Budget 2021 was the first ever digital Union Budget presented in the Parliament by Hon'ble Finance Minister Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman on Monday, February 1st, 2021. Former Finance Minister, Sh. Arun Jaitley, while presenting his first budget in 2014 said that "I would like to convey to this August House and also the investors community at large that we are committed to provide a stable and predictable taxation regime that would be investor friendly and spur growth". In order to reduce the litigations and creating an investor friendly environment the government has initiated several measures in the recent past. Use of technology has been encouraged to reduce the human intervention in the tax system to the extent possible. Another big step in this direction is the re-institution of section 147 and 148 i.e. re-assessment of income vide budget proposal 2021.

As per the proposed amendment instead of recording & forming reasons to belief, the Assessing Officer can issue notice under section 148 only when there is information which suggests that the income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment in the case of the assessee for the relevant assessment year. The proposed section 148 also elucidates that the following information suggests that the income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment:

i.

any information flagged in the case of the assessee for the relevant assessment year in accordance with the risk management strategy formulated by the Board from time to time;

ii.

any final objection raised by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India to the effect that the assessment in the case of the assessee for the relevant assessment year has not been made in accordance with the provisions of this Act

Further, the scope of assessment/reassessment under section 147 has been increased by inserting a deeming provision to include the assessment or reassessment or re-computation in cases where search is initiated under section 132 or requisition is made under 132A, after 31st March 2021. Precisely, the following suggests that the income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment in the case of the assessee:

i.

a search is initiated under section 132 or books of account, other documents or any assets are requisitioned under section 132A, on or after the 1st day of April, 2021, in the case of the assessee; or

ii.

a survey is conducted under section 133A in the case of the assessee on or after the 1st day of April, 2021; or

iii.

the Assessing Officer is satisfied, with the prior approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, that any money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article or thing, seized or requisitioned in case of any other person on or after the 1st day of April, 2021, belongs to the assessee; or

iv.

the Assessing Officer is satisfied, with the prior approval of Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, that any books of account or documents, seized or requisitioned in case of any other person on or after the 1st day of April, 2021, pertains or pertain to, or any information contained therein, relate to, the assessee.

One more section proposed to be inserted in the family of reassessment provisions is section 148A. This new section provides that before issuance of notice the Assessing Officer shall conduct enquiries, if required, and provide an opportunity of being heard to the assessee. After considering assessee's reply, the Assessing Office shall decide, by passing an order, whether it is a fit case for issue of notice under section 148 and serve a copy of such order along with such notice on the assessee. The Assessing Officer shall before conducting any such enquiries or providing opportunity to the assessee or passing such order obtain the approval of specified authority. However, this procedure of enquiry, providing opportunity and passing order, before issuing notice under section 148 of the Act, shall not be applicable in search or requisition cases.

Besides these proposed amendment in law the Union Budget 2021 has also proposed other remarkable change i.e. reducing the time limit of issuance of notice under section 148. The time limitation for issuance of notice of reassessment is proposed as below:

Generally, no notice of re-assesment shall be issued if 3 years have passed from the end of the relevant assessment year;

However, where the Assessing Officer has in his possession evidence which reveal that the income escaping assessment, represented in the form of asset, amounts to or is likely to amount to rupees 50 lakhs or more, notice can be issued beyond the period of 3 years but not beyond the period of 10 years from the end of the relevant assessment year.

Hon'ble Income-tax Tribunal Decision

Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the Hon'ble ITAT held that it is not disputed that search was conducted and 'Panchnama' was executed in the present case. However, the 'Panchnama' did not disclose that any incriminating material to conclude that the bank account with HSBC Bank, Geneva was maintained by assessee.

The Hon'ble ITAT relied on the case of Kabul Chawla (supra), wherein it was observed that "AO can make amendments to already concluded assessments under section 153A on the basis of incriminating material made known during the course of search which were not produced or disclosed earlier."

Further, reliance was placed on Pr. CIT v. Meeta Gutgutia [2017] 82 taxmann.com 287/248 Taxman 384/395 ITR 526 (Delhi), wherein it was held that 'there was no justification at all for the AO to proceed on surmises and estimates without there being any incriminating material qua the AY for which he sought to make additions of franchisee commission.'

Furthermore, the Hon'ble ITAT held that the Swiss authorities could have provided information post the period 2011-12 but not for relevant period under consideration in the present case. Letter issued by Swiss Authorities to the Government of India specifically states that information could be provided for years commencing from 2011-12.

Therefore, the required information for the period prior to 2011 could not have been provided by the authorities as per Article 26 of DTAA between India and Switzerland. Thus, the ITAT held that the assessment order passed was beyond limitation period as the reference sought by the Income-tax authorities was erroneous and bad in law.

Our Comments

Back in 2016, when Panama Papers blew the lid off how money is parked in offshore tax haven jurisdictions, a number of countries including India introduced financial reforms and took a number of corrective actions to set things right. However, after the Panama Paper leak, even stringent laws and penalties were not sufficient to deter offenders from indulging in financial jugglery.

Panama Paper rocked the world in 2016 but the recent investigations under Pandora Papers provides twice as much information and is even larger and more global in scope than the earlier ICIJ's landmark Panama Paper Investigation.

There's nothing illegal with holding an offshore account unless it is done with the malafide intent of tax evasion. The courts while dwelling on the issue of "unaccounted money stashed outside India" would look into various aspects that are integral to the process.

The ITAT in the aforecited recent decision of Bhushan Lal Sawhney's case (supra) had observed that if no incriminating material could be found during the course of search to establish Assesee's connection with respect to foreign bank account, the additions would not sustain.

The Hon'ble ITAT, Kolkata Benches in Bishwanath Garodia v. Dy. CIT [2016] 76 taxmann.com 81, held the similar view and it observed that 'But in a case or circumstances where the proceedings have reached finality, assessment under section 143(3) read with section 153(3) has to be made as was originally made and in case certain incriminating materials were found indicating undisclosed income, then addition shall only be restricted to these documents/incriminating material.'

It is noteworthy to mention here that in the case of Bhushan Lal Sawhney (supra), the statement of Assesee's son was recorded by the AO who had admitted that Assessee had maintained bank account with HSBC Geneva. However, the same was denied by the assessee in his statement recorded by the AO.

It was observed by Delhi High court in Smt. Dayawanti v. CIT [2016] 75 taxmann.com 308/[2017] 245 Taxman 293/390 ITR 496 that "while adjudging the probative value of these statements, it is to be seen whether the assessee was able to give any explanation for the statement, its connection with the material seized, all are relevant, to judge if it is to be considered in an assessment."

[Civil Appeal Nos. 2506 to 2521 of 2016, dated 4-3-2016]: The issue involved in this case was regarding interpretation of provisions of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948 (the Act). In terms of Section 11(3) of the Act, 1948, time-limit for completing the assessment provided is three years from the end of the year. In this case, the Assessing Officer, however, sent notices after the expiry of three years. The Assessing Officer relied on Section 11(10) of the Act whereby the Commissioner is empowered to extend the period of three years for passing the order of assessment for such further period as he may deem fit, after recording in writing the reasons for extending such period.

The question before the Supreme Court was "Whether the power to extend time is to be necessarily exercised before the normal expiry of the said period of three years run out?"

Three judge bench of the Supreme Court relying on income-tax decisions observed that once statutory period of limitation expires, the assessee is protected from being subject to assessment again, as the right to make assessment gets extinguished.

Thus, once an assessment is time barred there would be no question of extending the time for assessment.

Due date for filing of belated and revised ITR

If a return of income is not filed on or before the specified due date, it is regarded as a belated return. Further, the taxpayer has an option to revise a return to correct any error or omission in the original return. An assessee may file a revised or belated return for any previous year at any time before the expiry of the relevant assessment year or before completion of the assessment, whichever is earlier. Thus, as per the existing provisions, the last date to file the revised or belated return is 31st March of the relevant Assessment Year.

The Finance Bill, 2021 proposed amendments to Section 139(4) and 139(5), with effect from the assessment year 2021-22, to provide that the belated and revised return can be filed at any time within three months prior to the end of the relevant assessment year or before completion of the assessment, whichever is earlier.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) has redrafted the wordings of the proposed amendment although the intent remains the same. Now, it has been provided that the belated and revised return can be filed before three months prior to the end of the relevant assessment year or before the completion of the assessment, whichever is earlier.

Thus, pursuant to the amendment, a belated and revised return in respect of assessment year 2021-22 and subsequent assessment years can be filed up to 31st December of that assessment year.

15. New scheme of Re-assessment

15.1. Changes proposed by the Finance Bill, 2021

The Finance Bill, 2021 proposed a new re-assessment procedure for an income which has escaped the assessment and in search and seizure cases. The Explanatory Memorandum stated that the new scheme of assessment would result in less litigation and would provide ease of doing business to the taxpayers. The Finance Bill substituted existing Sections 147, 148, 149 and 151 and inserted a new section 148A making a complete change in the assessment proceedings relating to income escaping assessment and search related cases. Consequential amendments have also been proposed to Sections 151A, 153A and 153C.

The new Section 147 provides that the Assessing Officer can make the re-assessment of an income escaping assessment if the following conditions are satisfied:

(a)

Any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year; and

(b)

The Assessing Officer follows the provisions of sections 148 to 153.

If the above conditions are satisfied, the Assessing Officer can assess or reassess such income or recompute the loss or the depreciation allowance or any other allowance or deduction for such assessment year. It is imperative to note that in view of Explanation to Section 147 the Assessing Officer can assess or reassess all those incomes which have escaped assessment and which come to his notice subsequently in the course of such proceeding notwithstanding that the procedure prescribed in section 148A was not followed before issuing such notice for such income.

15.2. Power to assess or reassess for assessment or reassessment or recomputation

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) has also covered 'recomputation' within the scope of the said Explanation to Section 147. Thus, the Assessing Officer for the purpose of assessment or reassessment or recomputation can assess or reassess all those incomes which have escaped assessment and which come to his notice subsequently in the course of such proceeding notwithstanding that the procedure prescribed in Section 148A was not followed before issuing such notice for such income.

15.3. Information suggests income escaping in case of Survey

The new scheme of reassessment proposes that the Assessing Officer can initiate the proceedings if he has the information which suggests that some income has escaped the assessment. Explanations 1 and 2 of the proposed Section 148 define the situation in which an Assessing Officer shall be deemed to have the information which suggests that the income chargeable to tax has escaped the assessment.

Explanation 2 applies in the case of search, survey or requisition of books, documents or other assets. Explanation 1 applies in other cases.

The reassessment provisions introduced in the Income Tax Bill, 2025 appear to be a classic case of old wine in a new bottle. After the substantial overhaul brought by the Finance Act, 2021 - which was lauded for streamlining procedures, reducing litigation, and fostering taxpayer confidence—the proposed rollback to earlier mechanisms in the 2025 Bill is both perplexing and concerning.

The 2021 Reform: A Promised Shift Toward Efficiency and Fairness

The Finance Act, 2021 ushered in a new era of reassessment jurisprudence. One of its key features was a significant curtailment of the reassessment window-from six years to three years under Section 148—except in cases involving serious tax evasion where income chargeable to tax, represented in the form of assets, exceeded ₹50 lakh. Such cases were allowed to be reopened up to ten years. The post 2021 act aligns with the enhanced access to third-party data under Sections 285BA and 285BB, including Annual Information Statements (AIS) and reports from enforcement agencies electronically and thereby, reducing reassessment notice period.

The Hon'ble Finance Minister had highlighted, in her 2021 Budget Speech, that the reduction in the time limit was necessitated by the digitization and real-time availability of taxpayer information. The goal was clear: reduce uncertainty, curb harassment, and bring reassessment in tune with modern-day data access and compliance norms.

2025 Bill: Reinstating the Past

In a surprising move, the Income Tax Bill, 2025 appears to have reintroduced several elements reminiscent of the pre-2021 reassessment regime. Notably:

Time Limit Re-Expansion: The Bill resurrects the 4-year and 6-year time bars for issuing reassessment notices—now cloaked under Section 282 and linked to the issuance under the erstwhile Section 148, now proposed as Section 280. This reversion dilutes the sharpness and precision that the post 2021 act reform aimed to achieve. The 2025 bill shows a mirror image of the Pre-amended 2021 act.

Sanction approval u/s 151 Hierarchy Watered Down: One of the keystones of the 2021 amendments was the elevation of the sanctioning authority under Section 151—from (Joint Commissioner or Commissioner) to Commissioner & Principal Chief Commissioner or Principal Director General. This was a deliberate policy safeguard meant to prevent arbitrary and unjustified reopening of cases. The 2025 Bill, however, devolves the sanctioning authority back to the level of Joint Commissioner or Additional Commissioner, under Section 282, thereby weakening the supervisory checks envisioned in even in the Pre-2021 reform.

A Legislative Contradiction

The regression is more than just procedural. It strikes at the very legislative intent articulated in the Memorandum to the Finance Bill, 2021, which had explicitly emphasized reduced litigation, ease of doing business, and use of technology as the foundation for reassessment reform.

The 2025 proposal, by contrast, creates a legislative paradox—rolling back reform without revising the rationale. It ignores the earlier commitment made to taxpayers and professionals alike, and worse, creates a legal structure that is vulnerable to arbitrariness, lack of consistency, and increased litigation.

Conclusion: A Call for Legislative Introspection

As professionals, we look not only for legislative consistency but also for policy continuity that respects prior commitments. The proposed reassessment provisions in the Income Tax Bill, 2025, by reviving elements of the very system that was consciously discarded in 2021, represent a legislative volte-face. The finance ministry owes stakeholders an explanation: has the information ecosystem deteriorated, or was the 2021 reform premature?

In a tax administration increasingly reliant on data, precision, and transparency, going back to broad-brush tools of reassessment seems anachronistic. The hope is that reason will prevail before this retrogressive shift becomes law.

Another question that has raged controversy in the interpretation of Explanation 2 to section 271(1)(c) would continue to remain so in the interpretation of sub section (4) (5) of section 270A that as to what is the meaning of the phrase appearing in these sub sections where 'no penalty was levied'. In our considered opinion, if penalty was levied but was cancelled for any reason including on legal grounds, yet it would be a case where penalty was levied and such intangible additions cannot be revisited with penalty under sub section (4)(5) of section 270A.

The SLP filed by Revenue was subsequently dismissed by the Supreme Court in Asstt. CIT v. AMW Auto Component Ltd. [2026] 184 taxmann.com 487 (SC) on 13.03.2026.

Summary of Present Legal Position Key Takeaways for Practitioners

First, the clean slate principle remains the dominant rule. Where a resolution plan extinguishes all past tax liabilities, reassessment under Section 148 is unjustified—now fortified by the Supreme Court's SLP dismissal in AMW Auto Component.

Second, the VRDV Traders exception carves a narrow window: reassessment for investigating fraud through shell entities and reversal trades may survive, though any resulting recovery against the corporate debtor remains impermissible. The remedy, per the Telangana HC, may lie against erstwhile directors.

Third, timely claim-filing by the Revenue during the CIRP is critical. Failure to submit claims before the Resolution Professional results in permanent extinguishment, as seen in V Hotels and Vaibhav Goel.

Fourth, resolution applicants should ensure comprehensive tax extinguishment clauses in the resolution plan covering assessed and unassessed liabilities, TDS demands, penalties, prosecution risks, and related-party implications as demonstrated by the exhaustive clauses in the AMW Auto Component plan.

Conclusion

The jurisprudence on the interplay between IBC resolution plans and income tax reassessment has reached substantial clarity through Ghanshyam Mishra, Vaibhav Goel, and the AMW Auto Component SLP dismissal. The clean slate principle is now the settled norm. However, the VRDV Traders exception permitting reassessment where mala fide transactions through shell entities are suspected creates a narrow but significant carve-out that the Supreme Court has not yet directly addressed.

Taxpayers and professionals must carefully evaluate each case on its facts particularly the nature of transactions, the comprehensiveness of the resolution plan's extinguishment clauses, and whether tax claims were duly filed during the CIRP to determine whether the clean slate holds or whether the wound remains open.

It has also been clarified that these instructions shall not be applicable to the Central charges and International Taxation charges for which separate instructions are being issued.

Interestingly, the said CBDT Instruction also clarifies that action u/s 148 of the Act shall be taken by the Assessing Officer in respect of the above categories of cases after forming a reasonable belief that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment and 'reasons to believe' shall be recorded and required sanction as per section 151 of the Act shall be obtained before issuing notice u/s 148 of the Act.

It is pertinent to mention here that amendments have been proposed in the Finance Bill 2021, to substitute the existing sections 147 and 148 of the Income Tax Act, to reduce the time period for reopening the already concluded assessments from existing 6 years to 3 years. However, where the escapement of income is suggested to be of Rs 50 lakhs or more in a financial year in the form of undisclosed asset, then the maximum time period for reopening the already concluded assessments is 10 years.

No doubt that the proposed reduction in time period for reopening of assessments from 6 years to 3 years is a welcome and appreciable initiative. However, the issue of concern is the fact that the existing mandatory condition of formation of an independent reason to believe by the assessing authority that income of the assessee has escaped assessment so as to assume lawful jurisdiction u/s 147, is proposed to be substituted with the presence of any flagged information as per the risk management strategy of CBDT or the final audit objection of C&AG, suggesting that income of the assessee has escaped assessment.

However, a further clarification is desirable from CBDT that whether all the present "information" generated in Annual Information Return (AIR) u/s 285BA of the Income tax Act like share transactions, mutual fund transactions, cash deposits, credit card transactions, foreign travel, purchase of immovable property etc. would be considered as the "flagged information" suggesting escapement of income, so as to warrant assumption of jurisdiction under the newly proposed sections 148 and 147. If that being so, then naturally these amendments are of a lot of concern and apprehension because in such cases, suspicion arising out of such flagged information will substitute the existing mandatory condition of formation of reason to believe by the assessing authority.

Also, the existing proviso to section 147 requiring the mandatory condition of failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for the purpose of assessments for reopening the already concluded assessments beyond a period of 4 years and uptill 6 years, has found no place in the newly proposed section 147 and 148.

Further, the newly proposed section 148A, requiring the assessing authority to provide a suitable opportunity of being heard to the assessee and also mandating prior approval of the competent income tax authority before issuing notice u/s 148, and as such being perceived by the Legislature as an adequate safeguard, authorises the assessing authority to proceed with the issuing of notice u/s 148 merely if he thinks it fit to do so and it nowhere requires the formation of an independent reason to believe by such assessing authority, of the escapement of income.

To cure such time barred assessments, the law has been amended retrospectively. Two new provisos to sub-section (1) have been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-10-1991 to provide as follows:

Section 13(1) of the IT Act, 2000 provides that unless otherwise agreed, the dispatch of an electronic record occurs when it enters into computer resources outside the control of the originator. The amendment has been made to neutralise the decision in Motorola Inc. v. Dy. CIT [2005] 95 ITD 269 (Delhi)(SB), where it was held that the notice under section 142(1) calling for a return of income has to be issued after end of the period in section 139(1) and before end of the relevant assessment year and if no return of income is filed by an assessee till the end of the assessment year, a notice issued after the said date is invalid.

The amendment thus regularises the notices which were not served within the stipulated time period under the pre-amendment law.

Time limit for issue of notice under section 143(2) for the purposes of making assessment or reassessment under section 147

7.3 Section 148(1) provides that before making any assessment, reassessment or re-computation under section 147, the Assessing Officer shall serve a notice under section 148, on the assessee, requiring him to furnish his return of income and the provisions of the Act shall apply as if the return furnished in response to such notice were a return required to be furnished under section 139.

The Tribunal has held that assessment under section 147 is invalid if the notice under section 143(2) is not issued within 12 months from the end of the month in which return under section 147 was filed (after issuance of notice under section 148). [See Raj Kumar Chawla v. ITO [2005] 94 ITD 1 (Delhi)(SB)]

To cure such time barred assessments, the law has been amended retrospectively. Two new provisos to sub-section (1) have been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-10-1991 to provide as follows:

(a) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2) as it stood immediately before the amendment of said sub-section by the Finance Act, 2002, but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

(b) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2)(ii) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2)(ii), but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

Further, an Explanation has been inserted, with effect from 1-10-2005 in section 148(1) so as to clarify that the provisions of the aforesaid provisos shall not apply in relation to any return which has been furnished on or after 1-10-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148(1).

Thus, so far as returns furnished on or after 1-10-2005 are concerned, the pre-amendment law will apply and the notices will have to be served within a period of 12 months specified in section 143(2).

Reduction of the time limits provided for completion of assessment and reassessment

7.4 Section 153 provides for time limit for completion of assessments and reassessments of total income and FBT. Section 153B provides for the time limit for completion of assessment in cases where search has been initiated under section 132 or books of account, other documents or any assets have been requisitioned under section 132A.

The time limits specified for completion of assessments and re-assessments in the aforesaid sections 153 and 153B have been amended with effect from 1-6-2006 to provide that the time limits specified under the aforesaid sections, shall be reduced by three months. To illustrate, for assessment year 2005-06, the regular assessment under section 143 or a best judgment assessment under section 144 would have to be completed by 31-12-2007 as against 31-3-2008 earlier.

However, where a notice under section 148 has been served after 1-4-2005, no reassessment order under section 147 can be passed after the expiry of nine months from the end of the financial year in which it has been served.

Defective return under section 139

-2h Section 151A - This provision empowers the Central Government to make a scheme for the faceless assessment under Section 147. The Central Government has notified12 the e-Assessment of Income Escaping Assessment Scheme, 2022 for the purpose of this provision. The Scheme is applicable with effect from 29-03-2022.

The scheme provides that assessment, reassessment or recomputation under Section 147 and issuance of notice under Section 148 shall be done:

(a) Through automated allocation, in accordance with the risk management strategy formulated by the Board as referred to in Section 148 for issuance of notice; and

(b)

In a faceless manner, to the extent provided in Section 144B with reference to making an assessment or reassessment of total income or loss of assessee.

7.4-2i Section 152 - This provision provides that where an assessment has been reopened, the assessee (if he has not preferred an appeal or applied for revision) can claim that the re-assessment proceedings shall be dropped if he shows that:

(a)

He had been assessed on an amount which is not lower than what he would be rightly liable for, even if income alleged to have escaped assessment had been taken into account;

(b)

The assessment or computation had been properly made.

7.4-2j Section 153 - The time limits have been prescribed in this provision for summary assessment, scrutiny assessment, best judgment assessment and income escaping assessment. If an assessment is not completed within the prescribed time limit, it becomes time-barred.

Reassessment ● Notice Period

5.2 Under section 148 of the Act, an assessment can be reopened and for the purpose a notice can be issued to an assessee for filing a return of his income within a specified period, not being less than thirty days. At present, in the printed form of notice under section 148, the assessee is required to furnish a return of his income 'within thirty days'. As per Memorandum explaining provision of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, notices issued under section 148 have been held to be invalid by the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal on the ground that whereas the statute allows the taxpayer a time, 'not being less than thirty days', the notice gives the direction to file a return 'within a period of thirty days'. The Bombay High Court in the case of CIT v. Ekbal & Co. [1945] 13 ITR154 (Bom.) decided a similar issue by laying down that the expressions within thirty days' and 'not less than thirty days' are two quite different things. The above legal position, as such, invalidates all the proceedings initiated through such printed notice(s), which could have been avoided by changing the form of notice.

However, to get over the situation, section 148 of the Act has been amended, with retrospective effect from 1-4-1989 whereby the words 'not being less than 30 days' have been omitted.

The effect of the deletion of the words is that now an Assessing Officer can require an assessee to file a return pursuant to a notice under section 148 of the Act within such period as may be specified in the notice. Thus, now, a notice could be for a shorter period as the minimum time constraint has been removed.

Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996 states that this amendment will also apply to any notice which has already been issued, on or after 1-4-1989.

However, one does not find any specific words or mention of it in the amendment so as to show that such notices have been validated.

The concerned assessees may be adversely affected and may have to agitate the proceedings afresh. In such a situation a question could arise as to whether a mere insertion of the amendment with retrospective effect is sufficient to validate the invalid notice which has been issued needs to be validated. It is felt that the latter action would be necessary. Otherwise, one can validate or invalidate an action at any point of time with no remedy for taxpayers.

Further, it appears that those assessees who had questioned such validity may be able to agitate this issue. However, in cases where pursuant to notices issued after 1-4-1989 reassessment is concluded, it may not be now possible to take a plea that the notices were invalid. In other words, in such cases, it appears that the retrospective amendment would support the case of revenue.

Limitation period for completion of assessments and reassessments

5.3 Section 153 of the Act lays down the time limit for making an order of assessment (two years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable). Also, Explanation 1 below section 153 of the Act sets out certain circumstances in which certain periods as specified are excluded from the period of limitation.

In a case where an audit under section 142(2A) is ordered, the assessee is required to furnish a report of such audit within the prescribed time. In such a case, the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited under section 142(2 A) and ending with the date on which the assessee furnishes a report of such audit is excluded while reckoning the period of limitation for completion of the assessment, as per Explanation 1(iii) below section 153 of the Act.

As per the Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, in a case where the report is not prepared and, therefore, not furnished, the normal time limit of two years is operative and the Assessing Officer does not get any additional time for the purpose of making an assessment because the time taken for furnishing the audit report is not excluded. Exclusion of the period in terms of Explanation 1(iii) could operate only if the report of such audit is furnished.

To obviate the difficulty, the said Explanation has been amended, with effect from 1-4-1997, to provide that the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited and ending on the date on which the report of such audit was required to be furnished, shall be excluded from the period of limitation.

This would enable extension of the limitation period, at least, by the time permitted, although, the audit report is not furnished.

Special procedure for assessment of search cases

5.4 The Finance Act, 1995, introduced a new scheme for assessment of Undisclosed Income ('UnI') determined as a result of search.*

The Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, provides as follows:

Service vs. issue of notice - Section 148 of enjoins that the AO must serve on the assessee a notice requiring him to furnish a return of his income, in respect of which he/she is assessable under the 1961 Act during the PY corresponding to the relevant AY. In stark contrast, s. 149 speaks only of the issuance of a notice under the preceding section within a prescribed period. S. 149 does not mandate that such a notice must also be served on the assessee within the prescribed period [Mayawati v. CIT [2010] 321 ITR 349 (Delhi)].

Limitation provided u/s 149 for issuance of notice commences from date when notice is issued and not when notice served [Synfonia Tradelinks (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2021] 127 taxmann.com 153/281 Taxman 557 (Del.); Sadhna Tolasariya v. ITO [2021] 127 taxmann.com 127/281 Taxman 354 (Mad.)].

Time-limit applies for issue of notice - The word 'issued' in section 149 should be given its natural meaning and not the strained wider meaning of 'served'. Consequently, where the notice was issued within time but was served on the assessee after the expiry of the time-limit, it could not be held to be invalid [Jai Hanuman Trading Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 110 ITR 36 (P&H - FB)].

It is date of issue of notice u/s 148, and not actual receipt of notice by assessee which is relevant to return a finding as to whether reassessment proceedings have been initiated within period of limitation [CIT v. K. G. Singhania [2012] 24 taxmann.com 208/209 Taxman 45 (P&H)].

Mere generation of notice do not constitute issue of notice – Function of generation of notice on ITBA portal and digital signing of notice is executed by Assessing Officer while function of drafting of e-mail to which notice is attached and triggering e-mail to assessee is performed by ITBA e-mail software system. Thus, mere generation of notice u/s 148 on ITBA software cannot in fact or in law constitute issue of notice, it is only upon due despatch that notice can be said to have been issued. 'Despatch' as per section 13 of Information Technology Act of 2000 is sine qua non for issuance of notice through electronic mail for purpose of s. 149 [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/[2023] 290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Date of issuance of notice in case of Postal department - Date of issue of notice would be the date on which the same was handed over for service to the proper officer or Postal Department. Since the Income-tax Department is covered by 'book now pay later' scheme, the further requirement of properly stamping envelope with adequate postal stamp, would not be germane. Therefore, where reassessment notice was handed over to Postal Department before stipulated time, it would not be barred by time factor [Rajesh Sunderdas Vaswani v. DCIT [2017] 88 taxmann.com 602 (Guj.)].

Where AO issued and dispatched a reopening notice against assessee on last date of expiry of period of limitation, even though notice was franked by Postal department later, said notice was not barred by limitation [Rajmannar Ramaswamy v. ITO [2021] 130 taxmann.com 431 (Mad.)].

Clarificatory amendment regarding the time limit for issue of notice under section 142

7.2 Section 142(1), inter alia, provides that for the purposes of making assessment in a case where a person has not made a return of his income within the time specified under section 139(1), the Assessing Officer may serve a notice under the said sub-section on such person requiring him to furnish the return of his income in the prescribed form and manner.

Clause (i) of section 142(1) has been amended with effect from 1-4-2006 to provide that in a case where a person has not made a return of his income before the end of the relevant assessment year, the Assessing Officer may serve a notice after the end of the relevant assessment year under the said sub-section requiring such person to furnish his return of income.

Further a proviso to the said clause (i) has been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-4-1990, so as to provide that where any notice has been served on or after 1-4-1990 under sub-section (1) after the end of the relevant assessment year to any person who has not made a return of his income before the end of the relevant assessment year, such notice shall be deemed to be a notice served in accordance with the provisions of the said sub-section (1).

The amendment has been made to neutralise the decision in Motorola Inc. v. Dy. CIT [2005] 95 ITD 269 (Delhi)(SB), where it was held that the notice under section 142(1) calling for a return of income has to be issued after end of the period in section 139(1) and before end of the relevant assessment year and if no return of income is filed by an assessee till the end of the assessment year, a notice issued after the said date is invalid.

The amendment thus regularises the notices which were not served within the stipulated time period under the pre-amendment law.

7.3 Section 148(1) provides that before making any assessment, reassessment or re-computation under section 147, the Assessing Officer shall serve a notice under section 148, on the assessee, requiring him to furnish his return of income and the provisions of the Act shall apply as if the return furnished in response to such notice were a return required to be furnished under section 139.

(a) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2) as it stood immediately before the amendment of said sub-section by the Finance Act, 2002, but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

(b) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2)(ii) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2)(ii), but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

ISSUE/SERVICE OF NOTICE

Service of notice is mandatory - The notice prescribed by section 148 cannot be regarded as a mere procedural requirement. It is only if the said notice is served on the assessee that the ITO would be justified in taking proceedings against the assessee. If no notice is issued or if the notice issued is shown to be invalid, then the proceedings taken by the ITO would be illegal and void [Y. Narayana Chetty v. ITO [1959] 35 ITR 388 (SC); CIT v. Thayaballi Mulla Jeevaji Kapasi [1967] 66 ITR 147 (SC); CIT v. Kurban Hussain Ibrahimji Mithiborwala [1971] 82 ITR 821 (SC)].

Section 148 provides for service of notice as a condition precedent to making the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested in the AO to proceed to reassess. The mandate of section 148 is that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued [R. K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 33 Taxman 229 (SC)].

Signature of authority – Where a reopening notice u/s. 148 was issued upon assessee without signature of Assessing Officer affixed on it either digitally or manually, said notice was invalid and same would not vest Assessing Officer with any further jurisdiction to proceed to reassess income of assessee [Prakash Krishnavtar Bhardwaj v. ITO [2023] 150 taxmann.com 60/293 Taxman 132/451 ITR 27 (Bom.)].

Date of issue/service of notice – While issuing notice u/s 148, date of issue of notice is not important, it is date of signing notice which is important [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices u/s 148 are sent through registered e-mail ID of respective Assessing Officers, though not digitally signed, it will be held to be valid service of notice. However, date and time of dispatch as recorded in ITBA portal will be taken as date of issuance of notice in this regard [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices u/s 148 were only uploaded in e-filing portal of assessees without any real time alert, date and time when assessees viewed notices in e-filing portal, as recorded in ITBA portal will be construed as date of service of notice [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices u/s 148 were manually despatched, date and time when notices were delivered to post office for dispatch was to be construed as date of issuance of notice [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices were sent to unrelated e-mail addresses, date on which notice was first viewed by assessee on e-filing portal was to be construed as date of issuance of notice [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Issue before getting approval u/s 151 – There is no need for paper containing approval being received physically before issuing notice and Assessing Officer can proceed to issue a notice u/s 148 if approving authority has granted his approval and approval has been communicated to Assessing Officer in any manner including by uploading approval on portal of department. Thus, reopening notice could not be vitiated on ground that paper containing approval u/s 151 was received by Assessing Officer after issuing notice [Sahara Credit Cooperative Society Ltd. v. DCIT/Asstt. CIT [2022] 141 taxmann.com 384 (All.)].

Where assessment proceedings are pending - Notice cannot be issued during pendency of assessment proceedings [Jhunjhunwala Vanaspati Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 137 Taxman 336 (All.)].

In the Ashish Agarwal ruling, the Supreme Court did not address whether or not the reassessment notices were issued within the time limits prescribed under the provisions of the 1961 Act, read with the relaxations provided under TOLA. Thus, in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC), setting aside various judgments1, the Supreme Court held that:

(a)

Section 3(1) of TOLA applies to the issuance of reassessment notices under section 148 of the 1961 Act. While TOLA did not amend the four and six-year time limits under the Act, it provided a relaxation for issuing reassessment notices during the COVID-19 period. TOLA does not apply if the time-limit under section 149 expires before 20-3-2020. When issuing a reassessment notice, the revenue must check both section 149 time limit and TOLA's relaxation period. For example, the six-year limit for AY 2013-14 expired on 31-3-2020, but TOLA extended it to 30-06-2021.Accordingly, after 1-4-2021, the 1961 Act has to be read along with the substituted provisions. TOLA will continue to apply to the Income-tax Act after 1-4-2021, if any action or proceeding specified under the substituted provisions of the 1961 Act falls for completion between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021.

(b)

TOLA will extend the time-limit for the grant of sanction by the authority specified under section 151. The test to determine whether TOLA will apply to section 151 of the new regime is this: if the time-limit of three years from the end of an assessment year falls between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021, then the specified authority under section 151(i) has extended time till 30-6-2021 to grant approval. In the case of section 151 of the old regime, the test is: if the time-limit of four years from the end of an assessment year falls between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021, then the specified authority under section 151(2) has extended time till 31-3-2021 to grant approval. Thus, the Assessing Officers were required to issue the reassessment notice under section 148 of the new regime within the time-limit surviving under the 1961 Act read with TOLA. All notices issued beyond the surviving period are time-barred and liable to be set aside.

Implementation of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183 1. Hon'ble Supreme Court, vide its judgment dated 04.05.2022 [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183, in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal has adjudicated on the validity of the issue of reassessment notices issued by the Assessing Officers during the period beginning on 1st April, 2021 and ending with 30th June 2021, within the time extended by the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 [hereinafter referred to as "TOLA"] and various notifications issued thereunder (these reassessment notices hereinafter referred to as "extended reassessment notices").

2. These extended reassessment notices were issued by the Assessing Officers under the provision of section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") following the procedure prescribed under various sections pertaining to reassessment namely sections 147 to 151, as they existed prior to their amendment by the Finance Act, 2021 (hereinafter referred to as "old law"). With effect from 1st April 2021, the old law has been substituted with new sections 147-151 (hereinafter referred to as the "new law").

3. Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that these extended reassessment notices issued under the old law shall be deemed to be the show cause notices issued under clause (b) of section 148A of the new law and has directed Assessing Officers to follow the procedure with respect to such notices. It has also held that all the defences available to assessees under section 149 of the new law and whatever rights are available to the Assessing Officer under the new law shall continue to be available. Hon'ble Supreme Court has passed this order in exercise of its power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India.

4. The implementation of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court is required to be done in a uniform manner. Accordingly, in exercise of its power under section 119 of the Act, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (hereinafter referred to as "the Board") directs that the following may be taken into consideration while implementing this judgment.

5. Scope of the judgment:

5.1 Taking into account the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in various paragraphs. it is clarified that the judgment applies to all cases where extended reassessment notices have been issued. This is irrespective of the fact whether such notices have been challenged or not.

6. Operation of the new section 149 of the Act to identify cases where fresh notice under section 148 of the Act can be issued:

6.1 With respect of operation of new section 149 of the Act, the following may be seen:

Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that the new law shall operate and all the defences available to assessees under section 149 of the new law and whatever rights are available to the Assessing Officer under the new law shall continue to be available.

Sub-section (1) of new section 149 of the Act as amended by the Finance Act, 2021 (before its amendment by the Finance Act, 2022) reads as under:-

"149. (1) No notice under section 148 shall be issued for the relevant assessment year.—

(a)

if three years have elapsed from the end of the relevant assessment year, unless the case falls under clause (b);

(b)

if three years, but not more than ten years, have elapsed from the end of the relevant assessment year unless the Assessing Officer has in his possession books of account or other documents or evidence which reveal that the income chargeable to tax, represented in the form of asset, which has escaped assessment amounts to or is likely to amount to fifty lakh rupees or more for that year:

Provided that no notice under section 148 shall be issued at any time in a case for the relevant, assessment year beginning on or before 1st day of April, 2021, if such notice could not have been issued at that time on account of being beyond the time limit specified under the provisions of clause (b) of sub-section (1) of this section, as they stood immediately before the commencement of the Finance Act, 2021."

Hon'ble Supreme Court has upheld the views of High Courts that the benefit of new law shall be made available even in respect of proceedings relating to past assessment years. Decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court read with the time extension provided by TOLA will allow extended reassessment notices to travel back in time to their original date when such notices were to be issued and then new section 149 of the Act is to be applied at that point.

6.2 Based on above, the extended reassessment notices are to be dealt with as under:

The substituted provision provides as follows:

(b)

Clause (a) of Section 150(2) imposes a restriction on the power given in section 150(1) in the situation when the assessment year was already time-barred at the time the order (subject matter of appeal, reference or revision) was passed. This provision is similar to pre-amended section 150(2).

(c)

Clause (b) of section 150(2), a new provision, imposes a restriction on the power given in section 150(1) in the situation when the assessment year was already time-barred at the time the assessment proceedings (subject matter before the court) were initiated [see Para 16.3C-4a].

Sub-section (3) of Section 150, a new provision, provides the time limit within which the notice under section 148 pursuant to the findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority [see Para 16.3C-4b].

16.3C-4a No reassessment if the assessment year was time-barred at the time the assessment proceedings were initiated - Section 150(2)(a) largely mirrors the existing provision of section 150(2). It refers to the time when the original order (which was subsequently challenged in appeal, reference, or revision) was made. The implication remains consistent with the current law: if, at the time the initial assessment order was passed, the assessment year was already time-barred under other provisions of the Act, then section 150(1) cannot be used to reopen it, even if a higher authority later gives a finding or direction.

Section 150(2)(b) introduces a new reference point for checking the time limitation for assessment proceedings that are the subject of court proceedings. This clause significantly broadens the circumstances under which section 150(1) cannot be invoked. It shifts the focus from the date of the final order to the date of initiation of proceedings relating to assessment or reassessment. If the proceedings were initiated at a time when the limitation period to issue notice for an assessment year had expired under the general provisions (like Section 149 or section 153), then even if a subsequent court order gives a finding or direction, section 150(1) would be rendered inapplicable. This would prevent the reopening of old cases based on findings from court proceedings.

It provides that the notice under section 148 shall be issued within 3 months from the end of the quarter in which the certified copy of the order of the authority or the Court, as the case may be, is received by the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. This provision puts the limitation period within which such notice should be issued, and if not issued within such period, the assessment becomes time-barred, and section 150(1) cannot come to its rescue.

Limitation period for completion of assessments and reassessments

5.3 Section 153 of the Act lays down the time limit for making an order of assessment (two years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable). Also, Explanation 1 below section 153 of the Act sets out certain circumstances in which certain periods as specified are excluded from the period of limitation.

In a case where an audit under section 142(2A) is ordered, the assessee is required to furnish a report of such audit within the prescribed time. In such a case, the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited under section 142(2 A) and ending with the date on which the assessee furnishes a report of such audit is excluded while reckoning the period of limitation for completion of the assessment, as per Explanation 1(iii) below section 153 of the Act.

As per the Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, in a case where the report is not prepared and, therefore, not furnished, the normal time limit of two years is operative and the Assessing Officer does not get any additional time for the purpose of making an assessment because the time taken for furnishing the audit report is not excluded. Exclusion of the period in terms of Explanation 1(iii) could operate only if the report of such audit is furnished.

To obviate the difficulty, the said Explanation has been amended, with effect from 1-4-1997, to provide that the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited and ending on the date on which the report of such audit was required to be furnished, shall be excluded from the period of limitation.

This would enable extension of the limitation period, at least, by the time permitted, although, the audit report is not furnished.

7.2-3f ABATEMENT OF PENDING ASSESSMENT OR REASSESSMENT - There could be several situations and implications. Some of them are discussed below :

Consider a case, where the search action takes place, say, on 1-7-2003. In the search, only certain documents are found showing receipts on sale of certain goods, relating to the financial year 2002 and 2003. Apart from that, nothing else is found. In this case, the Assessing Officer will have to issue the notice under section 153A to the assessee for filing the return for the specified period, i.e., assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04. The assessee has already filed returns under section 139 for all the above assessment years. Further, in respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments have been reopened pursuant to notice under section 148. In respect of assessment year 2001-02, the assessee has not received any notice for assessment under section 143(2). Further, for the assessment year 2000-01 no assessment was done under section 143(3). In respect of assessment year 1999-2000, the assessment was made under section 143(3). The assessment is pending in appeal. In respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, against the assessments made under section 143(3), an appeal was filed. In the appeal, the assessment for assessment year 1997-98 was set aside and the appeal for assessment year 1998-99 was decided with a direction to examine the claim of the assessee, for certain facts, and accordingly allow the claim.

The position, in respect of the above assessment years, as per the new procedure, could be as follows :

The Assessing Officer has to make assessments or reassessments for each of the assessment years under the new procedure. Thus, prima facie, the Assessing Officer will make assessments or reassessments for all the years covered in the specified period, that is, assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04.

In respect of the assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments whereof are reopened but reassessments are not completed, the reassessments can now be completed, pursuant to section 153A. The effect would be extension in the limitation period for making reassessment, since section 153A overrides the provisions of section 153.

The assessments for assessment years 2000-01 and 2001-02, though barred by limitation under section 153, can be made under section 153A. In the assessment, normal disallowance, etc., can be made. This may attract interest, if any, under section 234B, etc.

The assessment for assessment year 1999-2000 is completed. All the same, a fresh assessment can be made under section 153A. The new procedure would not affect the pending appeal.

The set aside assessment for the assessment year 1997-98 shall abate and the Assessing Officer will make the assessment under section 153A. However, while making reassessment, it may not be possible for him to ignore the directions, if any, of the Appellate Authority, in respect of the issue covered by the appellate order.

7.2-3f ABATEMENT OF PENDING ASSESSMENT OR REASSESSMENT - There could be several situations and implications. Some of them are discussed below :

Consider a case, where the search action takes place, say, on 1-7-2003. In the search, only certain documents are found showing receipts on sale of certain goods, relating to the financial year 2002 and 2003. Apart from that, nothing else is found. In this case, the Assessing Officer will have to issue the notice under section 153A to the assessee for filing the return for the specified period, i.e., assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04. The assessee has already filed returns under section 139 for all the above assessment years. The assessment is pending in appeal. In respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, against the assessments made under section 143(3), an appeal was filed. 11.4 Exclusion of 15 days from the limitation period for the issue of notice under Section 148 [Section 149]

11.4-1 Background

The existing provision of Section 149 provides the limitation period for the issue of notice under Section 148 for the reassessment under Section 147. Section 148A specifies the procedure to be followed before issuing a notice under Section 148. It provides that the Assessing Officer shall conduct enquiries, if required, and provide an opportunity of being heard to the assessee. After considering his reply, the Assessing Officer shall decide, after passing an order, whether it is a fit case for the issue of notice under Section 148 and serve a copy of such order along with such notice on the assessee.

This procedure does not apply where a search is carried out under Section 132 or requisition is made under Section 132A and in cases initiated on the basis of information emanating from search and requisition proceedings. In such cases, a notice under Section 148 is issued without conducting proceedings under Section 148A. However, in cases resulting from material gathered during survey operations under Section 133A, the AO is required to carry out proceedings under Section 148A before issuing notice under Section 148.

11.4-2 Difficulty in existing provision

It is observed that when a search or requisition is conducted after 15th March of a financial year, there is very little time left to collate the material and issue notice under Section 148. Also, where a statement of a person recorded during a search indicating tax evasion is received late by the jurisdictional AO, due to a shortage of time, it becomes difficult to carry out necessary verification before the issue of notice under Section 148. Therefore, to facilitate the AO carrying out necessary verification before the issue of notice under Section 148, the Finance Act, 2023 has amended Section 149 to provide 15 days extra time to AO to issue notice under section 148 in such cases.

11.4-3 Amendment by the Finance Act, 2023

The Finance Act, 2023 has inserted the Third and Fourth proviso (after the existing Second Proviso and the existing Third and Fourth Proviso are renumbered as Fifth and Sixth Proviso) in Section 149 with effect from the assessment year 2023-24.

(c)

Section 150(1), with a non obstante clause, overrides the general time limits prescribed in section 149 for issuing notices under section 148. This provision enables issuing a notice under section 148 for re-assessment at any time for the purpose of giving effect to any finding or direction contained in an order passed by any authority in any proceeding by way of appeal, reference or revision or by a Court. While section 150(1) grants a broad power, section 150(2) imposes a restriction on that power. It states that the provisions of sub-section (1) (i.e., the power to issue notice "at any time") shall not apply in any case where the assessment, reassessment, or recomputation relates to an assessment year in respect of which such reassessment could not have been made at the time the order (which was the subject-matter of the appeal, reference, or revision) was made, by reason of any other provision limiting the time within which any action for reassessment may be taken. This provision ensures that this power cannot be used to revive an assessment year that was already time-barred when the original order (which was the subject of appeal or revision) was made.

The existing provision covered the scenario where an order (the subject of appeal or revision) was made, but did not cover the situation in which proceedings for assessment, reassessment, or recomputation had been initiated by the Assessing Officer, but no order had been passed. Further, section 150 did not specify the time limit within which the notice under section 148 pursuant to the findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority must be issued.

16.12 Direction by approving panel to invoke GAAR and finding or direction of the court is included in 'information' to initiate the reassessment [Section 280 of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 148 of the ITA 1961)]

16.12-1 Position under the ITA 1961

To make an assessment, reassessment, or re-computation in section 147 of the ITA 1961, a notice was required to be issued to the assessee under section 148, requiring him to furnish a return of his income or the income of any other person in respect of which he is assessable under this Act. A notice under section 148 could be issued only when the Assessing Officer has information suggesting that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for the relevant assessment year. In the following situations, information shall be deemed to be suggesting that income has escaped assessment:

(a)

any information in the case of the assessee for the relevant assessment year in accordance with the risk management strategy formulated by the Board from time to time;

(b)

any audit objection to the effect that the assessment in the case of the assessee for the relevant assessment year has not been made in accordance with the provisions of this Act;

(c)

any information received under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A of the Act;

(d)

any information made available to the Assessing Officer under the scheme notified under section 135A;

(e)

any information which requires action in consequence of the order of a Tribunal or a Court;

(f)

any information emanating from a survey conducted under section 133A (other than conducted under section 133A(2A) for verifying TDS and TCS) on or after 1-9-2024.

While issuing such a notice, the Assessing Officer is not required to obtain prior approval of the specified authority. However, the procedure prescribed under section 148A must be followed. However, if the Assessing Officer receives information in a faceless manner under the e-Verification Scheme, 2021 (notified under section 135A), the notice can be issued without following the procedure under section 148A. In such cases, prior approval of the specified authority is mandatory before issuing the notice under section 148.

HEADNOTE: Section 148, read with section 149, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reassessment - Issue of notice - Assessment year 1966-67 - Whether, where reassessment notice under section 148 was issued within period of limitation prescribed under section 149 but was served on assessee after expiry of period of limitation, initiation of reassessment proceedings by ITO was barred by limitation and, therefore, invalid - Held, no

FACT: For the assessment year 1966-67, assessment was reopened under section 148 by the ITO in the case of assessee, an individual. In the reassessment, the ITO included certain amount as unexplained investment in the income assessed earlier in the original assessment. The notice under section 148 was issued on 29-3-1975 but it was served on the assessee on 7-4-1975. On appeal before the AAC, the assessee contended that the notice having been served after the expiry of period of limitation, the reassessment proceedings were barred by limitation. The AAC rejected the assessee's contention. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the notice under section 148 was not only to be issued but served within the period of limitation as laid down in section 149, and since the notice was served on the assessee after the expiry of 8 years, the order of reassessment was set aside.

On reference:

HELD: In R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 166 ITR 163, the Supreme Court categorically held that a clear distinction has been made out under the Income-tax Act, 1961 between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice'. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It prohibits issue of notice under section 148 after the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested with the ITO to proceed to reassess. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued Section 148(1) deals with making of the reassessment and mandates that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. Under the Act, service is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the ITO to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to the making of the order of assessment.

In the Instant case, notice under section 148 was issued by the ITO within the period of limitation prescribed under section 149. There was also no controversy about the fact that the order of reassessment was made only after service of notice on the assessee. The ratio of the decision in R.K. Upadhyaya's case (supra ) of the Supreme Court squarely applied to the present case. The ITO having issued the notice under section 148 within limitation, the order of reassessment was valid. Therefore, the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the initiation of reassessment proceedings by the ITO was barred by limitation and in setting aside the orders of the AAC and the ITO.

As held by the Apex Court in Krishan Lal's case (supra ) it was not an irregularity committed by the Assessing Officer but an illegality which would render assessments bad in law. [Para 30] From these judicial pronouncements it is clear that where the reassessment proceeding initiated under section 147 were not concluded to a logical end, the Assessing Officer cannot issue fresh reassessment notice under section 148. HEADNOTE: Section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income escaping assessment - Issue of notice for - Assessment years 1994-95 to 1996-97 - Whether if a proper notice is issued but not served on assessee or if it is found that notice is not at all issued, then it cannot be stated that Assessing Officer assumed jurisdiction for making reassessment validly- Held, yes - When assessee received notice under section 142(1) requiring it to furnish information relating to reassessment to be done by Assessing Officer, it came to know that notice under section 148 dated 30-3-2001 was issued to it and same was allegedly served on it on 28-4-2001 - Assessee’s case was that no valid notice was served on it as signature of recipient from some ‘V’ although resembled with name of managing director of company ‘VK’ but that was not actual signature of ‘VK’; limitation period of issuing notice under section 148 for assessment year in question was to expire on 31-3-2001 and since department had not issued any notice by 31-3-2001 and by realizing its mistake, Assessing Officer made out a notice dated 30-3-2001 and took stand that it had been served by a notice server on 28-4-2001 - Assessing Officer, however, completed reassessment - Whether since there was no evidence for issuance of notice and signature of ‘V’ was not verifiable, it could be said that Assessing Officer made out notice on 30-3-2001 only to save his wrong action - Held, yes - Whether since proper service of notice was not done by Assessing Officer, assessment proceedings conducted consequent thereon were invalid - Held, yes

FACT: When the assessee received notice under section 142(1) requiring it to furnish information relating to the reassessment to be done by the Assessing Officer, it came to know that notice under section 148 dated 30-3-2001 was issued to it and same was allegedly served on it on 28-4-2001.The assessee brought to the notice of the Assessing Officer that no notice under section 148 had been served upon him and required the Assessing Officer to supply the notice and in response to this letter, notice issued under section 148 dated 30-3-2001, duly signed by some ‘V’ was provided to the assessee and thereafter the assessee participated in the assessment proceedings. During the assessment proceedings, the assessee’s case was that no valid notice was served on it as signature of the recipient from some ‘V’ although resembled with the name of the managing director ‘VK’ of the company but that was not actually signature of ‘VK’. The Assessing Officer, however, completed the reassessment. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the reassessment order.

In second appeal, the assessee contended that limitation period of issuing notice under section 148 for the assessment year in question was to expire on 31-3-2001 and since the department had not issued any notice by 31-3-2001 and by realizing its mistake, the Assessing Officer made out a notice dated 30-3-2001 and took the stand that it had been served by a notice server on 28-4-2001; it was against preponderance of probability that a notice server could have taken 28 days to serve a notice, which was impractical, and revealed that the Assessing Officer only to cover his inaction for issuing of notice within time, made out a notice dated 30-3-2001 after the expiry date, i.e., 30-3-2001 and had just delivered the notice to someone and recorded signatures, namely ‘V’, which was not resembling with the signatures of ‘VK’, managing director of the company. The assessee further contended that requirement of section 148 was that notice should be issued; in its case, no evidence for issuance of notice, as such, had been produced by the department; in view of fact that without adducing any evidence of the issuance of notice, as such it was stated to have been served on 28th April after 28 days, it could well be assumed that said service of notice was an afterthought; and since there was no service of notice under section 148, the assessment made in pursuance of such notice was illegal and without jurisdiction.

On second appeal :

HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had observed in the order for the assessment year 1998-99 'the Assessing Officer is, however, free to take action in assessment year 1997-98'. The above observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) could not be held as a direction. Following the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajinder Nath v. CIT [1979] 120 ITR 14 / 2 Taxman 204, it could safely be held that the Commissioner (Appeals) had not given any direction to the Assessing Officer to initiate reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98. Therefore, the notice issued under section 148 on 16-11-2004 was beyond the time-limit prescribed in the Act. In this case the assessment year ended on 31-3-1998 and, therefore, no notice under section 148 could have been issued after 31-3-2004. The appellate order for the assessment year 1998-99 had been passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) on 10-6-2004 and as per law, no reassessment for the assessment year 1997-98 could have been made after 31-3-2004. For argument's sake if it was admitted that the Commissioner (Appeals) had given direction to the Assessing Officer to initiate reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98 in his order dated 10-6-2004, even then under the law, the direction given by the Commissioner (Appeals) on 10-6-2004 was against the provisions of section 150(2).

In the instant case, initiation of the reassessment proceedings was barred by other provision of the Act on 10-6-2004 when the appellate order for the assessment year 1998-99 was passed. The assessment year 1997-98 had ended on 31-3-1998. Reopening of the assessment for the assessment year 1997-98 was permissible under the Act upto 31-3-2004. However, the appellate order, on the basis of which reassessment was initiated, had been passed on 10-6-2004. On the said date initiation of reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98 was prohibited by law, and, hence, reassessment proceeding initiated after 31-3-2004 was clearly barred by limitation.

Therefore, the reassessment order was time barred by limitation and, hence, was liable to be quashed.

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.
