Therefore, the Assessing Officer had issued notices under section 148 on 25-9-2006 and 24-11-2006 for assessment year 2001-02 and on 24-11-2006 for assessment years 2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-05 during pendency of assessment proceedings under section 147. [Para 29] It had to be examined as to whether issue of notice under section 148 during the period when assessment/reassessment is pending is a 'nullity' or an 'irregularity'. The Supreme Court in the case of Krishan Lal v. State of J&K [1994] 4 SCC 422 had an occasion to examine the difference between the expressions 'irregularity' and 'nullity'. The Supreme Court referred to the meaning as given in words and phrases (Permanent Edition) where as to 'irregularity' it has been stated that it is 'want of adherence to some prescribed rule or mode of proceeding;' whereas 'nullity' is 'a void act or an act having no legal force or validity.' The safest rule of distinction between 'irregularity' and 'nullity' is to see whether 'a party can waive the objection; if he can waive, it amounts to irregularity and if he cannot, it is nullity.' Further a waiver is an intentional relinquishment of a known right, but obviously an objection to jurisdiction cannot be waived, for consent cannot give a Court jurisdiction where there is none. The power to assess get vested in the Assessing Officer the moment he issues notice under section 148. The contention of the revenue that no such plea was taken by the assessee would not mean that the Assessing Officer got jurisdiction to issue of notice under section 148 during the currency of assessments. As held by the Apex Court in Krishan Lal's case (supra ) it was not an irregularity committed by the Assessing Officer but an illegality which would render assessments bad in law. [Para 30]

From these judicial pronouncements it is clear that where the reassessment proceeding initiated under section 147 were not concluded to a logical end, the Assessing Officer cannot issue fresh reassessment notice under section 148. Therefore, the assessment for the assessment years 2001-02 to 2004-05 framed with reference to the notice issued under section 148 on 24-11-2006 during the pendency of assessment were bad in law. The notices issued under section 148 on 23-9-2005 were deemed to have been served on the assessee and since assessments were to be completed by 31-12-2006 the assessments completed on 24-12-2007 with reference to notices issued on 24-11-2006 were barred by limitation. Hence, the assessments made under section 147 deserved to be annulled on both counts. [Para 44]

The Commissioner (Appeals) had observed in the order for the assessment year 1998-99 'the Assessing Officer is, however, free to take action in assessment year 1997-98'. The above observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) could not be held as a direction.

Following the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajinder Nath v. CIT [1979] 120 ITR 14 / 2 Taxman 204, it could safely be held that the Commissioner (Appeals) had not given any direction to the Assessing Officer to initiate reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98. Therefore, the notice issued under section 148 on 16-11-2004 was beyond the time-limit prescribed in the Act. In this case the assessment year ended on 31-3-1998 and, therefore, no notice under section 148 could have been issued after 31-3-2004. The appellate order for the assessment year 1998-99 had been passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) on 10-6-2004 and as per law, no reassessment for the assessment year 1997-98 could have been made after 31-3-2004. For argument's sake if it was admitted that the Commissioner (Appeals) had given direction to the Assessing Officer to initiate reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98 in his order dated 10-6-2004, even then under the law, the direction given by the Commissioner (Appeals) on 10-6-2004 was against the provisions of section 150(2).

In the instant case, initiation of the reassessment proceedings was barred by other provision of the Act on 10-6-2004 when the appellate order for the assessment year 1998-99 was passed. The assessment year 1997-98 had ended on 31-3-1998. Reopening of the assessment for the assessment year 1997-98 was permissible under the Act upto 31-3-2004. However, the appellate order, on the basis of which reassessment was initiated, had been passed on 10-6-2004. On the said date initiation of reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98 was prohibited by law, and, hence, reassessment proceeding initiated after 31-3-2004 was clearly barred by limitation.

Therefore, the reassessment order was time barred by limitation and, hence, was liable to be quashed.

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.

The amendment made to sub-section (1) of section 150 which intends to lift embargo of period of limitation under section 149 to enable Authorities to reopen assessments not only on the basis of Orders passed in proceedings under the Act but also on Order of a Court in any proceedings under any law has to be applied prospectively. It appears that the Deputy Commissioner has issued the impugned reassessment notice, dated 21-7-2022, under section 148 pursuant to passing of the impugned order dated 21-7-2022, under section 148A(d), for the alleged income, which has escaped assessment, amounting to Rs. 39 lakhs for the assessment year 2016-17.

It is evident that the notice dated 30-5-2022, under section 148A(b), clearly indicates that the alleged income, which has escaped assessment, is only Rs. 39 lakhs. Further, from the impugned order dated 21-7-2022, under section 148A(d), it is also evident that the alleged income, which has escaped assessment, is only Rs. 39 lakhs. As per section 149, the limitation period for issuance of notice under section 148 is normally three years from the end of the relevant assessment year (in instant case assessment year 2016-17) and extendable beyond 3 years till 10 years provided the income which has escaped assessment is Rs. 50 lakhs or more and the permission of the concerned authority is taken. The three-year time period of assessment year 2016-17 had ended on 31-3-2020. Accordingly, the impugned notice, dated 21-7-2022, is beyond 3 years' time period. Further, the said notice is for alleged escaped income of Rs. 39 lakhs which is less than Rs. 50 lakhs and thus, the said notice cannot take the benefit of extended period of limitation which is beyond three years till ten years. [Para 10]

Thus, it is to be held that the very initiation of reassessment proceeding is wholly without jurisdiction. [Para 12]

Accordingly, the impugned notice dated 21-7-2022, issued under section 148, is barred by the limitation period prescribed under section 149 and is illegal, unsustainable and void ab initio and is liable to be set aside. It is a well-established principle of law that if the foundation of any proceeding is illegal and unsustainable in law, then all consequential proceedings or order are also bad in law. Since the impugned notice dated 21-7-2022, under section 148, is illegal and unsustainable in law, accordingly, the impugned reassessment order dated 31-5-2023 passed under section 147 and the notice of demand dated 31-5-2023 issued under section 148 are also bad in law and unsustainable and the same, is to be quashed and set aside. [Para 13]

On perusal of and after a conjoint reading of the provisions under sections 143(2) and 148, it can be safely gathered that at the relevant point of time i.e., assessment year 2015-16, the time limit of issuance of notice under section 143(2) within a period of one year but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment, which was prescribed under the Act in clause (b) of 1st proviso to section 148 was no more applicable in the year under consideration as have become otiose by insertion of explanation effective from 1-10-2005 that, “For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that nothing contained in the first proviso or the second proviso shall apply to any return which has been furnished on or after the 1-10-2005 in response to a notice served under this section.” In view of the said explanation, the issuance of notice under section 143(2) which is qua the returns filed under section 139 shall apply in cases where the returns are filed under section 148 also, as going by the provisions of section 148, it is clarified that, the provisions of the Act shall, so far as may be, apply accordingly as if such return (under section 148 read with section 139) were a return required to be furnished under section 139. [Para 15]

■

Accordingly, in the instant case which pertains to assessment year 2015-16, for issuance of notice under section 143(2), the time limitation as provided proviso to sub clause (ii) of section 143(2) shall be applied, which have come into existence effective from 1-4-2021. [Para 16]

■

Adverting the facts of instant case, the return of income in response to notice under section 148 was filed by the assessee on 31-3-2021, and the notice under section 143(2) was issued on 20-11-2021, which in accordance with the applicable provisions of proviso to sub-clause (ii) of section 143(2) was to be issued within 3 months i.e., on or before 30-6-2021, however, the notice was issued on 20-11-2021, beyond the prescribed time as per aforesaid provisions, thus, was barred by limitation. The explanation by the revenue that the notice under section 143(2) was issued within period of 1 year from the end of the month in which the return was furnished cannot be accepted as the same was not substantiated or supported by any material, decision or the mandatory provisions of the Act. Therefore, undoubtedly, the notice issued under section 143(2) was beyond the prescribed time under the provisions of section 143(2), which needs to be strictly adhered to by the revenue. In the instant case, the notice was issued belatedly beyond the prescribed time of 3 months applicable in the instant case, as the notice was issued after 1-4-2021, i.e., on 20-11-2021, the same falls under the category of any invalid notice, which is the foundation of passing a valid assessment order, therefore, the assessment order passed in the instant case on the strength of an invalid notice under section 143(2), cannot sustained and liable to be struck down. [Para 17]

■

In absence of any plausible explanation or contradictory material or decision to dislodge the aforesaid view, the contention of the assessee in the cross objection that in absence of a valid notice under section 143(2), which was not issued within the prescribed time limit for the purpose of making the assessment is a violation of mandatory provisions of law is acceptable, therefore, the reassessment impugned order passed under section 147 read with section 144B dated 30-3-2022, dehors a valid notice under section 143(2) is a nullity and liable to be quashed. [Para 16]

Hence, to give meaning to the proviso it has to be interpreted to be applicable for assessment years up to 2021-2022. The interpretation canvassed by the revenue would render the following parts of the proviso redundant -

Section has to be interpreted so as to give meaning to all the words/phrases used in the section and it should not be interpreted in such a way so as to render any part or phrase in the section otiose. As stated foresaid, if the interpretation canvassed by the revenue is to be accepted then, not only various parts of the section would be rendered otiose, one would have to also substitute one phrase with another phrase in the said section, which is clearly not permissible in law. Whether the notice dated 27th August 2022 issued under section 148 of the Act is barred by limitation as per the first proviso to section 149 of the Act?

It was submitted on behalf of revenue that the period of limitation for the purposes of section 149 has to be seen with respect to the original notice under section 148 which was issued to petitioner on 8th April, 2021 and as the said notice was issued within the period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year, which was expiring on 31st March, 2022, the reassessment proceedings are within the period of limitation prescribed in section 149. It is not acceptable. Section 149 sets out, inter alia, the time limit for issuing notice under section 148. Apart from the period of limitation set out in the said Section, the first proviso lays down a further restriction on the issue of a notice under section 148. The period of limitation as well as the said further restriction is framed/provided in respect of a notice under 148 and not for a notice under section 148A. The notice dated 8th April, 2021, which though originally issued as a notice under section 148 of the Act, (under the provisions of the Act prior to the amendments made by the Finance Act, 2021), has now been treated as a notice issued under section 148A(b). Once the notice dated 8th April, 2021, has been treated as having been issued under section 148A(b), the said notice is no longer relevant for the purpose of determining the period of limitation prescribed under section 149 or the restriction as per the first proviso below Section 149. Therefore, for considering the restriction on issue of a notice under section 148 prescribed in the first proviso to section 149, the fresh/presently impugned notice dated 27th August, 2022 issued under section 148 is required to be considered. The said notice is admittedly beyond the erstwhile period of limitation of six years prescribed by the Act prior to its amendment by the Finance Act, 2021. For the assessment year 2015-2016, the erstwhile time limit of six years expired on 31st March, 2022 and, the impugned notice under section 148 has been issued on 27th August, 2022 and, therefore, the impugned notice dated 27th August, 2022 is barred by the restriction of the first proviso to section 149. [Para 29]

on 28-7-2022 under section 148 of the new regime is barred by limitation and hence bad in law, liable to be quashed, resulting in impugned reassessment proceedings as well as the impugned reassessment order bad in law. Accordingly, ground nos. 1 and 2 raised by the revenue are dismissed. Resultantly, grounds raised on the merits of the case are rendered academic and hence not adjudicated upon. [Para 10.2]

■ Now, with respect to the appeal by the revenue and cross objection by the assessee for assessment year 2015-16. Appeal by the revenue is on the merits of the case whereas cross objection by the assessee is on challenging the legal issue of notice under section 148 as bad in law, invalid, void ab initio, to be quashed. Accordingly, the legal issue raised by the assessee through its cross objection is taken up as it goes to the root of the matter. [Para 11]

■

Identical chronology of events exists for assessment year 2015-16 as discussed while adjudicating appeal for assessment year 2014-15 in the above paragraphs, except for date of filing of return. Notice under section 148 of the old regime was issued on 30-6-2021. Later, pursuant to the judgment in case of Ashish Agarwal (supra), it was directed among other things that notice issued under section 148 shall be deemed to have been issued under section 148A as substituted by the Finance Act, 2021 and construed or treated to be the show cause notice in terms of section 148A(b). In view of this direction, the said notice under section 148, dated 30-6-2021 was deemed to be a show cause notice under section 148A(b) for which another one was issued on 26-5-2022, complying with the direction given in the case of Ashish Agarwal (supra). [Para 12]

■

Thereafter, provisions of section 148A(d) were complied with by passing an order, dated 28-7-2022 and issuing a notice under section 148 of the same date (under the new regime). Assessee has contested by raising a ground of cross objection that the notice so issued is bad in law, invalid, void ab initio, to be quashed. The assessee strongly submitted that it is barred by limitation making the impugned reassessment proceedings and resultant reassessment order bad in law. [Para 12.1]

■

At the outset, it is found that this issue has been settled in the case of Rajeev Bansal (supra) wherein reference is made to the submissions made on behalf of the revenue which is relevant. [Para 12.2]

■

Thus, it can be seen that revenue conceded before the Supreme Court for dropping all the notices issued on or after 1-4-2021 for assessment year 2015-16 as they will not fall for completion during the period prescribed under TOLA. [Para 12.3]

■

In the case of present assessee, since the notice issued under section 148 is dated 28-7-2022, period of six years expired on 31-3-2022 and is thus barred by limitation. Accordingly, notice so issued and re-assessment completed thereafter under section 147 is liable to be quashed, in view of the decision of Supreme Court in the case of Rajeev Bansal (supra). [Para 12.5]

■

In view of above stated deliberation, both on facts and law including the applicable jurisprudence, it is held that notice for assessment year 2015-16 issued on 28-7-2022 under section 148 of the new regime is barred by limitation and hence bad in law, liable to be quashed, resulting in impugned reassessment proceedings as well as the impugned reassessment order bad in law. Accordingly, grounds of cross objection raised by the assessee are allowed. Resultantly, grounds of appeal raised on the merits of the case by the revenue are rendered academic and are therefore, dismissed. [Para 12.7]

■

In the result, for assessment year 2015-16, appeal by the revenue is dismissed and cross objection by the assessee is allowed. For assessment year 2014-15, appeal by the revenue is dismissed. [Para 13]

Unlike the position under the 1922 Act, an order passed under section 163 of the 1961 Act treating an assessee as an agent of a non-resident has been specifically appealable under section 246(1)(g ). If this right of appeal of the assessee is to have any real meaning, the decision under section 163 must be given previous to the notice under section 148 being issued to an assessee on the basis that the alleged income, which had escaped assessment, was the income on which the assessee was liable to be assessed as the agent of a non-resident covered by section 163. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that order under section 163 is to be passed in the first place and, thereafter, a notice under section 148 is to be served on the assessee who is sought to be made liable as a representative assessee, viz., as agent of a non-resident.

In the instant case, after the determination under section 163 took place on 28-3-1969 for the three assessment years under three separate orders, a fresh notice under section 148 was required to be issued. By that time, however, the period of limitation under section 149(3) had expired making the issue of any notice invalid. The earlier notice dated 31-3-1965 issued under section 148 was clearly not in order and any assessment, reassessment or recomputation done in pursuance of such invalid notice was also invalid. Thus, the Tribunal was justified in holding that the earlier notice issued under section 148 was void in law rendering the reassessment invalid.

■

Similar issue pertaining to the challenge of notice issued under section 148 for the assessment year 2015-16, on the ground that the same was beyond the limitation period prescribed under section 149 was decided in favour of the taxpayer in various cases by following the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70 /301 Taxman 238 /469 ITR 46 (SC). [Para 7]

■

In the present case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 29-7-2022. In view of the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Rajeev Bansal (supra) as well as in the case of Deepak Steel and Power Ltd. v. CBDT [2025] 174 taxmann.com 144 (SC), it is held that the notice issued on 29-7-2022 under section 148 in instant case for the assessment year 2015-16 was void ab initio and bad in law. As the notice was barred by limitation, accordingly, the entire reassessment proceeding and the assessment order passed under section 147 read with section 144B was to be quashed. [Para 7.4]

that the income was assessable in the assessment year 1977-78 Thus, it was a finding within the meaning of section 150(1) read with Explanation 2 below section 153(3). The first plea raised by the assessee was, therefore, found to be devoid of any merit. The Assessing Officer was within his jurisdiction to issue a notice under section 148 for the purposes of reassessment so as to give effect to the finding contained in the Tribunal’s order. As regards question of limitation section 150(1) removes the bar of limitation enacted in section 149 against the issuance of any notice under section 148. Generally, the time limit of four years prescribed in section 149(1)(b) shall not apply where reassessment proceedings are initiated by a notice to give effect to any finding or direction, under section 150(1). B ut under section 150(2), the period of limitation, as laid down in section 149, shall come into play. According to section 150(2) the provisions of sub-section (1) shall not apply where, by virtue of any other provision limiting the time within which action for assessment or reassessment may be initiated, issuance of notice for such assessment or reassessment is barred on the date of the order, which is the subject-matter of appeal, reference or revision, in which the finding or direction is contained. It would, thus, mean that an appellate or revisional authority cannot give a direction for assessment or reassessment, which goes to the extent of conferring jurisdiction upon the Assessing Officer if his jurisdiction had ceased due to the bar of limitation. If the issuing of a notice for assessment or reassessment for a particular assessment year had become time-barred at the time of the order, which was the subject-matter of the appeal, the provisions of section 150(1) cannot be invoked to the aid of the Revenue for making an assessment or reassessment.

In the light of the provision of section 149 specifying the period of limitation as four years from the end of the relevant assessment year, the case of the assessee for the purposes of issuance of notice for reassessment for the assessment year 1977-78 was found to be barred by limitation. The period of four years from the end of the assessment year 1977-78 expired on 31-3-1982. The assessment for the assessment year 1978-79 which was the subject-matter of appeal before the Tribunal, was made in the case of the first assessee on 23-3-1989. The appellate order was passed by the Commissioner on 27-12-1989. Thus, the subject-matter of appeal before the Tribunal was the order of the Commissioner dated 27-12-1989. On the date of the appellate order of the Commissioner, i.e., 27-12-1989, the Assessing Officer had no jurisdiction to issue a notice under section 148 for the assessment year 1977-78 inasmuch as the period of four years had already expired on 31-3-1982.

In the case of the second assessee, the last assessment order for the assessment year 1978-79 had been passed by the Assessing Officer on 30-1-1989 and the appellate order annulling the assessment was passed by the Commissioner on 29-3-1990. In this case also, the period of limitation for the purposes of reassessment for the assessment year 1977-78 had expired on 31-3-1982. The appellate order of the Commissioner dated 29-3-1990, was the subject-matter of appeal before the Tribunal. On that date, the Assessing Officer had no jurisdiction to issue a notice to the assessee under section 148 for the assessment year 1977-78. Section 150(2) refers to the subject matter of the appeal, reference or revision. In that light, it is actually the appellate order of the Commissioner (Appeals) which can be said to be the subject-matter of appeal before the Tribunal. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner was the order which was the subject-matter of appeal before the Tribunal. The period of limitation should have been available on the date of the appellate order of the Commissioner. In that view of the matter. Since the notices under section 148 had been issued by the Assessing Officer to both the assessees on 1-3-1996 these notice were beyond the period of limitation as laid down in section 149(1)(b ) read with section 150(2) and said notices deserved to be quashed.

The writ petitions were, therefore, to be allowed.

or order of the appellate authority or revision authority then the limitation provided under section 149 would not be applicable. However, the said extension of time limit under section 150(1) is also not absolute but is subject to the condition and restrictions as envisaged in sub-section (2) of section 150. Further, section 151 contemplates requirement of sanction where the notice under section 148 is issued after expiry of four years from the end of the assessment year. [Para 5] The plain reading of these provisions of section 149 to 151 reveals that section 150(1) provides exception to the limitation provided under section 149 for issuing notice under section 148. Therefore, section 150 can be pressed into service in a particular case of reopening based on the directions or giving effect to the order of the appellate authority only when the time limitation provided under section 149 has already expired. In the case in hand, the time limit provided under section 149 was certainly not expired as on 31-4-2011, however, it is certainly after the expiry of four years from the end of the assessment year and, therefore, as per the provisions of section 151, the notice under section 148 cannot be issued unless the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner is satisfied on the reasons recorded by the Assessing Officer that it is a fit case for issue of such notice. Therefore, the condition set out in section 151 and particularly in the proviso to section 150(1) as existed at relevant time is a mandatory condition for issuing notice under section 148. If such notice is issued after expiry of four years from end of the relevant assessment year section 151 gives jurisdiction to the Assessing Officer to initiate the proceedings under section 147 and in absence of the sanction of the authority provided under section 151, the notice issued by the Assessing Officer is invalid. The provisions of section 150 is only an exception to the limitation provided under section 149 and, therefore, the said section cannot be taken as an exception to section 151. Hence, even if the assessment is reopened to make reassessment in consequence of or to give effect to any finding or direction of the appellate authority the requirement of sanction under section 151 is mandatory for issuing notice under section 147. Even otherwise from the plain reading of section 150(1), it is clear that it begins with non-obstante clause as far as the limitation provided under section 149 and, therefore, section 150(1) has an overriding effect on section 149 and not over section 151. The requirement of sanction under section 151 is in the nature of check and balance and it is a measure against the misuse of power by the assessing authority for assessment or reassessment based the reasons not found satisfactory by the authorities provided under section 151. Accordingly, when the Assessing Officer admittedly issued notice under section 148 after the four years from the end of the assessment year and without obtaining the sanction under section 151 then such notice issued under section 148 is in violation of provisions of section 151 and, consequently, the same was invalid and the entire reassessment proceedings stand vitiated. Hence, the reopening of the assessee is not valid and the same is quashed. The consequential reassessment is also quashed. [Para 5]

once a notice under section 148 has been issued to assess or reassess a particular income then unless and until those proceedings are concluded by way of a valid order, fresh notice under section 148 to assess or reassess, the same income cannot be issued and if issued, it will be illegal and bad in law. Therefore, there is no provision for issuing second notice under section 148 during the pendency of notice under section 148 already issued but pending for service. [Para 13] As regards the question of the validity of the notices under section 148 issued on 29-3-1988 and 12-5-1988 without approval of the CBDT but with the approval of the Commissioner, the revenue’s case was that the notices having been issued in consequence upon the directions of the Commissioner (Appeals) they were saved by the provisions of section 150(1) and no approval of any higher authority was required.

As already observed, the observations of the Commissioner (Appeals) in his orders dated 25-5-1987, while annulling the first set of reassessments, were not directions. Therefore, the provisions of section 150(1) did not come into picture and revenue’s case was not saved. [Paras 14.2 and 15]

In the instant case, notices for the assessment years 1976-77, 1977-78 and 1978-79 issued on 29-3-1988 were issued after the expiry of 8 years but before the expiry of 16 years from the relevant assessment year which were not valid notices because, as per section 151, the notices for these years could be issued only with the prior sanction of the CBDT. Notices for these 3 years were, therefore, invalid and bad in law.

So far as assessment year 1979-80 was concerned, the old notice, being valid notice, could be served on or before 31-3-1988 and if Assessing Officer was to issue fresh notice, then proceedings on the basis of old notice should have been dropped for want of service. Admittedly, the Assessing Officer having not dropped the proceedings, the issuance of second notice for assessment year 1979-80 on 29-3-1988 was not in accordance with law. Even if it was taken that the Assessing Officer could issue fresh notice then also the same having been issued after the expiry of a period of 8 years for the end of the relevant assessment year without the sanction of the CBDT was invalid and bad in law. So far as notices for assessment years 1980-81, 1981-82 and 1982-83 were concerned, the same having been issued after the expiry of a period of 4 years but before the expiry of a period of 8 years from the end of the relevant assessment years and with the prior sanction of the Commissioner, were valid notices. [Para 16.5]

In view of above, the notices for the assessment years 1976-77 to 1979-80 issued on 29-3-1988 were bad in law and illegal, whereas notice of assessment year 1980-81 issued on 29-3-1988 and notices for the assessment years 1981-82 and 1982-83 issued on 12-5-1988 were valid notices. Since it is well-settled that once the notices under section 148 are held to be illegal and bad in law all subsequent proceedings are rendered non est bad-in law, the reassessments for the assessment years 1976-77 to 1979-80 were quashed being void-ab-initio, whereas assessments for the assessment years 1980-81, 1981-82 and 1982-83 were sustained.

Consequently, the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) for the assessment years 1980-81 to 1982-83 were to be confirmed whereas for the assessment years 1976-77 to 1979-80 were to be set aside. [Paras 17 to 19]

Examination of the notice issued under section 148 dated 23.04.2022 in the light of section 149 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, including the first proviso, shows that the first proviso to section 149 clearly provides that no notice under section 148 shall be issued at any time in a case for the relevant assessment year beginning on or before 01.04.2021, if such notice could not have been issued at that time on account of being beyond the time limit specified under the provisions of the Act as it stood prior to amendment. [Para 7]

■

In the present case, the assessment year involved is 2015-16 and as per the unamended provisions of section 149 of the Act, where income escaping assessment exceeds the prescribed limit, the time limit for issuance of notice under section 148 of the Act, was six years from the end of the relevant assessment year. Accordingly, for the assessment year 2015-16, the notice under section 148 of the Act, could have been issued on or before 31.03.2022. However, it is an undisputed fact that the notice under section 148 of the Act, has been issued on 23.04.2022, which is beyond the period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year. Therefore, in the considered view of the Tribunal, in light of the first proviso to section 149 of the Act, the A.O. could not have issued notice under section 148 of the Act, after 31.03.2022 for the assessment year 2015-16. [Para 8]

■

The Tribunal further finds that, although the Revenue has contended that as per the amended provisions of section 149 of the Act, where income escaping assessment exceeds Rs.50,00,000/-, the time limit for issuance of notice under section 148 of the Act, has been extended up to ten years, such extended time limit cannot be applied to cases where the limitation under the old regime had already expired. The first proviso to section 149 restricts issuance of notice under the new regime in cases where such notice was already time barred under the earlier provisions. Therefore, once the limitation has expired on 31.03.2022, the extended time limit of ten years under the amended provisions cannot be invoked to reopen the assessment. [Para 9]

■

In the present case, since the limitation for issuance of notice under section 148 of the Act, had already expired on 31.03.2022, in the considered view of the Tribunal, the notice issued by the A.O. under section 148 of the Act, dated 23.04.2022 is barred by limitation and consequently the assessment order passed by the A.O. under section 147 r.w.s. 144 r.w.s. 144B of the Act, is bad in law and liable to be quashed. Therefore, it is held that the notice issued under section 148 of the Act, is invalid and the consequent assessment order passed by the A.O. is liable to be quashed. Since the reassessment proceedings have been quashed on the legal issue, the other grounds raised by the assessee on merits become academic in nature and are not adjudicated. [Para 10]

■

In the result, the appeal filed by the assessee is allowed. [Para 11]

In the instant case, the respondent reopened the assessment of the appellant for the assessment year 2011-12, through notice dated 31-3-2018 under section 148. Admittedly, the limitation period of six years for reopening the assessment, came to an end on 31-3-2018. The main plank of contention of the appellant is that the notice under section 148 dated 31-3-2018 has been received by the appellant through e-mail only on 18-4-2018 i.e., after the expiry of six years from the end of the assessment year under consideration and hence, the same is clearly barred by limitation, whereas the department contended that mere signing of notice by the respondent on 31-3-2018 amounts to issuance of notice under section 149 and therefore, the same is within the limitation period. [Para 8]

It is clear from the provision of section 149 that the maximum time limit for issuance of notice under section 148 for reopening the assessment is six years from the end of the relevant assessment year. In the instant case, the relevant assessment year is 2011-12; the limitation of six years for initiation of reassessment proceedings expired on 31-3-2018; and notice under section 148 signed by the respondent was dated 31-3-2018. In such circumstances, this court is required to examine that such notice is in adherence to the compliance of section 149 for reassessment proceedings. [Para 9]

While the appellant stated that notice under section 148 was received by her through e-mail only on 18-4-2018 and hence, the same is clearly barred by limitation, it is stated on the side of the department that notice under section 148 was signed by the respondent on 31-3-2018 and the same was given to the process server to be served on the appellant on the same day, but it was returned on 6-4-2018 stating that there was no such person in the given address. After ascertaining her address from the last return of income filed by her, the said notice was sent to the appellant's registered mail ID, which was also served on 18-4-2018. Thus, according to the respondent, the reassessment proceedings commenced from the moment, when the notice was signed by the respondent on 31-3-2018 and hence, the same is well within limitation. [Para 10]

It is apparent that the issuance of notice under section 149 is complete only when the same is issued in the manner as prescribed under section 282 read with rule 127 prescribing the mode of service of notice under the Act. The signing of notice would not amount to issuance of notice as contemplated under section 149. In other words, the requirement of issuance of notice under section 149 is not mere signing of the notice under section 148, but is sent to the proper person within the end of the relevant assessment year. [Para 12]

Concededly, the notice dated 31-3-2018 issued by the respondent was served on the appellant through mail, only on 18-4-2018. Though the respondent produced the relevant pages of notice server book maintained by the department to show that the notice of the respondent dated 31-3-2018 under section 148 is within the limitation period, but the same only disclosed that the notice dated 31-3-2018 was returned on 6-4-2018.

In instant case, there is no document made available to prove that the notice under section 148 dated 31-3-2018 was sent for despatch to the appellant, within the end of the relevant assessment year i.e., 31-3-2018. Thus, it is crystal clear that the notice under section 148 for reopening the assessment was not sent to the appellant, within the time stipulated under section 149 and hence, the same vitiates the reassessment proceedings initiated under section 147. [Para 13]

In such view of the matter, the order of the Judge as well as the notice issued by the respondent are liable to be set aside. As a sequitur, the writ appeal stands allowed. [Para 14]

The reason to believe primarily indicates that it was based on the observations made by the 1st Appellate Authority while passing the order for the assessment year 1992-93. The reasons to believe for re-initiating assessment proceeding was primarily on the basis of the documents seized, which were contended to be bogus purchases and, consequently, there was a reason to believe that there was an omission or failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for assessment. It is found that the original assessment order considered all the seized documents, which were observed in the reasons to believe. Explanation given by the assessee was also considered in the original assessment proceeding. [Para 11]

Consequently, all the necessary explanation and information were furnished by the assessee and, therefore, there was no failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts for making assessment. [Para 13]

First proviso to section 147 makes it apparently clear that the reassessment proceedings after four years could only be initiated if the assessee failed to disclose fully or truly all material facts necessary for making the assessment. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the Tribunal has given a categorical finding that the assessee had disclosed all the material facts necessary for making the assessment and there was no failure on his part. This finding of the Tribunal is perfectly correct and, the Assessing Officer in his original assessment proceedings had considered each and every document and the explanation given by the assessee on the seized documents. Therefore, it was not a case where the assessee failed to disclose fully or truly all material facts necessary for making the assessment. The notice issued under section 148 was invalid. [Para 15]

Insofar as the period of limitation is concerned, the present dispute relates to the assessment year 1992-93 and as per the then existing provision of limitation specified under section 149, the period of limitation was10 years. Accordingly, the reassessment notice could be issued on or before 31-5-2001 whereas in the instant case reassessment notice under section148 was issued on 11-4-2001, which was within the period of limitation. Consequently, the notice issued under section148 was issued within the period of limitation. [Para 16]

In the light of the aforesaid, the question of invoking the provision of section 150(1) does not arise. However, section 150 provides that the power to issue a notice under section 148 in consequence of or giving effect to any finding or direction of the Appellate or Revisional Authority or the Court is subject to the provisions contained in section 150(2). Section 150(2) provides that the direction issued under section 150(1) cannot be given by the Appellate or Revisional Authority or by the Court if on the date on which the order in appeal or revision was passed, the reassessment proceeding had become barred by time. Under section 150(2) the Appellate or the Revisional Authority or the Court could give direction for reassessment only in respect of that assessment year. In respect of reassessment, proceedings could be initiated on the date of passing of the order in appeal. Since the notice was issued within the period of limitation, the provision of section 150(1) is not applicable in the instant case. [Para 17]

In R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 166 ITR 163, the Supreme Court categorically held that a clear distinction has been made out under the Income-tax Act, 1961 between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice'. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It prohibits issue of notice under section 148 after the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested with the ITO to proceed to reassess. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued Section 148(1) deals with making of the reassessment and mandates that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. Under the Act, service is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the ITO to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to the making of the order of assessment.

In the Instant case, notice under section 148 was issued by the ITO within the period of limitation prescribed under section 149. There was also no controversy about the fact that the order of reassessment was made only after service of notice on the assessee. The ratio of the decision in R.K. Upadhyaya's case (supra ) of the Supreme Court squarely applied to the present case. The ITO having issued the notice under section 148 within limitation, the order of reassessment was valid. Therefore, the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the initiation of reassessment proceedings by the ITO was barred by limitation and in setting aside the orders of the AAC and the ITO.

Section 148 provides provisions for initiation of the reassessment proceedings. The initiation has to be made with the issue of a notice under section 148 on the assessee concerned. In the instant case from the facts alone, the notice for the assessment year 1981-82 was barred by limitation under section 149(1)(a)(ii ) and as such the assessment done in pursuance of time-barred notice was liable to be quashed. Mere acceptance, acquiescence and participation in such a proceeding where notice is served beyond the period of statutory limitation cannot remedy the defect for not issuing the notice within the period of limitation, and that does not confer authority on the Assessing Officer to assume jurisdiction. Service of notice within the statutory period is a sine qua non and is an indispensable requisite for the initiation of assessment proceeding under section 148 where income has escaped assessment. The Assessing Officer, in the instant case, having failed to comply with the statutory requirement, could not assume jurisdiction and as such, the assessment order for the assessment year 1981-82 in the assessment proceedings passed by him pursuant to such time-barred notice for the said assessment year could not be sustained and no appellate authority including the Tribunal could give authority or jurisdiction to the Assessing Officer in such cases, as no life could be given to a dead horse. Further, in all the notices of the assessment years 1982-83 to 1986-87 including the assessment year 1981-82, there was no mention as to the status of the assessee even though the department was aware of the status of the assesee as individual having already assessed the assessee in the said status, i.e., in the ‘individual’ capacity only on salary income.

If the department sought to assess him in the status of ‘oral trust’, the status should have been mentioned in the notice itself. Without mentioning the status in the notice itself, the said notice could not be taken advantage of to start proceedings under section 148 against the ‘oral trust’. Therefore, the assessment for all the years under consideration made pursuant to such invalid notice, must be quashed.

Whatever and howsoever noble may be the purpose of any trust (religious or evangelic), they cannot escape themselves from the responsibility of accountability before the revenue. Otherwise, the very purpose of the existence of the revenue to control the source of funds and expenditures of any person/assessee would be futile.

The primary onus to furnish the accounts to the Income-tax Department like all other law-abiding citizens irrespective of caste, creed, colour, community and religion heavily lies on the person/assessee. In the instant case the assessee as an individual might be receiving salary for the work done by him sincerely on propagation of Christianity but that did not mean that the department would close its eyes to the accounts maintained by him for the funds received from abroad and expenditures thereof.

In the result, the appeals were to be allowed.

From a perusal of section 151 the following propositions emerge :— (i )if an assessment has been made under sub-section (3) of section 143 or section 147 and four years have not expired from the end of the relevant assessment year, a notice under section 148 has to be issued by the Assessing Officer who is not below the rank of the Assistant Commissioner or the Joint Commissioner but before issuing any such notice, the Joint Commissioner is to be satisfied with the reasons recorded by such Assessing Officer that it is a fit case for issue of such notice. Here ‘Joint Commissioner’, would also include an Additional Commissioner, in view of the definition of the phrase ‘Joint Commissioner’ as contained in section 2(28C). The satisfaction has to be necessarily recorded by the Additional Commissioner or the Joint Commissioner, as the case may be. However, if the Assessing Officer is the Additional Commissioner or the Joint Commissioner, then in that case prior approval of any higher officer is not required in case he has recorded the reasons for issuing notice in view of the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 120;

(ii )if, however, the period of four years has expired and the assessment order has been made under sub-section (3) of section 143 or section 147, the notice is to be issued only after the satisfaction has been recorded by either the Chief Commissioner or the Commissioner about the reasons recorded by the Assessing Officer that it is a fit case for issue of such notice. Thus, the Assessing Officer not below the rank of the Assistant Commissioner can issue a notice but before issuing the notice, the satisfaction of the Commissioner or the Chief Commissioner of the Income-tax is necessarily to be obtained. This would be the position after 1-4-1988 in view of the omission of the words ‘Additional Commissioner’ in section 2(16) by the Direct Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 1987; and

(iii )where an assessment has not been made under sub-section (3) of section 143 or section 147 and the period of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year has expired, notice under section 148 can be issued only by an officer of the rank of the Joint Commissioner after being satisfied with the reasons recorded by the Assessing Officer that it is a fit case for issue of such notice. Here, the term ‘Joint Commissioner’ is inter-changeable with the words ‘Additional Commissioner’ in view of the definition of the term ‘Joint Commissioner’, as given in section 2(28C). [Para 39]

In view of the various provisions of the Act defining jurisdiction of the various authorities and the powers, procedure to be adopted and the limitations imposed upon such authorities for making assessment or reassessment, it is clear that if under the provisions of the Act an authority is required to exercise powers or to do an act in a particular manner, then that power has to be exercised and the act has to be performed in that manner alone and not in any other manner. [Para 40]

Thus, if the assessment has been made under sub-section (3) of section 143 or section 147 and the proceedings for reassessment are to be initiated after a period of four years, then the notice can be issued only after the Chief Commissioner or Commissioner of Income-tax, as the case may be, has recorded his satisfaction, for issuance of notice as provided under the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 151. [Para 41]

It is well-settled that a notice issued without obtaining the prior sanction of the authority mentioned in the provisions of section 151, whether it is the proviso to sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), would be, invalid and the entire proceeding taken in pursuance thereof is liable to be quashed as the same would be without jurisdiction. [Para 51]

Applying the principles laid down to the facts of the instant case, there was no dispute between the parties that the impugned notices dated 12-9-2000 had been issued without obtaining the prior sanction of the Chief Commissioner or the Commissioner of Income-tax which was obligatory on the part of the Assessing Officer, as in all those assessment years, assessment/reassessment had been completed under sub-section (3) of section 143 or section 147 and the notice under section 148, dated 12-9-2000 had been issued much after the expiry of the period of four years from the end of the relevant assessment years. Any notices to the transferor company (which included VBPPL) that may be issued thereafter would be responded to by the Petitioner. This is not be understood to mean that proceedings initiated against any of the transferor companies, including VBPPL, by the Department prior to that date would be continued against the petitioner. What it meant was that notices issued thereafter to VBPPL after it ceased to exist would be responded to by the petitioner. That condition has been complied with since in fact the petitioner answered the notices issued to VBPPL after 1-4-2012. [Para 20]

It is trite law that the issue of a notice under section 148 is a condition precedent to the validity of any assessment under section 147, and, therefore, if no such notice is issued or if the notice issued is invalid or vague or is not served in accordance with law, the assessment would be bad. Assessing authority had not followed the time-limit prescribed while notice under section 148 was issued on 1-10-1993. The assessee filed his return of income on 27-3-1995. The assessee had also pointed out to the ITO that in the notice dated 1-10-1993 which was issued under section 148, the assessee was not given the statutory minimum period of time for filing the return of income. The law that was in force at the relevant point of time cast a statutory duty on the assessing authority to give minimum 30 days’ time. The Assessing Officer cancelled the notice when it was pointed out to him and, therefore, notice under section 148 was issued on 28-3-1996. Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 enacted by the Parliament and received the assent of the President on 28-9-1996. The Act omitted the words ‘not being less than 30 days’ from section 148 with effect from 1-4-1989. When notice dated 1-10-1993 and the fresh notice dated 28-3-1996 were issued, the Finance Act (No. 2) was not in force. The assessing authority had, therefore, rightly applied the then existing law. [Para. 5]

Section 148 provides for initiation of assessment proceedings which starts with the issue of notice. Initiation of proceedings by the assessing authority on 1-10-1993 was not valid and consequently it was dropped. Fresh notice was, therefore, issued under section 148 in conformity with the time prescribed under section 148. When the Finance Act was passed a legally valid proceeding was in existence. Notice prescribed under section 148 for the purpose of initiating reassessment proceedings is a condition precedent to the validity of an assessment made. The assessing authority was only curing the defect of not following the time-limit when it was pointed out by the assessee and, therefore, notice was issued strictly on the basis of the then existing statutory provision. The mere fact that the time-limit prescribed under section 148(1) was taken away would not make an invalid notice valid so as to render the assessment order dated 26-3-1997 invalid in terms of section 153(2). The assessee could not be allowed to raise such a plea after having persuaded the assessing authority to withdraw notice dated 1-10-1993 pointing out that it was not in conformity with the statutory provision. The assessee could not be allowed to take advantage of the plea of limitation in terms of section 153(2) contending that the notice dated 1-10-1993 was valid due to the omission of time-limit vide the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 with effect from 1-4-1989. [Para 6]

On the strength of notice dated 28-3-1996, the return of income was filed and such return could not be ignored. [Para 7]

The mere fact that the time-limit has been taken away with effect from 1-4-1989 would not vitiate the proceedings validly initiated applying the then existing law. The object and purpose of the amendment is only to take away the time-limit for giving time for the assessee to file a return which the Legislature thought unnecessary. If the Legislature wanted to undo all that was done by the assessing authority applying the then existing law, it should have been specifically provided in the statute. In the absence of specific provision in the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 invalidating those proceedings initiated by the ITO, it could not be said that the action taken by the ITO applying the then existing law was invalid. Once the notice issued under section 148 on 28-3-1996 was upheld the plea of limitation raised by the assessee under section 153(2) had to be rejected. The Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 as amended would not validate an invalid notice which was issued under section 148(1). [Para 9]

Once notices under section 148 have been issued, the proceedings initiated through them have to be taken to their logical end. In other words, either assessments should be framed on the basis of those proceedings or the Assessing Officer may specifically drop the proceedings, may be on the ground that no sufficient material was available for holding that income liable to tax had escaped assessment. Even if an assessee does not comply with those notices by fling the income-tax returns, the remedy which is open to the revenue is not to issue fresh notices under section 148 but to issue notices under section 142(1) or to have completed the assessments under section 144. Thus, if the assessments have got barred by limitation, they cannot be revived by issuing fresh notices. In the instant case, this position was clear to the Assessing Officer and other officers of the department as could be gathered from a DO letter written by ITO to his IAC in which he had written that in this case, the assessment for the assessment year 1972-73 had been completed on a total income of Rs. 2,53,400 on 20-2-1985 as a result of which a demand was created. He had further written that the assessment was completed in pursuance of action initiated under section 148 subsequent to an action under section 148 got time- barred. He had further mentioned that this matter was discussed with the Commissioner and that according to the Commissioner the demand was unrealisable and assessment was likely to be annulled.

In the circumstances, it was to be held that since in the instant case valid Notices for the assessment years under consideration had been issued by The Assessing Officer on 9-10-1973 but he failed to complete the assessments within the time allowed under law, the assessments got barred by time for both the years. Further, the assessments dated 29-3-1984 for the assessment year 1971-72 and 20-2-1985 for the assessment year 1972-73 were invalid, because they were completed on the basis of fresh notices issued under section 148 dated 31-3-1980 and 17-3-1981, i.e., at a time when the original proceedings initiated under section 148 were still pending.

Hence, both the assessments framed by the Assessing Officer for those two assessment years had to be annulled.

The facts as available to the Assessing Officer at the time of reopening of the assessment have only to be seen for justifying or otherwise of the reopening of the assessment. The information should have direct nexus with the escapement of income. The information available should be relevant and belief of the officer should be rational. The Court can only examine as to whether the process of formation of belief is in accordance with law. Adequacy of material is not relevant. It is also not relevant as to whether in the ultimate analysis, same amount of addition was made. Further, the belief at the time of reassessment of the assessment is only prima facie and not final. Similarly, the amount of escaped amount is also tentative and not final. There is always possibility of the quantum of escaped income varying in final analysis on the basis of particulars given to the assessee for explaining the case. It is possible that the assessee may be able to explain the entire amount or part of amount or the Assessing Officer may discover greater amount of concealed income. As regards the validity of notice issued under section 148, the first condition laid down in section 148(1) for issuance of notice is that it should be issued before making assessment, re-assessment and re-computation of income. In the instant case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 25-10-1988 and the assessment was completed on 22-8-1990. Thus, the notice issued under section 148 was valid as it was issued before the assessment was made. Then, according to the provisions envisaged and limitation laid down in section 149(1), no notice under section 148 would be issued in cases falling under clause (a) of section 147 for the relevant assessment year if eight years had elapsed from the end of that year. In the instant case, the relevant assessment year was 1987-88 and 8 years from the end of that year would elapse in 1996. But the notice under section 148 was already issued on 25-10-1988 and was, therefore, well within the prescribed time limit of eight years, i.e., before 31-3-1990. The assessee’s contention that the notice under section 148 issued prior to 31-3-1990 could not take the right of the assessee to file the return under section 139(4) was also not tenable as, in the instant case, no return was furnished before the issuance of notice under section 148. Moreover, there was no provision in the Act to invalidate the notice under section 148 by furnishing of return after the issue of such notice.

The notice issued under section 148 was in the nature of notice under section 139(2) and it was issued as no return was filed by the assessee and the Assessing Officer had reason to believe that income had escaped assessment as per section 147(a) of the Act. The notice under section 148 was issued on 25-10-1988 and the return of income was filed by the assessee on 30-3-1989. As the return was filed after the issue of notice under section 148, it was certainly a return submitted in response to the notice under section 148. Although the return was filed before 31-3-1990 and it was a belated return, it could not be treated as a return furnished under section 139(4), as it was not filed voluntarily by the assessee. There was no clash between the provisions of sections 139(1) and 139(4) on the one hand and section 139(2), on the other. A person who has not furnished a return under section 139(1) and (2) is authorised to file the return under section 139(4). In the instant case, as the assessee has furnished the return in response to a notice under section 148 which was treated as a notice under section 139(2), the assessee was not entitled to furnish a return under section 139(4). Therefore, the return furnished by the assessee was to be treated as a return filed under section 139(2)/section 148 and not a return under section 139(4). The assessee had contended that the assessment was barred by limitation, as the return was filed on 30-3-1989 and the assessment should have been completed by 31-3-1990 while it was completed on 22-8-1990. This contention of the assessee was based on the argument that the return furnished on 30-3-1989 should be treated as a return under section 139(4). As the latter contention of the assessee was rejected and the return furnished on 30-3-1989 was treated as a return under section 148/139(2), the former contention was also not tenable and could not be accepted under any provisions of law. As the assessment was re-opened under section 147(a), provisions of section 153(2)(a) were applicable. According to these provisions, no assessment is to be made after the expiry of four years from the end of the assessment year in which the notice under section 148 was served. In the instant case, as the notice under section 148 was served on 26-10-1988, the limitation for assessment expired on 31-3-1993, i.e., four years from the end of assessment year 1988-89. In view of the foregoing, it was to be held that the notice issued under section 148 was a valid notice, the return furnished in compliance with the notice under section 148 was to be treated as a return furnished under section 139(2) and the assessment made was within limitation and, therefore, was a valid assessment.

As regards the point of commencement of limitation, a plain reading of the provisions contained in clause (i) of sub-section (1)(a) of section 149 conveys the message that the relative adjective ‘that’ used in that provision has reference to the words ‘assessment year’ used in the opening lines of sub-clause (i). It suggests that the period of eight years is to commence from the end of the relevant assessment year. Nowhere in section 149(1)(a)(i ) has the term ‘financial year’ been used The position has been made clear by the use of the same term ‘assessment year’ in both sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 151. It is, thus, abundantly clear that the prescribed period of eight years or 16 years, as the case may be, is to be reckoned from the end of the relevant assessment year and not the financial year.

As regards the question of issue and service of notice, for the purposes of application of the provisions of section 149, a notice under section 148 should be issued and served within the time prescribed by section 149. For proper administration of sections 149 and 153 and to satisfy the legislative intention in enacting those provisions, the words `issued’ and ‘served’ used in sections 149 and 153, respectively, should be regarded and interpreted as inter-changeable. It is difficult to accept that the Legislature would have intended that the issuance of notice under section 148 within the period of limitation prescribed by section 149 without there being the effective service of such notice as required by section 153 within the prescribed period, would satisfy the pre-condition for making a valid assessment as per the provisions of section 147 read with sections 149 and 153. Such an interpretation of the word ‘issued’ used in section 149 would be too oppressive for the assessees. For the decision to issue notice under section 148 is taken by the ITO behind the back of an assessee as there is no requirement of law to hear the assessee before the issue of a notice under section 148 to him If the meaning of the word ‘served’ as used in section 153 is not considered to be hidden in the meaning of the word ‘issued’ used in section 149 and vice versa, it may lead to unwanted consequences. For, before the end of eight or sixteen years, as the case may be, from the relevant assessment year, an ITO may issue a notice under section 148 and allow it to be kept in his file for an indefinite period, for the period of limitation prescribed by section 153 for completing the assessment is to commence from the date of service of the notice under section 148 and not before. The ITO may, thus, keep the sword of democles, hanging on the head of an assessee for an indefinite period, Such could not be the intention of the Legislature in enacting the provisions of sections 149 and 153. Both the sections prescribe limitation for an integrated purpose. They should, therefore, be read together in order to meet that purpose.

It therefore, logically follows that the word issued’ used in section 149 is required to carry the meaning of the expression ‘issued and served’ within the prescribed period of limitation.

As regards the validity of notice under section 148, the relevant assessment year in this appeal was 1975-76 which came to an end on 31-3-1976. The starting point of limitation under section 149(1)(c) was 1-4-1976 and the eighth year from that date expired on 31-3-1984. Since the notice under section 148, according to the assessee himself, was served on him by affixation on 30-3-1984, the notice issued and the assessment proceedings initiated on the basis of such notice were not hit by the provisions of section 149. Since the service of the notice under section 148 on 30-3-1984 was proved, the subsequent service on 3-4-1984 of another notice of the same type would not adversely affect the validity of the notice served on 30-3-1984. Therefore, the notice issued in this case under section 148 was quite valid and not hit by the provisions of section 149.

Under the Surtax Act the limitation is to be spelt out from service of the notice rather than issuance of the same. Since the impugned notice was served on the assessee after the limitation date, it was not valid, and the consequential reassessment should be cancelled.

No return had been filed by the assessee as per the provisions of the Act and the so-called return filed beyond the time-limit prescribed under section 139(4) on 16-2-2000 was an invalid and non est return in the eyes of law. The proceedings to fasten liability on the assessee-company was commenced by the department for the assessment year 1997-98 by issue of a notice under section 142(1) dated 24-8-1998 for the first time. Prior to it, no notice or proceeding had started. Subsequently, several notices had been issued by the department under section 142(1) but all these notices were apparently issued after the end of the assessment year, i.e., 31-3-1998. As per the provisions of section 147, the income would be treated as escaped assessment at the end of the assessment year where no return had been filed. In the instant case, in the absence of return, the provisions were to tax income that escaped assessment and not to tax income which was not assessed as on 1-4-1998. Thus, the income could be assessed only by issuance of notice under section 148 and in the instant case, no such notice had been issued by the department under section 148. Mere issuance of notice under section 142(1) after the end of the assessment year in the absence of voluntary return by the assessee could not give rise to valid proceedings under the Act.

Explanation 2(a ) to section 147 includes non-filing of return in the expression ‘escaped assessment’. The scope of Explanation 2(a) has to be restricted to the failure of the assessee to file a return suo motu or a voluntary return under section 139(1) or section 139(4) within the prescribed time-limit and not to cases where a notice under section 142(1) requiring the assessee to file return has already been issued. Otherwise even on the first day of the assessment year itself the Assessing Officer can issue notice under section 148 when the process of assessment itself has not yet come into being. It would thus be too wide a proposition to be accepted. As regards the outer limit of issuing notice under section 142(1)(i), there is apparently no time-limit prescribed, but other provisions give an impression that the outer limit is one year from the end of the assessment year. Otherwise, the assessee’s failure to submit the return under section 142(1) would not entitle him to file the return thereafter. Once that time-limit is over and the assessee has not filed any return, it becomes a case of income escaping assessment and for that, issuance of notice under section 148 is a must. As per section 153, time-limit for completing assessment is two years from the end of the assessment year in which it was first assessable. This limit comes into play when the proceedings for assessment have been initiated by filing a return suo motu under section 139(1) or by issuance of a valid notice under section 142(1). Clause (i) of sub-section (1) of section 142 was amended by Finance Act, 1990, so that if a person fails to furnish a return of income by the due date mentioned in section 139(1), a notice calling upon him to file the return can be sent to him within the relevant assessment year itself. If no such initiation was taken within the assessment year, it would be a case of escaped assessment within the meaning of Explanation 2 to section 147 and, therefore, a notice under section 148 would be a must to empower the Assessing Officer to proceed with the assessment.

In the instant case, the assessee had not filed the return suo motu within a time prescribed under section 139(1), the revenue had not issued any notice under section 142(1) before the end of the assessment year and return furnished by the assessee under section 139(4) on 16-2-2000 had been filed beyond the time-limit prescribed under section 139(4) and was invalid return. Therefore, a notice under section 148 had to be issued when an assessment, reassessment or recomputation was to be made under section 147 to tax income which had escaped assessment. This was a case of assessment without there being an earlier assessment. Therefore, the assessment completed without issuing notice under section 148 was invalid and bad in law.

Accordingly, the assessment order stood annulled.

VALIDITY OF NOTICE UNDER SECTION 148 ISSUED DURING PENDENCY OF REASSESSMENT PROCEEDINGS :

In CIT v. Ram Kishan Leela [2007] 207 CTR (Raj.) 463, the Rajasthan High Court considered similar issue and held that second notice issued during the pendency of the reassessment proceedings cannot be treated to be legally justified.

In view of the said decision and on the facts and circumstances of the case, it was to be held that the reopening of the assessment by the second notice could not be justified and the assessment completed on the basis of such illegal notice did not have legal legs to stand on. The assessment was, therefore, liable to be quashed on this ground.

VALIDITY OF NOTICE UNDER SECTION 148 ISSUED BEYOND PERIOD OF 4 YEARS FROM RELEVANT ASSESSMENT YEAR :

Subsequent notice under section 148 was issued on 31-3-2003. The assessment pertained to the assessment year 1996-97. Notice issued on 31-3-2003 was, therefore, after the expiry of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year as the fourth year had expired on 31-3-2001.

In view of the proviso to section 147, no action can be taken for reassessment after the expiry of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year, unless any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for such assessment year by reason of the failure on the part of the assessee to make a return under section 139 or in response to a notice issued under sub-section (1) of section 142 or section 148 or to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment, for that assessment year.

In the instant case, the assessee had disclosed all the facts relating to deduction under section 80HHC during the original assessment and the Assessing Officer had preferred to accept her claim. Therefore, it could not be said that there was any failure on the part of the assessee in disclosing material facts. Since the instant case was covered by the proviso to section 147, both the conditions, viz., firstly, the Assessing Officer must have reason to believe that income, profit or gains chargeable to income-tax have escaped assessment, and secondly, he must also have reason to believe that such escapement has occurred by reason of either omission or failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully or truly all material facts necessary for his assessment of that year, were required to be satisfied. As the assessee had disclosed the material facts, the second condition was not satisfied and, therefore, it could be said that the reassessment had been made only on the basis of change of opinion.

Thus, the reassessment made after the expiry of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year could not be justified in law because the department had not been able to bring out any material to show that there was any failure on the part of the assessee to disclose material facts truly and fully to the Assessing Officer during the assessment proceedings. Thus, in view of the proviso to section 147, the reopening of the assessment could not be justified and, consequently, the notice issued under section 148 was to be held to be invalid. The entire reassessment proceedings were, therefore, null and void and on this basis, the reassessment order was liable to be quashed. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be set aside and the reassessment was to be quashed.

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.

The Settlement Commission directed the Assessing Officer having jurisdiction in the matter to take action in accordance with law. Even if the direction issued by the Settlement Commission was the reason which impelled the Assessing Officer to issue notice under section 148, he could have recorded that reason either in the notice issued to the assessee, or even in the file maintained by him in his office. Though a counter-affidavit had been filed on behalf of the Revenue, there was no averment in the counter-affidavit that reasons had been separately recorded in the file. On this short ground alone the notice issued under section 148, must be quashed.

There was yet another reason why the notice and the order passed consequent thereto, could not be upheld. It was not disputed that so far as the assessment year 1981-82 was concerned, the period of limitation prescribed was ten years for the issuance of notice under section 148. The said period, therefore, expired on 31-3-1992. The notice was, therefore, ex-facie barred by limitation. The Revenue, however, relied upon section 150 and submitted that in view of the direction issued by the Settlement Commission, the question of limitation could not stand in the way of the Assessing Officer issuing a notice under section 148. No doubt the submission was misconceived.

Resort to sub-section (1) of section 150 can be taken only in cases where it becomes necessary to make assessment or reassessment or recomputation in consequence of, or to give effect to, any finding or direction pursuant to an appellate order passed by the appellate authority or pursuant any order in reference or revision or by a court in any proceeding under any other law.

Obviously, the appeal, reference or revision or any other proceeding before a court must relate to the assessee in question, and not any direction or assessment made in appeal, reference or revision in the case of any other assessee, or in a proceeding in which the assessee in question is not a party. The assessee before the Settlement Commission was different and distinct from the assessee in the instant case. Certain findings were arrived at by the Settlement Commission and that gave rise to a belief in the mind of the Settlement Commission that the petitioner and others might have earned income which had escaped assessment. It was, therefore, observed that necessary action be taken in accordance with law. Such an order could not be construed to be an order passed under this Act by way of appeal, reference or revision so as to necessitate reassessment for the assessment year 1981-82. Sub-section (2) of section 150 makes it quite clear that the provisions of sub-section (1) shall not apply in any case if the order which was the subject-matter of the appeal, reference or revision, could not have been made by reason of any other provision limiting the time with in which any action for assessment, reassessment or recomputation may be taken.

It, therefore, follows that if the original order which was the subject-matter of the appeal, reference or revision could not have been passed, when it was purported to have been passed by reason of its being barred by limitation, the same cannot be revived under sub-section (1) of section 150. In the instant case, that question did not arise, because there was no assessment order for the assessment year 1981-82, which had been taken in appeal, reference or revision before any authority under the Act. The order of the Settlement Commission could have only justified issuance of the notice, if that was the reason for issuance of the notice, but beyond that it could not operate to revive a proceeding which was barred by limitation.

In these circumstances, the notice issued under section 148 and the assessment made pursant thereto was wholly without juriseiction being barred by limitation. The notice issued under section 148 was bad for non-compliance with the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 148, as the Assessing Officer failed to record his reasons while issuing the said notice.

The instant petition was accordingly allowed and the impugned notice issued under section 148 was quashed.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The ingredients of the proviso could be broken down for analysis as follows:
