Quoting of PAN

7.1 Section 139A has been amended with effect from 1-6-2006 to provide that the requirement of quoting of PAN is now extended to all quarterly statements prepared and delivered or caused to be delivered in accordance with section 200(3) or proviso to section 206C(3).

Clarificatory amendment regarding the time limit for issue of notice under section 142

7.2 Section 142(1), inter alia, provides that for the purposes of making assessment in a case where a person has not made a return of his income within the time specified under section 139(1), the Assessing Officer may serve a notice under the said sub-section on such person requiring him to furnish the return of his income in the prescribed form and manner.

Clause (i) of section 142(1) has been amended with effect from 1-4-2006 to provide that in a case where a person has not made a return of his income before the end of the relevant assessment year, the Assessing Officer may serve a notice after the end of the relevant assessment year under the said sub-section requiring such person to furnish his return of income.

Further a proviso to the said clause (i) has been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-4-1990, so as to provide that where any notice has been served on or after 1-4-1990 under sub-section (1) after the end of the relevant assessment year to any person who has not made a return of his income before the end of the relevant assessment year, such notice shall be deemed to be a notice served in accordance with the provisions of the said sub-section (1).

The amendment has been made to neutralise the decision in Motorola Inc. v. Dy. CIT [2005] 95 ITD 269 (Delhi)(SB), where it was held that the notice under section 142(1) calling for a return of income has to be issued after end of the period in section 139(1) and before end of the relevant assessment year and if no return of income is filed by an assessee till the end of the assessment year, a notice issued after the said date is invalid.

The amendment thus regularises the notices which were not served within the stipulated time period under the pre-amendment law.

Time limit for issue of notice under section 143(2) for the purposes of making assessment or reassessment under section 147

7.3 Section 148(1) provides that before making any assessment, reassessment or re-computation under section 147, the Assessing Officer shall serve a notice under section 148, on the assessee, requiring him to furnish his return of income and the provisions of the Act shall apply as if the return furnished in response to such notice were a return required to be furnished under section 139.

The Tribunal has held that assessment under section 147 is invalid if the notice under section 143(2) is not issued within 12 months from the end of the month in which return under section 147 was filed (after issuance of notice under section 148). [See Raj Kumar Chawla v. ITO [2005] 94 ITD 1 (Delhi)(SB)]

To cure such time barred assessments, the law has been amended retrospectively. Two new provisos to sub-section (1) have been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-10-1991 to provide as follows:

(a) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2) as it stood immediately before the amendment of said sub-section by the Finance Act, 2002, but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

(b) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2)(ii) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2)(ii), but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

ISSUE/SERVICE OF NOTICE

Service of notice is mandatory - The notice prescribed by section 148 cannot be regarded as a mere procedural requirement. It is only if the said notice is served on the assessee that the ITO would be justified in taking proceedings against the assessee. If no notice is issued or if the notice issued is shown to be invalid, then the proceedings taken by the ITO would be illegal and void [Y. Narayana Chetty v. ITO [1959] 35 ITR 388 (SC); CIT v. Thayaballi Mulla Jeevaji Kapasi [1967] 66 ITR 147 (SC); CIT v. Kurban Hussain Ibrahimji Mithiborwala [1971] 82 ITR 821 (SC)].

Section 148 provides for service of notice as a condition precedent to making the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested in the AO to proceed to reassess. The mandate of section 148 is that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued [R. K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 33 Taxman 229 (SC)].

Signature of authority – Where a reopening notice u/s. 148 was issued upon assessee without signature of Assessing Officer affixed on it either digitally or manually, said notice was invalid and same would not vest Assessing Officer with any further jurisdiction to proceed to reassess income of assessee [Prakash Krishnavtar Bhardwaj v. ITO [2023] 150 taxmann.com 60/293 Taxman 132/451 ITR 27 (Bom.)].

Date of issue/service of notice – While issuing notice u/s 148, date of issue of notice is not important, it is date of signing notice which is important [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices u/s 148 are sent through registered e-mail ID of respective Assessing Officers, though not digitally signed, it will be held to be valid service of notice. However, date and time of dispatch as recorded in ITBA portal will be taken as date of issuance of notice in this regard [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices u/s 148 were only uploaded in e-filing portal of assessees without any real time alert, date and time when assessees viewed notices in e-filing portal, as recorded in ITBA portal will be construed as date of service of notice [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices u/s 148 were manually despatched, date and time when notices were delivered to post office for dispatch was to be construed as date of issuance of notice [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices were sent to unrelated e-mail addresses, date on which notice was first viewed by assessee on e-filing portal was to be construed as date of issuance of notice [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Issue before getting approval u/s 151 – There is no need for paper containing approval being received physically before issuing notice and Assessing Officer can proceed to issue a notice u/s 148 if approving authority has granted his approval and approval has been communicated to Assessing Officer in any manner including by uploading approval on portal of department. Thus, reopening notice could not be vitiated on ground that paper containing approval u/s 151 was received by Assessing Officer after issuing notice [Sahara Credit Cooperative Society Ltd. v. DCIT/Asstt. CIT [2022] 141 taxmann.com 384 (All.)].

Where assessment proceedings are pending - Notice cannot be issued during pendency of assessment proceedings [Jhunjhunwala Vanaspati Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 137 Taxman 336 (All.)].

In the Ashish Agarwal ruling, the Supreme Court did not address whether or not the reassessment notices were issued within the time limits prescribed under the provisions of the 1961 Act, read with the relaxations provided under TOLA. Thus, in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC), setting aside various judgments1, the Supreme Court held that:

(a)

Section 3(1) of TOLA applies to the issuance of reassessment notices under section 148 of the 1961 Act. While TOLA did not amend the four and six-year time limits under the Act, it provided a relaxation for issuing reassessment notices during the COVID-19 period. TOLA does not apply if the time-limit under section 149 expires before 20-3-2020. When issuing a reassessment notice, the revenue must check both section 149 time limit and TOLA's relaxation period. For example, the six-year limit for AY 2013-14 expired on 31-3-2020, but TOLA extended it to 30-06-2021.Accordingly, after 1-4-2021, the 1961 Act has to be read along with the substituted provisions. TOLA will continue to apply to the Income-tax Act after 1-4-2021, if any action or proceeding specified under the substituted provisions of the 1961 Act falls for completion between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021.

(b)

TOLA will extend the time-limit for the grant of sanction by the authority specified under section 151. The test to determine whether TOLA will apply to section 151 of the new regime is this: if the time-limit of three years from the end of an assessment year falls between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021, then the specified authority under section 151(i) has extended time till 30-6-2021 to grant approval. In the case of section 151 of the old regime, the test is: if the time-limit of four years from the end of an assessment year falls between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021, then the specified authority under section 151(2) has extended time till 31-3-2021 to grant approval. Thus, the Assessing Officers were required to issue the reassessment notice under section 148 of the new regime within the time-limit surviving under the 1961 Act read with TOLA. All notices issued beyond the surviving period are time-barred and liable to be set aside.

Implementation of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183 1. Hon'ble Supreme Court, vide its judgment dated 04.05.2022 [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183, in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal has adjudicated on the validity of the issue of reassessment notices issued by the Assessing Officers during the period beginning on 1st April, 2021 and ending with 30th June 2021, within the time extended by the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 [hereinafter referred to as "TOLA"] and various notifications issued thereunder (these reassessment notices hereinafter referred to as "extended reassessment notices").

2. These extended reassessment notices were issued by the Assessing Officers under the provision of section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") following the procedure prescribed under various sections pertaining to reassessment namely sections 147 to 151, as they existed prior to their amendment by the Finance Act, 2021 (hereinafter referred to as "old law"). With effect from 1st April 2021, the old law has been substituted with new sections 147-151 (hereinafter referred to as the "new law").

3. Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that these extended reassessment notices issued under the old law shall be deemed to be the show cause notices issued under clause (b) of section 148A of the new law and has directed Assessing Officers to follow the procedure with respect to such notices. It has also held that all the defences available to assessees under section 149 of the new law and whatever rights are available to the Assessing Officer under the new law shall continue to be available. Hon'ble Supreme Court has passed this order in exercise of its power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India.

4. The implementation of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court is required to be done in a uniform manner. Accordingly, in exercise of its power under section 119 of the Act, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (hereinafter referred to as "the Board") directs that the following may be taken into consideration while implementing this judgment.

5. Scope of the judgment:

5.1 Taking into account the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in various paragraphs. it is clarified that the judgment applies to all cases where extended reassessment notices have been issued. This is irrespective of the fact whether such notices have been challenged or not.

6. Operation of the new section 149 of the Act to identify cases where fresh notice under section 148 of the Act can be issued:

6.1 With respect of operation of new section 149 of the Act, the following may be seen:

Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that the new law shall operate and all the defences available to assessees under section 149 of the new law and whatever rights are available to the Assessing Officer under the new law shall continue to be available.

Sub-section (1) of new section 149 of the Act as amended by the Finance Act, 2021 (before its amendment by the Finance Act, 2022) reads as under:-

"149. (1) No notice under section 148 shall be issued for the relevant assessment year.—

(a)

if three years have elapsed from the end of the relevant assessment year, unless the case falls under clause (b);

(b)

if three years, but not more than ten years, have elapsed from the end of the relevant assessment year unless the Assessing Officer has in his possession books of account or other documents or evidence which reveal that the income chargeable to tax, represented in the form of asset, which has escaped assessment amounts to or is likely to amount to fifty lakh rupees or more for that year:

Provided that no notice under section 148 shall be issued at any time in a case for the relevant, assessment year beginning on or before 1st day of April, 2021, if such notice could not have been issued at that time on account of being beyond the time limit specified under the provisions of clause (b) of sub-section (1) of this section, as they stood immediately before the commencement of the Finance Act, 2021."

Hon'ble Supreme Court has upheld the views of High Courts that the benefit of new law shall be made available even in respect of proceedings relating to past assessment years. Decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court read with the time extension provided by TOLA will allow extended reassessment notices to travel back in time to their original date when such notices were to be issued and then new section 149 of the Act is to be applied at that point.

The substituted provision provides as follows:

(a) Sub-section (1) of section 150, with a non obstante clause, overrides the general time limits prescribed in section 149 for issuing notices under section 148. This provision is similar to pre-amended section 150(1).

(b)

Clause (a) of Section 150(2) imposes a restriction on the power given in section 150(1) in the situation when the assessment year was already time-barred at the time the order (subject matter of appeal, reference or revision) was passed. This provision is similar to pre-amended section 150(2).

(c)

Clause (b) of section 150(2), a new provision, imposes a restriction on the power given in section 150(1) in the situation when the assessment year was already time-barred at the time the assessment proceedings (subject matter before the court) were initiated [see Para 16.3C-4a].

Sub-section (3) of Section 150, a new provision, provides the time limit within which the notice under section 148 pursuant to the findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority [see Para 16.3C-4b].

16.3C-4a No reassessment if the assessment year was time-barred at the time the assessment proceedings were initiated - Section 150(2)(a) largely mirrors the existing provision of section 150(2). It refers to the time when the original order (which was subsequently challenged in appeal, reference, or revision) was made. The implication remains consistent with the current law: if, at the time the initial assessment order was passed, the assessment year was already time-barred under other provisions of the Act, then section 150(1) cannot be used to reopen it, even if a higher authority later gives a finding or direction.

Section 150(2)(b) introduces a new reference point for checking the time limitation for assessment proceedings that are the subject of court proceedings. This clause significantly broadens the circumstances under which section 150(1) cannot be invoked. It shifts the focus from the date of the final order to the date of initiation of proceedings relating to assessment or reassessment. If the proceedings were initiated at a time when the limitation period to issue notice for an assessment year had expired under the general provisions (like Section 149 or section 153), then even if a subsequent court order gives a finding or direction, section 150(1) would be rendered inapplicable. This would prevent the reopening of old cases based on findings from court proceedings.

16.3C-4b Time-limit to issue notice under section 148 - Sub-section (3) of section 150 provides the time limit within which the notice under section 148 can be issued pursuant to the findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority. It provides that the notice under section 148 shall be issued within 3 months from the end of the quarter in which the certified copy of the order of the authority or the Court, as the case may be, is received by the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. This provision puts the limitation period within which such notice should be issued, and if not issued within such period, the assessment becomes time-barred, and section 150(1) cannot come to its rescue.

16.3C-4a No reassessment if the assessment year was time-barred at the time the assessment proceedings were initiated - Section 150(2)(a) largely mirrors the existing provision of section 150(2). It refers to the time when the original order (which was subsequently challenged in appeal, reference, or revision) was made. The implication remains consistent with the current law: if, at the time the initial assessment order was passed, the assessment year was already time-barred under other provisions of the Act, then section 150(1) cannot be used to reopen it, even if a higher authority later gives a finding or direction.

Section 150(2)(b) introduces a new reference point for checking the time limitation for assessment proceedings that are the subject of court proceedings. This clause significantly broadens the circumstances under which section 150(1) cannot be invoked. It shifts the focus from the date of the final order to the date of initiation of proceedings relating to assessment or reassessment. If the proceedings were initiated at a time when the limitation period to issue notice for an assessment year had expired under the general provisions (like Section 149 or section 153), then even if a subsequent court order gives a finding or direction, section 150(1) would be rendered inapplicable. This would prevent the reopening of old cases based on findings from court proceedings.

16.3C-4b Time-limit to issue notice under section 148 - Sub-section (3) of section 150 provides the time limit within which the notice under section 148 can be issued pursuant to the findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority. It provides that the notice under section 148 shall be issued within 3 months from the end of the quarter in which the certified copy of the order of the authority or the Court, as the case may be, is received by the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. This provision puts the limitation period within which such notice should be issued, and if not issued within such period, the assessment becomes time-barred, and section 150(1) cannot come to its rescue.

Limitation period for completion of assessments and reassessments

5.3 Section 153 of the Act lays down the time limit for making an order of assessment (two years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable). Also, Explanation 1 below section 153 of the Act sets out certain circumstances in which certain periods as specified are excluded from the period of limitation.

In a case where an audit under section 142(2A) is ordered, the assessee is required to furnish a report of such audit within the prescribed time. In such a case, the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited under section 142(2 A) and ending with the date on which the assessee furnishes a report of such audit is excluded while reckoning the period of limitation for completion of the assessment, as per Explanation 1(iii) below section 153 of the Act.

As per the Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, in a case where the report is not prepared and, therefore, not furnished, the normal time limit of two years is operative and the Assessing Officer does not get any additional time for the purpose of making an assessment because the time taken for furnishing the audit report is not excluded. Exclusion of the period in terms of Explanation 1(iii) could operate only if the report of such audit is furnished.

To obviate the difficulty, the said Explanation has been amended, with effect from 1-4-1997, to provide that the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited and ending on the date on which the report of such audit was required to be furnished, shall be excluded from the period of limitation.

This would enable extension of the limitation period, at least, by the time permitted, although, the audit report is not furnished.

7.2-3f ABATEMENT OF PENDING ASSESSMENT OR REASSESSMENT - There could be several situations and implications. Some of them are discussed below :

Consider a case, where the search action takes place, say, on 1-7-2003. In the search, only certain documents are found showing receipts on sale of certain goods, relating to the financial year 2002 and 2003. Apart from that, nothing else is found. In this case, the Assessing Officer will have to issue the notice under section 153A to the assessee for filing the return for the specified period, i.e., assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04. The assessee has already filed returns under section 139 for all the above assessment years. Further, in respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments have been reopened pursuant to notice under section 148. In respect of assessment year 2001-02, the assessee has not received any notice for assessment under section 143(2). Further, for the assessment year 2000-01 no assessment was done under section 143(3). In respect of assessment year 1999-2000, the assessment was made under section 143(3). The assessment is pending in appeal. In respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, against the assessments made under section 143(3), an appeal was filed. In the appeal, the assessment for assessment year 1997-98 was set aside and the appeal for assessment year 1998-99 was decided with a direction to examine the claim of the assessee, for certain facts, and accordingly allow the claim.

The position, in respect of the above assessment years, as per the new procedure, could be as follows :

The Assessing Officer has to make assessments or reassessments for each of the assessment years under the new procedure. Thus, prima facie, the Assessing Officer will make assessments or reassessments for all the years covered in the specified period, that is, assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04.

In respect of the assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments whereof are reopened but reassessments are not completed, the reassessments can now be completed, pursuant to section 153A. The effect would be extension in the limitation period for making reassessment, since section 153A overrides the provisions of section 153.

The assessments for assessment years 2000-01 and 2001-02, though barred by limitation under section 153, can be made under section 153A. In the assessment, normal disallowance, etc., can be made. This may attract interest, if any, under section 234B, etc.

The assessment for assessment year 1999-2000 is completed. All the same, a fresh assessment can be made under section 153A. The new procedure would not affect the pending appeal.

The set aside assessment for the assessment year 1997-98 shall abate and the Assessing Officer will make the assessment under section 153A. However, while making reassessment, it may not be possible for him to ignore the directions, if any, of the Appellate Authority, in respect of the issue covered by the appellate order.

11.2-8e Notice can be issued if incomes escaping assessment spread over more than 1 year [Section 149(1A)]

After sub-section (1) the following sub-section is inserted:

"(1A) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where the income chargeable to tax represented in the form of an asset or expenditure in relation to an event or occasion of the value referred to in clause (b) of sub-section (1), has escaped the assessment and the investment in such asset or expenditure in relation to such event or occasion has been made or incurred, in more than one previous years relevant to the assessment years within the period referred to in clause (b) of sub-section (1), a notice under section 148 shall be issued for every such assessment year for assessment, re-assessment or recomputation, as the case may be."

The amended section 149(1)(b) provides that notice under Section 148 can be issued after 3 years but before 10 years if escaped income of Rs. 50 lakhs or more is represented in the form of an asset, expenditure, or entry. Sub-section (1A) introduced by the Finance Act, 2022 provides that if such escaped income, represented in the form of asset or expenditure in respect of transaction, event or occasion, is spread over more than 1 year and the total escaped income in all these years is Rs. 50 lakhs or more, then AO gets jurisdiction to issue a notice under Section 148 for all those years. It is now no longer necessary that escaped income of Rs. 50 lakh should be only in 1 year. It is only to be seen that the aggregate of such escaped income is Rs. 50 lakh or more, and in such a situation, notice under Section 148 can be issued for all such years.

After sub-section (1) the following sub-section is inserted:

The amended section 149(1)(b) provides that notice under Section 148 can be issued after 3 years but before 10 years if escaped income of Rs. 50 lakhs or more is represented in the form of an asset, expenditure, or entry. It is now no longer necessary that escaped income of Rs. 50 lakh should be only in 1 year. It is only to be seen that the aggregate of such escaped income is Rs. 50 lakh or more, and in such a situation, notice under Section 148 can be issued for all such years.

7.2-3e RETURN PURSUANT TO THE NOTICE - As per the provisions, the return is required to be filed within the time specified in the notice. The Assessing Officer does not have any power to vary the time specified in the notice, unless such power is assumed as inherent power.

In practical life, it is observed that a substantial time is lost in obtaining the relevant particulars and information from the Tax Department from and out of seized material. Accordingly, the assessee will have to be careful in complying with the time limit.

The non-compliance, if any, may result in best judgment assessment. It may also result in prosecution.

The requirement contemplates filing of return in respect of each of the assessment years, in the prescribed form and verified in the prescribed manner as well as giving such particulars as may be prescribed. Further, it may be noted that the pending assessment, if any, shall abate. 7.2-3f ABATEMENT OF PENDING ASSESSMENT OR REASSESSMENT - There could be several situations and implications. Some of them are discussed below :

Consider a case, where the search action takes place, say, on 1-7-2003. In the search, only certain documents are found showing receipts on sale of certain goods, relating to the financial year 2002 and 2003. Apart from that, nothing else is found. In this case, the Assessing Officer will have to issue the notice under section 153A to the assessee for filing the return for the specified period, i.e., assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04. The assessee has already filed returns under section 139 for all the above assessment years. Further, in respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments have been reopened pursuant to notice under section 148. In respect of assessment year 2001-02, the assessee has not received any notice for assessment under section 143(2). Further, for the assessment year 2000-01 no assessment was done under section 143(3). In respect of assessment year 1999-2000, the assessment was made under section 143(3). The assessment is pending in appeal. In respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, against the assessments made under section 143(3), an appeal was filed. In the appeal, the assessment for assessment year 1997-98 was set aside and the appeal for assessment year 1998-99 was decided with a direction to examine the claim of the assessee, for certain facts, and accordingly allow the claim.

The position, in respect of the above assessment years, as per the new procedure, could be as follows :

◆ The Assessing Officer has to make assessments or reassessments for each of the assessment years under the new procedure. Thus, prima facie, the Assessing Officer will make assessments or reassessments for all the years covered in the specified period, that is, assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04.

◆ In respect of the assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments whereof are reopened but reassessments are not completed, the reassessments can now be completed, pursuant to section 153A. The effect would be extension in the limitation period for making reassessment, since section 153A overrides the provisions of section 153.

◆ The assessments for assessment years 2000-01 and 2001-02, though barred by limitation under section 153, can be made under section 153A. In the assessment, normal disallowance, etc., can be made. This may attract interest, if any, under section 234B, etc.

◆ The assessment for assessment year 1999-2000 is completed. All the same, a fresh assessment can be made under section 153A. The new procedure would not affect the pending appeal.

11.4 Exclusion of 15 days from the limitation period for the issue of notice under Section 148 [Section 149]

11.4-1 Background

The existing provision of Section 149 provides the limitation period for the issue of notice under Section 148 for the reassessment under Section 147. Section 148A specifies the procedure to be followed before issuing a notice under Section 148. It provides that the Assessing Officer shall conduct enquiries, if required, and provide an opportunity of being heard to the assessee. After considering his reply, the Assessing Officer shall decide, after passing an order, whether it is a fit case for the issue of notice under Section 148 and serve a copy of such order along with such notice on the assessee.

This procedure does not apply where a search is carried out under Section 132 or requisition is made under Section 132A and in cases initiated on the basis of information emanating from search and requisition proceedings. In such cases, a notice under Section 148 is issued without conducting proceedings under Section 148A. However, in cases resulting from material gathered during survey operations under Section 133A, the AO is required to carry out proceedings under Section 148A before issuing notice under Section 148.

11.4-2 Difficulty in existing provision

It is observed that when a search or requisition is conducted after 15th March of a financial year, there is very little time left to collate the material and issue notice under Section 148. Also, where a statement of a person recorded during a search indicating tax evasion is received late by the jurisdictional AO, due to a shortage of time, it becomes difficult to carry out necessary verification before the issue of notice under Section 148. Therefore, to facilitate the AO carrying out necessary verification before the issue of notice under Section 148, the Finance Act, 2023 has amended Section 149 to provide 15 days extra time to AO to issue notice under section 148 in such cases.

11.4-3 Amendment by the Finance Act, 2023

The Finance Act, 2023 has inserted the Third and Fourth proviso (after the existing Second Proviso and the existing Third and Fourth Proviso are renumbered as Fifth and Sixth Proviso) in Section 149 with effect from the assessment year 2023-24.

11.4-3a Extension of limitation period by 15 days in search and requisition cases [third proviso to Section 149(1)] - A third proviso has been inserted to Section 149(1), which provides as under:

"Provided also that for cases referred to in clauses (i), (iii) and (iv) of Explanation 2 to section 148, where,--

(a)

a search is initiated under section 132; or

(b)

a search under section 132 for which the last of authorisations is executed; or

(c)

requisition is made under section 132A,

after the 15th day of March of any financial year and the period for issue of notice under section 148 expires on the 31st day of March of such financial year, a period of fifteen days shall be excluded for the purpose of computing the period of limitation as per this section and the notice issued under section 148 in such case shall be deemed to have been issued on the 31st day of March of such financial year."

The effect of the third proviso is that 15 days will be excluded while computing the limitation period under Section 149 for the issue of notice under Section 148 if the following conditions are satisfied:

(a)

A search is initiated, the last warrant is executed, or requisition is made after 15th March of the financial year; and

(b)

Notice under Section 148 is required to be issued for an assessment year on or before 31st March of that financial year.

If the above conditions are satisfied, the notice so issued under Section 148 within the extended limitation period of 15 days will be deemed to have been issued on 31st March of such financial year.

For example, a search is initiated on 16th March 2024 (or where the search is initiated before 15th March 2024, but the last warrant was executed on 20th March 2024), and it revealed the acquisition of undisclosed assets during the financial year 2016-17 relevant to the assessment year 2017-18. The time period for the issue of notice under Section 148 read with section 153A expire on 31st March 2024. As per the amended law, such notice can be issued on or before 15th April 2024.

Section 150(1), with a non obstante clause, overrides the general time limits prescribed in section 149 for issuing notices under section 148. This provision enables issuing a notice under section 148 for re-assessment at any time for the purpose of giving effect to any finding or direction contained in an order passed by any authority in any proceeding by way of appeal, reference or revision or by a Court. While section 150(1) grants a broad power, section 150(2) imposes a restriction on that power. It states that the provisions of sub-section (1) (i.e., the power to issue notice "at any time") shall not apply in any case where the assessment, reassessment, or recomputation relates to an assessment year in respect of which such reassessment could not have been made at the time the order (which was the subject-matter of the appeal, reference, or revision) was made, by reason of any other provision limiting the time within which any action for reassessment may be taken. This provision ensures that this power cannot be used to revive an assessment year that was already time-barred when the original order (which was the subject of appeal or revision) was made.

The existing provision covered the scenario where an order (the subject of appeal or revision) was made, but did not cover the situation in which proceedings for assessment, reassessment, or recomputation had been initiated by the Assessing Officer, but no order had been passed. Further, section 150 did not specify the time limit within which the notice under section 148 pursuant to the findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority must be issued.

16.3C-2 Corresponding provisions of ITA 1961 and ITA 2025

The pre-amended section 150 of the ITA 1961 and section 283 of the ITA 2025 contain similar provisions with respect to powers to issue notices pursuant to findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority, and the restrictions on exercising such powers.

16.3C-3 Amendment by the Finance Act, 2026

The Finance Act, 2026 has made amendments to section 283 of the ITA 2025 and section 150 of the ITA 1961 to provide the time limit within which a notice of reassessment must be issued pursuant to the findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority.

16.12-1 Position under the ITA 1961

To make an assessment, reassessment, or re-computation in section 147 of the ITA 1961, a notice was required to be issued to the assessee under section 148, requiring him to furnish a return of his income or the income of any other person in respect of which he is assessable under this Act. A notice under section 148 could be issued only when the Assessing Officer has information suggesting that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for the relevant assessment year. In the following situations, information shall be deemed to be suggesting that income has escaped assessment:

(a)

any information in the case of the assessee for the relevant assessment year in accordance with the risk management strategy formulated by the Board from time to time;

(b)

any audit objection to the effect that the assessment in the case of the assessee for the relevant assessment year has not been made in accordance with the provisions of this Act;

(c)

any information received under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A of the Act;

(d)

any information made available to the Assessing Officer under the scheme notified under section 135A;

(e)

any information which requires action in consequence of the order of a Tribunal or a Court;

(f)

any information emanating from a survey conducted under section 133A (other than conducted under section 133A(2A) for verifying TDS and TCS) on or after 1-9-2024.

While issuing such a notice, the Assessing Officer is not required to obtain prior approval of the specified authority. However, the procedure prescribed under section 148A must be followed. However, if the Assessing Officer receives information in a faceless manner under the e-Verification Scheme, 2021 (notified under section 135A), the notice can be issued without following the procedure under section 148A. In such cases, prior approval of the specified authority is mandatory before issuing the notice under section 148.

The first proviso to Section 149(1)(b) requires the determination of whether the time limit prescribed under section 149(1)(b) of the old regime continues to exist for the assessment year 2021-2022 and before. Resultantly, a notice under Section 148 of the new regime cannot be issued if the period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year has expired at the time of issuance of the notice. This also ensures that the new time limit of ten years prescribed under section 149(1)(b) of the new regime applies prospectively. For example, for the assessment year 2012-2013, the ten year period would have expired on 31 March 2023, while the six year period expired on 31 March 2019. Without the proviso to Section 149(1)(b) of the new regime, the Revenue could have had the power to reopen assessments for the year 2012-2013 if the escaped assessment amounted to Rupees fifty lakhs or more. The proviso limits the retrospective operation of Section 149(1)(b) to protect the interests of the assesses.

HEADNOTE: Section 148, read with section 149, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reassessment - Issue of notice - Assessment year 1966-67 - Whether, where reassessment notice under section 148 was issued within period of limitation prescribed under section 149 but was served on assessee after expiry of period of limitation, initiation of reassessment proceedings by ITO was barred by limitation and, therefore, invalid - Held, no

FACT: For the assessment year 1966-67, assessment was reopened under section 148 by the ITO in the case of assessee, an individual. In the reassessment, the ITO included certain amount as unexplained investment in the income assessed earlier in the original assessment. The notice under section 148 was issued on 29-3-1975 but it was served on the assessee on 7-4-1975. On appeal before the AAC, the assessee contended that the notice having been served after the expiry of period of limitation, the reassessment proceedings were barred by limitation. The AAC rejected the assessee's contention. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the notice under section 148 was not only to be issued but served within the period of limitation as laid down in section 149, and since the notice was served on the assessee after the expiry of 8 years, the order of reassessment was set aside.

On reference:

HELD: In R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 166 ITR 163, the Supreme Court categorically held that a clear distinction has been made out under the Income-tax Act, 1961 between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice'. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It prohibits issue of notice under section 148 after the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested with the ITO to proceed to reassess. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued Section 148(1) deals with making of the reassessment and mandates that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. Under the Act, service is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction on the ITO to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to the making of the order of assessment.

In the Instant case, notice under section 148 was issued by the ITO within the period of limitation prescribed under section 149. There was also no controversy about the fact that the order of reassessment was made only after service of notice on the assessee. The ratio of the decision in R.K. Upadhyaya's case (supra ) of the Supreme Court squarely applied to the present case. The ITO having issued the notice under section 148 within limitation, the order of reassessment was valid. Therefore, the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the initiation of reassessment proceedings by the ITO was barred by limitation and in setting aside the orders of the AAC and the ITO.

Having said so, in merits embargo enshrined in section 149 is operative and here within six years notice should have been issued but in the case of the assessee, it was not done and the appellate order itself, which is the basis of issue of notice under section 148 and very basis for invoking provisions of section 150(1), was passed on 28/2/2013. Notice under section 148 was issued thereafter, therefore, it is beyond the period of limitation. 12. We further take guidance from the decision of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of K.M. Sharma v. ITO [2002] 122 Taxman 426/254 ITR 772 wherein it was held that fiscal statute more particularly on a provision such as the present one regulating period of limitation must receive strict construction. Law of limitation is intended to give certainty and finality to legal proceedings and to avoid exposure to risk of litigation to litigant. Proceedings, which have attained finality under existing law due to bar of limitation cannot be held to be open for revival unless the amended provision is clearly given retrospective operation so as to allow upsetting of proceedings, which had already been concluded and attained finality. The amendment to sub-section (1) of Section 150 is not expressed to be retrospective and, therefore, has to be held as only prospective. The amendment made to sub-section (1) of Section 150 which intends to lift embargo of period of limitation under Section 149 to enable Authorities to reopen assessments not only on the basis of Orders passed in proceedings under the I.T. Act but also on Order of a Court in any proceedings under any law has to be applied prospectively. Therefore, even as per rule, strict construction and limitation of section 149 applies until and unless ingredients of section 150(1) is fulfilled. In the case before us, the ingredients of section 150(1), which the Revenue has made the basis for issue of notice under section 148, itself is not satisfied, therefore, issuance of notice under section 148 is directly hit by the provisions of section 149 limitation. We are, therefore, of the considered view that since issuance of 148 notice is barred by limitation, serving of notice itself is invalid and bad in law and, therefore, any consequent assessment or re-assessment is obviously null and void. We, therefore, set aside the order of the ld. CIT (A) and direct quashing of the re-assessment proceedings. Since the legal ground of validity of proceedings under section 147/148 itself is decided in favour of the assessee, all other grounds in the grounds of appeal becomes infructuous.

13. In the result, appeal of the assessee is allowed.

The Supreme Court referred to the meaning as given in words and phrases (Permanent Edition) where as to 'irregularity' it has been stated that it is 'want of adherence to some prescribed rule or mode of proceeding;' whereas 'nullity' is 'a void act or an act having no legal force or validity.' The safest rule of distinction between 'irregularity' and 'nullity' is to see whether 'a party can waive the objection; if he can waive, it amounts to irregularity and if he cannot, it is nullity.' Further a waiver is an intentional relinquishment of a known right, but obviously an objection to jurisdiction cannot be waived, for consent cannot give a Court jurisdiction where there is none. The power to assess get vested in the Assessing Officer the moment he issues notice under section 148. HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had observed in the order for the assessment year 1998-99 'the Assessing Officer is, however, free to take action in assessment year 1997-98'. The above observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) could not be held as a direction. Following the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajinder Nath v. CIT [1979] 120 ITR 14 / 2 Taxman 204, it could safely be held that the Commissioner (Appeals) had not given any direction to the Assessing Officer to initiate reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98. Therefore, the notice issued under section 148 on 16-11-2004 was beyond the time-limit prescribed in the Act. In this case the assessment year ended on 31-3-1998 and, therefore, no notice under section 148 could have been issued after 31-3-2004. The appellate order for the assessment year 1998-99 had been passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) on 10-6-2004 and as per law, no reassessment for the assessment year 1997-98 could have been made after 31-3-2004. For argument's sake if it was admitted that the Commissioner (Appeals) had given direction to the Assessing Officer to initiate reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98 in his order dated 10-6-2004, even then under the law, the direction given by the Commissioner (Appeals) on 10-6-2004 was against the provisions of section 150(2).

In the instant case, initiation of the reassessment proceedings was barred by other provision of the Act on 10-6-2004 when the appellate order for the assessment year 1998-99 was passed. The assessment year 1997-98 had ended on 31-3-1998. Reopening of the assessment for the assessment year 1997-98 was permissible under the Act upto 31-3-2004. However, the appellate order, on the basis of which reassessment was initiated, had been passed on 10-6-2004. On the said date initiation of reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98 was prohibited by law, and, hence, reassessment proceeding initiated after 31-3-2004 was clearly barred by limitation.

Therefore, the reassessment order was time barred by limitation and, hence, was liable to be quashed.

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.

FACT: For the assessment year 1997-98, the Assessing Officer, on 24-8-1998, issued notice to assessee under section 142(1). The assessee filed his return on 16-2-2000. As the return filed by assessee was beyond time-limit prescribed under section 139(4), i.e., on or before 31-3-1999, the Assessing Officer initiated reassessment proceedings against the assessee under section 147 and completed the assessment. The assessee filed the instant miscellaneous application and contended that no notice under section 148 was ever issued before passing the assessment order. Hence, the assessment under section 147 became invalid.

HELD: No return had been filed by the assessee as per the provisions of the Act and the so-called return filed beyond the time-limit prescribed under section 139(4) on 16-2-2000 was an invalid and non est return in the eyes of law. The proceedings to fasten liability on the assessee-company was commenced by the department for the assessment year 1997-98 by issue of a notice under section 142(1) dated 24-8-1998 for the first time. Prior to it, no notice or proceeding had started. Subsequently, several notices had been issued by the department under section 142(1) but all these notices were apparently issued after the end of the assessment year, i.e., 31-3-1998. As per the provisions of section 147, the income would be treated as escaped assessment at the end of the assessment year where no return had been filed. In the instant case, in the absence of return, the provisions were to tax income that escaped assessment and not to tax income which was not assessed as on 1-4-1998. Thus, the income could be assessed only by issuance of notice under section 148 and in the instant case, no such notice had been issued by the department under section 148. Mere issuance of notice under section 142(1) after the end of the assessment year in the absence of voluntary return by the assessee could not give rise to valid proceedings under the Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 148, read with section 147, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reassessment - Notice of - Assessment years 1971-72 and 1972-73 - Whether, where a valid notice under section 148 had been issued but no assessment had been completed nor were proceedings dropped by the Assessing Officer, he was disentitled to initiate fresh assessment proceedings by issuing another notice under section 148 - Held, yes - Whether assessment completed on the basis of second notice under section 148 would be invalid - Held, yes - Whether, where assessment proceedings initiated on the basis of first notice under section 148 got barred by limitation, they could be revived by issuing fresh notice under section 148 - Held, no

FACT: For the assessment years 1971-72 and 1972-73, notices under section 148 were issued to the assessee-firm. These notices were served on 9-10-1973 on the Receiver who was appointed on 28-7-1972 on a suit for rendition of accounts filed by one of the partners 'V'. No assessment order was passed on the basis of these notices. Thereafter, another set of notices under section 148 was issued for both the assessment years on 31-3-1980 and 17-3-1981. respectively. The assessment for the assessment year 1971-72 was completed ex parte under section 144 on 29-3-1984 while, for the assessment year 1972-73, the assessment was completed under section 143(3) on 20-2-1985. On appeal, the assessee contended before the first appellate authority that assessments had become time-barred as they could not have been framed on the aforesaid dates on the basis of first set of notices issued on 9-10-1973. The appellate authority took the view that perusal of record did not reveal that any notice under section 148 had been issued on 9-10-1973 and the photocopy of the notices produced did not give reasons for initiating the proceedings. Therefore, it was held that the initiation of proceedings under section 148 vide subsequent notices as valid. However, the assessments were set aside for further examination and for fresh assessments.

On second appeal:

HELD: Once notices under section 148 have been issued, the proceedings initiated through them have to be taken to their logical end. In other words, either assessments should be framed on the basis of those proceedings or the Assessing Officer may specifically drop the proceedings, may be on the ground that no sufficient material was available for holding that income liable to tax had escaped assessment. Even if an assessee does not comply with those notices by fling the income-tax returns, the remedy which is open to the revenue is not to issue fresh notices under section 148 but to issue notices under section 142(1) or to have completed the assessments under section 144. Thus, if the assessments have got barred by limitation, they cannot be revived by issuing fresh notices. In the instant case, this position was clear to the Assessing Officer and other officers of the department as could be gathered from a DO letter written by ITO to his IAC in which he had written that in this case, the assessment for the assessment year 1972-73 had been completed on a total income of Rs. 2,53,400 on 20-2-1985 as a result of which a demand was created. He had further written that the assessment was completed in pursuance of action initiated under section 148 subsequent to an action under section 148 got time- barred. He had further mentioned that this matter was discussed with the Commissioner and that according to the Commissioner the demand was unrealisable and assessment was likely to be annulled.

In the circumstances, it was to be held that since in the instant case valid Notices for the assessment years under consideration had been issued by The Assessing Officer on 9-10-1973 but he failed to complete the assessments within the time allowed under law, the assessments got barred by time for both the years. Further, the assessments dated 29-3-1984 for the assessment year 1971-72 and 20-2-1985 for the assessment year 1972-73 were invalid, because they were completed on the basis of fresh notices issued under section 148 dated 31-3-1980 and 17-3-1981, i.e., at a time when the original proceedings initiated under section 148 were still pending.

Hence, both the assessments framed by the Assessing Officer for those two assessment years had to be annulled.

However, the learned Judge failed to appreciate the same in a proper perspective and erred in dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant herein.

It appears that the Deputy Commissioner has issued the impugned reassessment notice, dated 21-7-2022, under section 148 pursuant to passing of the impugned order dated 21-7-2022, under section 148A(d), for the alleged income, which has escaped assessment, amounting to Rs. 39 lakhs for the assessment year 2016-17.

It is evident that the notice dated 30-5-2022, under section 148A(b), clearly indicates that the alleged income, which has escaped assessment, is only Rs. 39 lakhs. Further, from the impugned order dated 21-7-2022, under section 148A(d), it is also evident that the alleged income, which has escaped assessment, is only Rs. 39 lakhs. As per section 149, the limitation period for issuance of notice under section 148 is normally three years from the end of the relevant assessment year (in instant case assessment year 2016-17) and extendable beyond 3 years till 10 years provided the income which has escaped assessment is Rs. 50 lakhs or more and the permission of the concerned authority is taken. The three-year time period of assessment year 2016-17 had ended on 31-3-2020. Accordingly, the impugned notice, dated 21-7-2022, is beyond 3 years' time period. Further, the said notice is for alleged escaped income of Rs. 39 lakhs which is less than Rs. 50 lakhs and thus, the said notice cannot take the benefit of extended period of limitation which is beyond three years till ten years. Thus, it is to be held that the very initiation of reassessment proceeding is wholly without jurisdiction. [Para 12]

Accordingly, the impugned notice dated 21-7-2022, issued under section 148, is barred by the limitation period prescribed under section 149 and is illegal, unsustainable and void ab initio and is liable to be set aside. It is a well-established principle of law that if the foundation of any proceeding is illegal and unsustainable in law, then all consequential proceedings or order are also bad in law. Since the impugned notice dated 21-7-2022, under section 148, is illegal and unsustainable in law, accordingly, the impugned reassessment order dated 31-5-2023 passed under section 147 and the notice of demand dated 31-5-2023 issued under section 148 are also bad in law and unsustainable and the same, is to be quashed and set aside. [Para 13]

The learned CIT-DR, on the other hand, submitted that the A.O. has issued notice under section 148A(b) of the Act, on 26.03.2022 and passed an order under section 148A(d) of the Act, and issued notice under section 142(1) of the Act, dated 24.03.2022, and as per section 148 of the Act, as amended by the Finance Act, 2021, if the income escaped from the assessment is more than Rs.50,00,000/-, then the notice under section 148 of the Act can be issued beyond three years and up to ten years, and therefore, the argument of the assessee is incorrect and cannot be accepted.

7. We have heard both parties, perused the material available on record and had gone through the orders passed by the authorities below. We have also carefully considered the notice issued by the A.O. under section 148 of the Act dated 23.04.2022 in light of the provisions of section 149 of the Act, including the first proviso thereto. The first proviso to section 149 clearly provides that no notice under section 148 shall be issued at any time in a case for the relevant assessment year beginning on or before 01.04.2021, if such notice could not have been issued at that time on account of being beyond the time limit specified under the provisions of the Act as it stood prior to amendment.

8. In the present case, the assessment year involved is 2015-16 and as per the unamended provisions of section 149 of the Act, where income escaping assessment exceeds the prescribed limit, the time limit for issuance of notice under section 148 of the Act, was six years from the end of the relevant assessment year. Accordingly, for the assessment year 2015-16, the notice under section 148 of the Act, could have been issued on or before 31.03.2022. However, it is an undisputed fact that the notice under section 148 of the Act, has been issued on 23.04.2022, which is beyond the period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year. Therefore, in our considered view, in light of the first proviso to section 149 of the Act, the A.O. could not have issued notice under section 148 of the Act, after 31.03.2022 for the assessment year 2015-16.

9. We further find that, although the Revenue has contended that as per the amended provisions of section 149 of the Act, where income escaping assessment exceeds Rs.50,00,000/-, the time limit for issuance of notice under section 148 of the Act, has been extended up to ten years, such extended time limit cannot be applied to cases where the limitation under the old regime had already expired. The first proviso to section 149 restricts issuance of notice under the new regime in cases where such notice was already time barred under the earlier provisions. Therefore, once the limitation has expired on 31.03.2022, the extended time limit of ten years under the amended provisions cannot be invoked to reopen the assessment.

10. In the present case, since the limitation for issuance of notice under section 148 of the Act, had already expired on 31.03.2022, in our considered view, the notice issued by the A.O. under section 148 of the Act, dated 23.04.2022 is barred by limitation and consequently the assessment order passed by the A.O. under section 147 r.w.s. 144 r.w.s. 144B of the Act, is bad in law and liable to be quashed. Therefore, we hold that the notice issued under section 148 of the Act, is invalid and the consequent assessment order passed by the A.O. is liable to be quashed. Since we have quashed the reassessment proceedings on legal issue, the other grounds raised by the assessee on merits become academic in nature and hence not adjudicated.

11. In the result, the appeal filed by the assessee is allowed.

Now let us examine as to whether issue of notice under section 148 during the period when assessment/reassessment is pending is a 'nullity' or an 'irregularity'. Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Krishan Lal v. State of J & K [1994] 4 SCC 422 had an occasion to examine the difference between the expressions "irregularity" and "nullity". The Supreme Court referred to the meaning as given in words and phrases (Permanent Edition) where as to 'irregularity' it has been stated that it is "want of adherence to some prescribed rule or mode of proceeding;" whereas 'nullity' is "a void act or an act having no legal force or validity." The safest rule of distinction between 'irregularity' and 'nullity' is to see whether "a party can waive the objection; if he can waive, it amounts to irregularity and if he cannot, it is nullity." Further a waiver is an intentional relinquishment of a known right, but obviously an objection to jurisdiction cannot be waived, for consent cannot give a court jurisdiction where there is none. As discussed above the power to assess get vested in the Assessing Officer the moment he issues notice under section 148. The contention of the Revenue that no such plea was taken by the assessee would not mean that the Assessing Officer got jurisdiction to issue of notice under section 148 during the currency of assessments. As held by Hon'ble Apex Court in Krishan Lal's case (supra) it is not an irregularity committed by the Assessing Officer but an illegality which will render assessments bad in law.

The assessment is re-opened when notice is issued under section 148. It is for the completion of the assessment the notice under section 148 should be served on the assessee. From these judicial pronouncements referred to above it is clear that where the reassessment proceedings initiated under section 147 were not concluded to a logical end the Assessing Officer cannot issue fresh reassessment notice under section 148. HEADNOTE: Section  149, read with section  147, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income escaping assessment -  Time limit for issue of notice (Reassessment) - Assessment year  2015-16 - Assessee filed return of income on 17-9-2015 - Based on information received under Risk Management Strategy of CBDT, notice under section 148 was issued on 23-6-2021 after obtaining prior approval of PCIT - Reassessment was completed under section 147 read with section 144B, disallowing short-term capital loss under section 94(7) - Assessee challenged reassessment on ground that subsequent notice issued under section 148 on 29-7-2022 was barred by limitation under amended provisions read with applicable judicial principles - It was noted that limitation period available to Assessing Officer for issuance of notice under section 148, as per section 149, was expired on 31-3-2022, however, notice under section 148 was issued on 29-7-2022 - Whether reassessment proceedings initiated beyond prescribed limitation period were void ab initio and unsustainable in law - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned reassessment proceedings initiated under section 148 vide notice dated 29-7-2022 are barred by limitation and deserve to be quashed and consequently, reassessment order passed under section 147 read with section 144B also deserved to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 5.1, 5.2 & 6] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee filed his return of income for assessment year 2015-16 on 17-9-2015 declaring total income of Rs. 11.87 crores. Subsequently, the case was taken up for reassessment proceedings based on the information received under Risk Management Strategy as formulated by the CBDT.

■

Notice under section 148 dated 23-6-2021 was issued after obtaining the prior approval of the PCIT.

■

The Assessing Officer vide order under section 147 read with section 144B dated 29-5-2023 completed the assessment at income of Rs. 36.25 crores by disallowing the short term capital loss under section 94(7) and adding the said amount.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee submitted that the Commissioner (Appeals) erred in law and facts of the matter while not quashing the notice issued on 29-7-2022 under section 148 being barred by limitation in view of the first proviso to section 149(1) and as such the notice issued under section 148 was bad in law and deserved to be quashed.

HELD: ■

From perusal of the records, it reveals that it is an undisputed fact that the year under consideration is relating to assessment year 2015-16, and accordingly, the limitation period available to the Assessing Officer for issuance of notice under section 148, as per section 149, was expired on 31-3-2022. However, the notice under section 148 was issued on 29-7-2022, thus, the issuance of notice under section 148 on 29-7-2022 is barred by limitation. Consequently, the reassessment proceedings culminating in the order under section 147 read with section 144B are rendered void ab initio, having been initiated beyond the prescribed statutory period and lacking legal sustainability. [Para 5]

■

In view of the aforesaid, the impugned order dated 29-7-2022 issued under section 148(A)(d) as well as the notice dated 29-7-2022 issued under section 148 in respect of assessment year 2015-16 deserve to be quashed. [Para 5.2]

■

It is further noted that even otherwise, the limitation period must be strictly construed in accordance with the statutory provisions of the Act as amended by the Finance Act, 2021, read with TOLA and judicial pronouncements of the Supreme Court.[Para 5.3]

So called reasons recorded by the Assessing Officer have been given in para 14 of the CIT(A)’s order. Admittedly, the notice under section 148 has been issued within four years so the question of taking approval of the CIT for the issue of such notice did not arise. It is also settled law that it is the Assessing Officer’s reason to believe which was relevant. The reading of the reasons itself makes it clear that the reasons were not recorded by the Assessing Officer. The words "hence if approved, notice under section 148 may be issued" itself was indicative of the fact that some staff member had put the note which was mechanically approved by the Assessing Officer without application of his mind. Needless to say, it is not the appraisal of the Assessing Officer but the subjective satisfaction of the Assessing Officer which is important for formation of belief. The CIT(A) has, therefore, rightly held that the Assessing Officer has initiated reassessment proceedings under section 147 without application of his mind. The initiation of reassessment proceedings on this count itself is illegal. We are, therefore, of the view that the CIT(A) has rightly held that the initiation of reassessment proceedings under section 147 of the Act was invalid.

23. The CIT(A) has also held that the reassessment was invalid as the same was made in consequence to a notice under section 143(2) of the Act which was issued beyond the period of limitation. Sub-section (2) of section 143 provides that when a return has been made under section 139 or in response to notice under section 142(1), the Assessing Officer, if considers necessary or expedient, shall issue a notice requiring the assessee to produce any evidence on which the assessee may rely in support of the return. A proviso has been attached to this sub-section. It provides that no notice under this sub-section shall be served on the assessee after expiry of 12 months from the end of the month in which the return is furnished. Admittedly, the notice under section 143(2) was issued on the original return. However, no order under section 143(3) of the Act was made within the limitation period. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148 for the re-assessment. The assessee vide letter dated 13-2-1993, intimated the Assessing Officer that the return of income filed originally may be treated as a return filed in response to notice under section 148 of the Act. Even the Assessing Officer has acted upon such letter by treating the return filed earlier to be a return in response to notice under section 148 of the Act. The question arises as to whether the limitation period for the issue of notice under section 143(2) of the Act as provided in proviso to section 143(2) will be applicable in the cases of returns filed in response to notice under section 148 or not. We have, therefore, examined the provision to section 148 of the Act which read as under :—

"148(1). Before making the assessment, reassessment or recomputation under section 147, the Assessing Officer shall serve on the assessee a notice requiring him to furnish within such period, as may be specified in the notice, a return of his income or the income of any other person in respect of which he is assessable under this Act during the previous year corresponding to the relevant assessment year, in the prescribed form and verified in the prescribed manner and setting forth such other particulars as may be prescribed; and the provisions of this Act shall, so far as may be, apply accordingly as if such return were return required to be furnished under section 139.

2. The Assessing Officer shall, before issuing any notice under this section, record his reasons for doing so."

■

On perusal of and after a conjoint reading of the provisions under sections 143(2) and 148, it can be safely gathered that at the relevant point of time i.e., assessment year 2015-16, the time limit of issuance of notice under section 143(2) within a period of one year but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment, which was prescribed under the Act in clause (b) of 1st proviso to section 148 was no more applicable in the year under consideration as have become otiose by insertion of explanation effective from 1-10-2005 that, “For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that nothing contained in the first proviso or the second proviso shall apply to any return which has been furnished on or after the 1-10-2005 in response to a notice served under this section.” In view of the said explanation, the issuance of notice under section 143(2) which is qua the returns filed under section 139 shall apply in cases where the returns are filed under section 148 also, as going by the provisions of section 148, it is clarified that, the provisions of the Act shall, so far as may be, apply accordingly as if such return (under section 148 read with section 139) were a return required to be furnished under section 139. [Para 15]

■

Accordingly, in the instant case which pertains to assessment year 2015-16, for issuance of notice under section 143(2), the time limitation as provided proviso to sub clause (ii) of section 143(2) shall be applied, which have come into existence effective from 1-4-2021. [Para 16]

■

Adverting the facts of instant case, the return of income in response to notice under section 148 was filed by the assessee on 31-3-2021, and the notice under section 143(2) was issued on 20-11-2021, which in accordance with the applicable provisions of proviso to sub-clause (ii) of section 143(2) was to be issued within 3 months i.e., on or before 30-6-2021, however, the notice was issued on 20-11-2021, beyond the prescribed time as per aforesaid provisions, thus, was barred by limitation. The explanation by the revenue that the notice under section 143(2) was issued within period of 1 year from the end of the month in which the return was furnished cannot be accepted as the same was not substantiated or supported by any material, decision or the mandatory provisions of the Act. Therefore, undoubtedly, the notice issued under section 143(2) was beyond the prescribed time under the provisions of section 143(2), which needs to be strictly adhered to by the revenue. In the instant case, the notice was issued belatedly beyond the prescribed time of 3 months applicable in the instant case, as the notice was issued after 1-4-2021, i.e., on 20-11-2021, the same falls under the category of any invalid notice, which is the foundation of passing a valid assessment order, therefore, the assessment order passed in the instant case on the strength of an invalid notice under section 143(2), cannot sustained and liable to be struck down. [Para 17]

■

In absence of any plausible explanation or contradictory material or decision to dislodge the aforesaid view, the contention of the assessee in the cross objection that in absence of a valid notice under section 143(2), which was not issued within the prescribed time limit for the purpose of making the assessment is a violation of mandatory provisions of law is acceptable, therefore, the reassessment impugned order passed under section 147 read with section 144B dated 30-3-2022, dehors a valid notice under section 143(2) is a nullity and liable to be quashed. Under the provisions of section 149 as applicable at the relevant time, the outer limitation for reopening AY 2008-09 expired on 31.03.2015. Thus, the notice issued under section 148 is admittedly time-barred. [Para 9.8]

■ The question then arises as to the point of time at which limitation is required to be examined under section 150(2). This issue is no longer res integra. The Jaipur Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Ramesh Chand Soni (HUF) v. ITO [2018] 89 taxmann.com 71 (Jaipur - Trib.) after considering the provisions of section 150(2) and the decision of the Hon'ble Kerala High Court in CIT v. Vaikundom Rubber Co. Ltd. [2001] 114 Taxman 378/249 ITR 19 (Kerala) held that where the Tribunal passes a finding or direction in second appeal, the relevant date for examining limitation under section 150(2) is not the date of the Tribunal order but the date of the order which was the subject matter of appeal before the Tribunal, namely the order of the CIT(A). The Tribunal categorically held that limitation under section 149 has to be reckoned up to the date of the appellate order which was under challenge before the Tribunal. [Para 9.9]

■

Respectfully following Ramesh Chand Soni (HUF) (supra), it is held that for the purposes of section 150(2), the relevant date in the present case is the date of the CIT(A)'s order for AY 2007-08, which was the subject matter of appeal before the Tribunal. [Para 9.10]

■

In the present case, the CIT(A) passed the order for AY 2007-08 on 02.02.2017. By that date, the limitation for reopening AY 2008-09 under section 149 had already expired on 31.03.2015. Therefore, on the date when the order which formed the subject matter of appeal before the Tribunal came into existence, the assessment for AY 2008-09 had already become time-barred. [Para 9.11]

■

Section 150(2) expressly provides that section 150(1) shall not apply in such circumstances. The legislative intent is clear. Section 150 cannot be utilised as a mechanism to revive a dead assessment or to reopen an assessment which had already become barred by limitation on the relevant date. The provision only saves those cases where the assessment was still alive and capable of being reopened on the date contemplated under section 150(2). Therefore, even assuming for the sake of argument that the Tribunal order contained a finding or direction, the Revenue would still be confronted with the statutory bar contained in section 150(2). Since the limitation for reopening AY 2008-09 had expired on 31.03.2015 and no time was available on 02.02.2017, the extended jurisdiction contemplated under section 150(1) stood expressly excluded by operation of section 150(2). [Para 9.12]

■

In view of the foregoing discussion, it is held that the Tribunal order for AY 2007-08 did not contain any finding or direction within the meaning of section 150(1). Consequently, invocation of section 150(1) by the AO for reopening AY 2008-09 was without jurisdiction. Even otherwise, the reopening is independently barred by section 150(2) since the limitation prescribed under section 149 had already expired on 31.03.2015 and no valid reassessment could have been made on the date of the CIT(A)'s order dated 02.02.2017, which was the order forming the subject matter of appeal before the Tribunal. Therefore, the notice issued under section 148 dated 19.03.2018 and the consequential reassessment framed pursuant thereto are void ab initio, barred by limitation and unsustainable in law. Accordingly, the notice issued under section 148 as well as the consequential reassessment order are quashed. Since the legal grounds challenging the assumption of jurisdiction itself have been allowed, the other grounds raised on merits become academic and do not call for adjudication. Hence, the legal grounds raised by the assessee are allowed. [Para 9.13]
