It is trite law that the issue of a notice under section 148 is a condition precedent to the validity of any assessment under section 147, and, therefore, if no such notice is issued or if the notice issued is invalid or vague or is not served in accordance with law, the assessment would be bad. Assessing authority had not followed the time-limit prescribed while notice under section 148 was issued on 1-10-1993. The assessee filed his return of income on 27-3-1995. The assessee had also pointed out to the ITO that in the notice dated 1-10-1993 which was issued under section 148, the assessee was not given the statutory minimum period of time for filing the return of income. The law that was in force at the relevant point of time cast a statutory duty on the assessing authority to give minimum 30 days’ time. The Assessing Officer cancelled the notice when it was pointed out to him and, therefore, notice under section 148 was issued on 28-3-1996. Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 enacted by the Parliament and received the assent of the President on 28-9-1996. The Act omitted the words ‘not being less than 30 days’ from section 148 with effect from 1-4-1989. When notice dated 1-10-1993 and the fresh notice dated 28-3-1996 were issued, the Finance Act (No. 2) was not in force. The assessing authority had, therefore, rightly applied the then existing law. [Para. 5]

Section 148 provides for initiation of assessment proceedings which starts with the issue of notice. Initiation of proceedings by the assessing authority on 1-10-1993 was not valid and consequently it was dropped. Fresh notice was, therefore, issued under section 148 in conformity with the time prescribed under section 148. When the Finance Act was passed a legally valid proceeding was in existence. Notice prescribed under section 148 for the purpose of initiating reassessment proceedings is a condition precedent to the validity of an assessment made. The assessing authority was only curing the defect of not following the time-limit when it was pointed out by the assessee and, therefore, notice was issued strictly on the basis of the then existing statutory provision. The mere fact that the time-limit prescribed under section 148(1) was taken away would not make an invalid notice valid so as to render the assessment order dated 26-3-1997 invalid in terms of section 153(2). The assessee could not be allowed to raise such a plea after having persuaded the assessing authority to withdraw notice dated 1-10-1993 pointing out that it was not in conformity with the statutory provision. The assessee could not be allowed to take advantage of the plea of limitation in terms of section 153(2) contending that the notice dated 1-10-1993 was valid due to the omission of time-limit vide the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 with effect from 1-4-1989. [Para 6]

On the strength of notice dated 28-3-1996, the return of income was filed and such return could not be ignored. [Para 7]

The mere fact that the time-limit has been taken away with effect from 1-4-1989 would not vitiate the proceedings validly initiated applying the then existing law. The object and purpose of the amendment is only to take away the time-limit for giving time for the assessee to file a return which the Legislature thought unnecessary. If the Legislature wanted to undo all that was done by the assessing authority applying the then existing law, it should have been specifically provided in the statute. In the absence of specific provision in the Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 invalidating those proceedings initiated by the ITO, it could not be said that the action taken by the ITO applying the then existing law was invalid. Once the notice issued under section 148 on 28-3-1996 was upheld the plea of limitation raised by the assessee under section 153(2) had to be rejected. The Finance Act (No. 2) of 1996 as amended would not validate an invalid notice which was issued under section 148(1). [Para 9]

During the survey, a printout of cash book of 'T' Ltd. for the period 1-4-2001 to 28-6-2001 was found. As per the said printout the Assessing Officer of the said company found that there was an excess payment of Rs. 11,44,658/- and accordingly, the addition of the said amount was made in the hands of the company for want of satisfactory explanation. The said addition was confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) vide his order dated 15-7-2009.

The Tribunal deleted said addition in the hands of 'T' Ltd. by holding that the said document belongs to 'T' proprietorship of the assessee HUF and the income if any arising from such transactions was held to be assessed in the hands of assessee instead of 'T' Ltd.

Based on the findings of the Tribunal in the case of 'T' Ltd. vide order dated 26-3-2010 the Assessing Officer initiated proceedings under section 147 and issued a notice under section 148 on 30-7-2010.

The assessee filed objections against the initiation of the proceedings under section 148 which was rejected by the Assessing Officer. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment under section 143(3) read with section 147 on 1-12-2011. The assessee challenged the action of the Assessing Officer including the validity of reopening before the Commissioner (Appeals) but could not succeed.

The assessee filed instant appeal submitting that the notice issued under section 148 on 30-7-2010 was barred by limitation as provided under section 149 read with section 150. It was further contended that the notice under section 148 was issued on 30-7-2010 and as per restrictions provided under section 150(2) the time limit prescribed under section 149 had already expired on 31-3-2009. Thus, reassessment proceedings were illegal and void.

HELD: The Assessing Officer proposed to reopen the assessment of the two assessment years i.e. 2001-02 & 2002-03 vide notice under section 148 dated 30-07-2010. Thus, it is apparent that the notice issued under section 148 for initiation of reassessment proceedings is beyond the limitation provided under section 149 as exists at the relevant point of time.

It is clear that no notice under section 148 shall be issued in any case after the expiry of 6 years, however, the limitation provided under section 149 is applicable in a situation where the Assessing Officer on its own on the basis of fresh material or information forms an opinion that the income assessable to tax has escaped assessment. Section 150 provides the assessment or reassessment in pursuant to an order of appeal, revision or reference and therefore, the limitation provided under section 149 for reopening of the assessment is not per se applicable when the reopening is based on the directions of the appellate or revisional authority or as per the directions of the Court.

Against such assessments, the assessee preferred appeals before the Commissioner (Appeals) mainly on the ground of unjustified issuance of notice under section 148 and denial of liability to be taxed in the status of oral trust, but the Commissioner (Appeals) remanded back the case to the Assessing Officer to re-examine the issues at length.

On appeal : HELD: Section 148 provides provisions for initiation of the reassessment proceedings. The initiation has to be made with the issue of a notice under section 148 on the assessee concerned. In the instant case from the facts alone, the notice for the assessment year 1981-82 was barred by limitation under section 149(1)(a)(ii ) and as such the assessment done in pursuance of time-barred notice was liable to be quashed. Mere acceptance, acquiescence and participation in such a proceeding where notice is served beyond the period of statutory limitation cannot remedy the defect for not issuing the notice within the period of limitation, and that does not confer authority on the Assessing Officer to assume jurisdiction. Service of notice within the statutory period is a sine qua non and is an indispensable requisite for the initiation of assessment proceeding under section 148 where income has escaped assessment. The Assessing Officer, in the instant case, having failed to comply with the statutory requirement, could not assume jurisdiction and as such, the assessment order for the assessment year 1981-82 in the assessment proceedings passed by him pursuant to such time-barred notice for the said assessment year could not be sustained and no appellate authority including the Tribunal could give authority or jurisdiction to the Assessing Officer in such cases, as no life could be given to a dead horse. Further, in all the notices of the assessment years 1982-83 to 1986-87 including the assessment year 1981-82, there was no mention as to the status of the assessee even though the department was aware of the status of the assesee as individual having already assessed the assessee in the said status, i.e., in the ‘individual’ capacity only on salary income.

If the department sought to assess him in the status of ‘oral trust’, the status should have been mentioned in the notice itself. Without mentioning the status in the notice itself, the said notice could not be taken advantage of to start proceedings under section 148 against the ‘oral trust’. Therefore, the assessment for all the years under consideration made pursuant to such invalid notice, must be quashed.

Whatever and howsoever noble may be the purpose of any trust (religious or evangelic), they cannot escape themselves from the responsibility of accountability before the revenue. Otherwise, the very purpose of the existence of the revenue to control the source of funds and expenditures of any person/assessee would be futile.

The primary onus to furnish the accounts to the Income-tax Department like all other law-abiding citizens irrespective of caste, creed, colour, community and religion heavily lies on the person/assessee. In the instant case the assessee as an individual might be receiving salary for the work done by him sincerely on propagation of Christianity but that did not mean that the department would close its eyes to the accounts maintained by him for the funds received from abroad and expenditures thereof.

In the result, the appeals were to be allowed.

The assessee sought that the reopening notice issued after expiry of six years from end of the relevant assessment year was barred by limitation as per provision of section 149 and thus needs to be quashed.

The Judge held that it was sufficient if the notice under section 147 had been signed and issued by authority within time period and therefore delay in receiving the same would not provide any ground to quash the entire proceedings.

On writ appeal : HELD: In the instant case, the respondent reopened the assessment of the appellant for the assessment year 2011-12, through notice dated 31-3-2018 under section 148. Admittedly, the limitation period of six years for reopening the assessment, came to an end on 31-3-2018. The main plank of contention of the appellant is that the notice under section 148 dated 31-3-2018 has been received by the appellant through e-mail only on 18-4-2018 i.e., after the expiry of six years from the end of the assessment year under consideration and hence, the same is clearly barred by limitation, whereas the department contended that mere signing of notice by the respondent on 31-3-2018 amounts to issuance of notice under section 149 and therefore, the same is within the limitation period. [Para 8]

It is clear from the provision of section 149 that the maximum time limit for issuance of notice under section 148 for reopening the assessment is six years from the end of the relevant assessment year. In the instant case, the relevant assessment year is 2011-12; the limitation of six years for initiation of reassessment proceedings expired on 31-3-2018; and notice under section 148 signed by the respondent was dated 31-3-2018. In such circumstances, this court is required to examine that such notice is in adherence to the compliance of section 149 for reassessment proceedings. [Para 9]

While the appellant stated that notice under section 148 was received by her through e-mail only on 18-4-2018 and hence, the same is clearly barred by limitation, it is stated on the side of the department that notice under section 148 was signed by the respondent on 31-3-2018 and the same was given to the process server to be served on the appellant on the same day, but it was returned on 6-4-2018 stating that there was no such person in the given address. After ascertaining her address from the last return of income filed by her, the said notice was sent to the appellant's registered mail ID, which was also served on 18-4-2018. Thus, according to the respondent, the reassessment proceedings commenced from the moment, when the notice was signed by the respondent on 31-3-2018 and hence, the same is well within limitation. [Para 10]

It is apparent that the issuance of notice under section 149 is complete only when the same is issued in the manner as prescribed under section 282 read with rule 127 prescribing the mode of service of notice under the Act. The signing of notice would not amount to issuance of notice as contemplated under section 149. In other words, the requirement of issuance of notice under section 149 is not mere signing of the notice under section 148, but is sent to the proper person within the end of the relevant assessment year. [Para 12]

Concededly, the notice dated 31-3-2018 issued by the respondent was served on the appellant through mail, only on 18-4-2018. Though the respondent produced the relevant pages of notice server book maintained by the department to show that the notice of the respondent dated 31-3-2018 under section 148 is within the limitation period, but the same only disclosed that the notice dated 31-3-2018 was returned on 6-4-2018.

In instant case, there is no document made available to prove that the notice under section 148 dated 31-3-2018 was sent for despatch to the appellant, within the end of the relevant assessment year i.e., 31-3-2018. Thus, it is crystal clear that the notice under section 148 for reopening the assessment was not sent to the appellant, within the time stipulated under section 149 and hence, the same vitiates the reassessment proceedings initiated under section 147. [Para 13]

In such view of the matter, the order of the Judge as well as the notice issued by the respondent are liable to be set aside. As a sequitur, the writ appeal stands allowed. [Para 14]

HELD: The case as put forth by the revenue was that the Commissioner (Appeals) had erred in quashing the order by holding that the re-assessment order passed under section 147 read with section 148 dated 30-12-2008 was invalid. The contention of the revenue was that the Tribunal's decision dated 11-7-2008 for block period from 1-4-1990 to 3-11-2000 had not become final and the High Court vide its order had granted liberty to the revenue to issue fresh notice if they wanted to do so and hence, the issue regarding validity of notice under section 148 pending with the subordinate judicial authorities was merged with the order of the High Court and as such fresh notice under section 148 dated 8-1-2008 issued by the Assessing Officer was in accordance with law. The Assessing Officer was, therefore, not liable to serve any demand notice upon the assessee pursuant to the reassessment order. The issue of the demand notice on 17-5-2002 was unnecessary and had to be ignored as superfluous. [Para 8]

The argument, that the assessee could not challenge the ‘nil’ demand order made by the Assessing Officer, could not be appreciated. Even if no demand is created, but the assessee feels aggrieved by the reassessment order, then it is open to it to file an appeal and challenge the correctness of the order. [Para 9]

However, the contention of the assessee, that the notice under section 148 had been issued beyond the period prescribed, had force and was required to be accepted. The reasons recorded in the notice showed that there was no allegation that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment because of the failure of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts. On the contrary, the assessee had disclosed the dividend income and interest income in the profit and loss account and was alleged to have claimed deduction thereon under section 80-I in respect of the ‘A’ unit. That was only a legal position taken by the assessee after furnishing all the material facts. It is open to the assessee to put forth a legal contention or claim after furnishing all the material particulars. The assessee cannot be shut out from doing so. He cannot be said to have furnished untrue particulars or incomplete particulars for having raised a legal plea. The inference from the facts is for the Assessing Officer to draw. The duty of the assessee, even under the proviso to section 147, extends only to the furnishing of all the material facts. It is not for him to advice the Assessing Officer as to what inference should be drawn therefrom. The assessee, having filed the basic facts, may raise his own inference therefrom and put forth the same to the Assessing Officer which the Assessing Officer may, in his wisdom, accept or reject. But rejection of the assessee’s inference from the material facts cannot be equated with furnishing of untrue or incomplete particulars necessary for the assessment. In that view of the matter, the assessment order passed on 28-3-2002 was invalid, the notice under section 148 having been issued beyond the period of limitation, prescribed under the proviso to section 147. It is now well-settled that the issue of a valid notice under section 148 is a condition precedent for the validity of the reassessment. Therefore, the assessee was right in saying that the limitation for rectification under section 154 should be reckoned from the date of the original assessment order passed on 29-11-1996. In that case, the 4 years period expired on 31-3-2001. The order under section 154 having been passed on 28-2-2003 was barred by limitation and, hence, invalid. [Para 10]

Detailed discussion is made in respect of applicable provisions on the issue in the present appeal as well as all the relevant judicial precedents have been discussed whereby the notice issued u/s.148 under the new regime was held to be barred by limitation and was thus, quashed resulting in the reassessment proceedings as well as the reassessment order as bad in law. There being no change in the relevant fact as in the present case, notice under section 148 is issued on 30-7-2022 which falls beyond the period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year. Following the above jurisprudence, it is held that notice for assessment year 2015-16, dated 30-7-2022 under section 148 is barred by limitation and hence, bad in law, liable to be quashed. Accordingly, the resultant reassessment proceeding as well as reassessment order are held to be bad in law, which are also quashed. [Para 7]

■

On perusal of the record, it is apparent that the impugned notice dated 14th March 2024 issued under section 148A(b), the order passed thereon under section 148A(d) dated 19 April 2024 and the consequent notice dated 19 April 2024 issued under section 148 are all issued by the Jurisdictional Assessing Officer and not by a Faceless Assessing Officer , as is required by the provisions of section 151A. [Para 3]

■

To give effect to the provisions of section 151A, the Central Government has issued a Notification dated 29 March 2022 whereby a faceless mechanism has been introduced. Thus, necessarily in resorting to a procedure under section 148A and the consequent notice to be issued under section 148 , the Assessing Officer is required to adhere to the provisions of section 151 read with the Notification. Thus, for a notice to be validly issued for reassessment under section 148, the Respondent-Revenue would need to be compliant with section 151A, which has been interpreted and analysed in detail by a Division Bench of this Court in the case of Hexaware Technologies Ltd. v. Asstt.CIT [2024] 162 taxmann.com 225/464 ITR 430. [Para 4]

■

There is yet another facet of the matter which also flows from the judgment rendered in the case of Hexaware Technologies Ltd.(supra), namely whether the notice issued under section 148 in the instant case is barred by limitation under section 149. In Hexaware Technologies Ltd.(supra), this was framed as issue No.2 and was empathetically answered by stating that the deadline for issuing a notice under section 148 must be considered by applying the provisions of section 149 at the time of issuance of the notice. Therefore, the version of section 149 as it stood at the time of issuance of the notice under section 148 must be examined. In the instant case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 19 April, 2014. By this time, the time limit for issuance of the notice as stipulated under section 149 had expired, i.e., three year period under section 149 expired on 31 March, 2021. Therefore, on this ground too, the re-assessment proceedings had called for interference. [Para 5]

In the instant case, the notice for re-opening, the assessment for returns for the Assessment Year 2017-18 had been issued more than after six years of the end of the relevant assessment year. The re-opening is purported to be on the basis of information available on the Revenue’s insight portal which is essentially based on the thesis of allegedly bogus artificial passing capital gains arising out of trading in the script of M/s. Frontline Business Solution Ltd. The six years period expired on 31 March, 2024 while the three year period expired on 31 March, 2021. In the result, on this ground too, the Petition deserves to be allowed. [Para 6]

■

In the present case, it is apparent that the Respondent-Revenue has not complied with the Scheme notified by the Central Government pursuant to section 151A(2) . The Scheme has also been tabled in Parliament and is in the character of subordinate legislation, which governs the conduct of proceedings under section 148A as well as section 148 . In view of the explicit declaration of the law in Hexaware Technologies Ltd.(supra), the grievance of the Petitioner-Assessee insofar as it relates to an invalid issuance of a notice is sustainable and consequently, the very manner in which the proceedings have been initiated, vitiates the proceedings. [Para 7]

■

Counsel for both the parties agree that the proceedings initiated under section 148 would not be sustainable in view of the judgment rendered in Hexaware. The assessee has also drawn attention to a recent decision of this Court in Nainraj Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. v. Dy.CIT [2024] 165 taxmann.com 674 whereby in similar circumstances, this Court has allowed the petition considering the provisions of section 151A. [Para 8]

■

Once notices under section 148 have been issued, the proceedings initiated through them have to be taken to their logical end. In other words, either assessments should be framed on the basis of those proceedings or the Assessing Officer may specifically drop the proceedings, may be on the ground that no sufficient material was available for holding that income liable to tax had escaped assessment. Even if an assessee does not comply with those notices by fling the income-tax returns, the remedy which is open to the revenue is not to issue fresh notices under section 148 but to issue notices under section 142(1) or to have completed the assessments under section 144. Thus, if the assessments have got barred by limitation, they cannot be revived by issuing fresh notices. In the instant case, this position was clear to the Assessing Officer and other officers of the department as could be gathered from a DO letter written by ITO to his IAC in which he had written that in this case, the assessment for the assessment year 1972-73 had been completed on a total income of Rs. 2,53,400 on 20-2-1985 as a result of which a demand was created. He had further written that the assessment was completed in pursuance of action initiated under section 148 subsequent to an action under section 148 got time- barred. He had further mentioned that this matter was discussed with the Commissioner and that according to the Commissioner the demand was unrealisable and assessment was likely to be annulled.

In the circumstances, it was to be held that since in the instant case valid Notices for the assessment years under consideration had been issued by The Assessing Officer on 9-10-1973 but he failed to complete the assessments within the time allowed under law, the assessments got barred by time for both the years. Further, the assessments dated 29-3-1984 for the assessment year 1971-72 and 20-2-1985 for the assessment year 1972-73 were invalid, because they were completed on the basis of fresh notices issued under section 148 dated 31-3-1980 and 17-3-1981, i.e., at a time when the original proceedings initiated under section 148 were still pending.

Hence, both the assessments framed by the Assessing Officer for those two assessment years had to be annulled.

■

In compliance with the directions issued by the Supreme Court in the case of Ashish Agarwal (supra), the Assessing Officer provided information and material to the assessee on 20-5-2022. The assessee was granted two weeks’ time to respond to the said notice i.e. by 2-6-2022. [Para 10]

■

According to section 149, period of six years from the end of relevant assessment year i.e. from 2013-14, got expired on 31-3-2020 and further time period was extended by the Taxation and Other Law Act, 2020 (TOLA) till 30-6-2021. [Para 10.1]

■

The next round of litigation arose before the Supreme Court, and in the landmark judgment of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70 (SC), it was held that notices issued under the erstwhile section 148 for assessment years 2013-14 and 2014-15 shall be deemed to be valid, provided they fall within the permissible time frame (surviving period) as preserved under the directions laid down in the said judgment. The Supreme Court, in the case of Rajeev Bansal, has elaborated upon the concept of the ‘surviving period’ for determining the validity of notices issued under section 148 after the pronouncement of the judgment in Union of India v. Ashish Aggarwal (supra). This interpretation is specifically discussed in the said judgment. The period from the date of the issuance of the erstwhile notice till 4-5-2022, the date on which the Supreme Court had rendered the decision in Ashish Agarwal (supra) is required to be excluded. Additionally, the time provided till the date of providing the material, which should have accompanied a notice under section 148A(b), as well as the time available to the assessee to respond to the said notice was also required to be excluded. The ‘surviving period’ is required to be computed and separately added to determine the validity of the notice issued under section 148. The surviving period is calculated by taking into account the number of days between the original date of issuance of the deemed notice under section 148 and 30-6-2021, as clarified in judicial pronouncements following the judgment in Ashish Agarwal and considering the entire facts of the case and the law laid down by the Apex court in the case of UOI v Rajeev Bansal (supra), it is opined that in the instant case the surviving period was of twenty four days and the revised timeline for issue of notice under section 148 (under the new regime) expired on 26-6-2022 and the notice issued in the instant case on 25-7-2022, is clearly barred by limitation and the impugned reassessment proceedings dated 23-5-2023, passed under section 147 read with section 144 (with 144B), is not legally valid and the same is quashed. [Para 10.2]

■

The arguments of the revenue revolved around the decision of the Apex court in the case of Union of India v. Ashis Agarwal (supra), and he has never concentrated on the next round of litigation in the case of Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal (supra) where it was held that notices issued under the erstwhile section 148 for assessment year 2013-14 and 2014-15, shall be deemed to be valid, provided they fall within the permissible time frame (surviving period) as preserved under the directions laid down in the said judgment (specially paragraph 108 of the said decision (already discussed above). The remaining case laws relied upon by the revenue are factually different and does not relate to the issue at hand. [Para 11]

■

Since the appeal of the assessee is allowed on the legal issue, the grounds of appeal on merits do not require any adjudication (more so considering the fact that the assessee has already withdrawn the grounds of appeal on merits in course of hearing). [Para 12]

The Assessing Officer was given 30 days from the date of judgment in Ashish Agarwal (supra), i.e. from 4-5-2022 to provide respective assessees, information and material relied upon, for reply by the assessee thereon. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer complied with this direction by issuing the letter of proceedings (show cause notice) on 26-5-2022. Similarly, the Court provided two weeks to the assessees to reply to the aforesaid show cause notices as noted in para 107 of Rajeev Bansal (supra). The Court while fixing the time limit of two weeks for the assessee to respond to the show cause notice, nowhere, in both the judgments of Ashish Agarwal and Rajeev Bansal (supra) considered any extension of time limit which can be granted by the Assessing Officer at the instance of the assessee. [Para 10]

■

By taking the date of 26-5-2022 from the show cause notice in the instant case, period of two weeks ended on 9-6-2022 for the assessee to furnish its reply. On this very date, when time limit of two weeks expires, assessee moved an application before the Assessing Officer, seeking adjournment for 2 to 3 weeks. The Assessing Officer accepted the same and granted adjournment on the same date, asking the assessee to submit the reply by 24-6-2022. Assessee did not comply with the extended time limit and furnished its response on 28-6-2022. On these given set of facts, one has to bear in mind the legal fiction within which one has to operate and the same has to be construed strictly. Since assessee did not file its response to the show cause notice within the permissible two weeks expiring on 9-6-2022, except for moving an application seeking adjournment, the clock started ticking for the revenue on expiry of permissible two weeks, i.e. on 9-6-2022. Surviving time period calculated by the assessee in the above extracted table is one day whereas according to the Commissioner (Departmental Representative), it is zero. The Assessing Officer has issued the impugned notice under section 148 on 28-7-2022 which does not meet the criteria of ''surviving time limit'' laid down by the Supreme Court, whether one or zero day is considered. [Para 10.1]

■

In view of above stated exhaustive deliberation, both on facts and law including the applicable jurisprudence, it is held that notice for assessment year 2014-15 issued on 28-7-2022 under section 148 of the new regime is barred by limitation and hence bad in law, liable to be quashed, resulting in impugned reassessment proceedings as well as the impugned reassessment order bad in law. Accordingly, ground nos. 1 and 2 raised by the revenue are dismissed. Resultantly, grounds raised on the merits of the case are rendered academic and hence not adjudicated upon. [Para 10.2]

The assessee, an individual, filed return of income for AY 2015-16 on 30-06-2016 declaring income of about Rs. 7 lakhs. The CIT(A)/NFAC upheld the re-assessment proceedings as well addition on merit. HEADNOTE: I. Section  149,  read with sections  147  and  148, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and section  3  of the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 -  Income escaping assessment  -  Time limit for issuance of notice (Illustrations)  - Assessment year  2015-16  - Assessee filed its return of income - Based on a departmental enquiry alleging coordinated and premeditated trades in illiquid BSE stock options leading to non-genuine profit/loss, reasons to believe were recorded and a notice under old regime Section 148 was issued on 21-6-2021 - Since this notice was issued under erstwhile regime of re-assessment as provided under section 148 read with section 147 which had undergone total revamp by Finance Act 2021, Assessing Officer passed an order under section 148A(d), dated 30-7-2022 recommending reopening of case under section 148 - Subsequently, a notice under section 148 was issued on 30-7-2022 - Whether since notice under section 148 was issued under new regime on 30-07 - 2022, which fell beyond period of six years from end of relevant assessment year 2015-16, such notice was barred by limitation and hence, bad in law, liable to be quashed, and consequently, resultant reassessment proceeding as well as reassessment order were also bad in law - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was a non-resident who filed his revised return of income.

On appeal to High Court:

The facts as available to the Assessing Officer at the time of reopening of the assessment have only to be seen for justifying or otherwise of the reopening of the assessment. The information should have direct nexus with the escapement of income. The information available should be relevant and belief of the officer should be rational. The Court can only examine as to whether the process of formation of belief is in accordance with law. Adequacy of material is not relevant. It is also not relevant as to whether in the ultimate analysis, same amount of addition was made. Further, the belief at the time of reassessment of the assessment is only prima facie and not final. Similarly, the amount of escaped amount is also tentative and not final. There is always possibility of the quantum of escaped income varying in final analysis on the basis of particulars given to the assessee for explaining the case. It is possible that the assessee may be able to explain the entire amount or part of amount or the Assessing Officer may discover greater amount of concealed income. The, subsequent, discovery of facts cannot undo the belief judiciously formed by the Assessing Officer on the basis of material available at that point of time. [Para 11]

Thus, merely because the Assessing Officer did not make any addition on account of disallowability of interest, it could not be said that reopening of the assessments were invalid because on the basis of material available at the time of reopening of the assessments/recording the reasons, the Assessing Officer was justified in reopening the assessments. Thus, this ground of the assessee was rejected. [Para 12]

However, since in the instant case, the notices under section 143(2) were issued for all the years on 12-9-2001, i.e., after the expiry of 12 months from the date of issuance of notice under section 148, such issuance of notice was beyond statutory limit and, therefore, reassessments framed in pursuance to these notices were barred by limitation. The reassessments for all the years were, therefore, to be cancelled. [Para 13]

From the perusal of the findings of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC), it is evident that the Supreme Court directed that while computing the time limit for issuance of notice under section 148, the time during which the show cause notice was stayed till the supply of relevant information or material by the Assessing Officer and further period of two weeks allowed to the assessee to respond to the show cause notice should be excluded. [Para 9]

■

Thus, the Supreme Court held that the surviving time under the Act read with the TOLA will be available to the revenue to complete the remaining proceedings in furtherance of the deemed notice, including issuance of a reassessment notice under section 148 under the new regime. [Para 10]

■

Therefore, the surviving/balance time limit can be calculated by computing the number of days between the date of issuance of the deemed notice and 30-6-2021. In the instant case, in order to compute the surviving/balance time as per the decision of the Supreme Court, it is relevant to note the various dates. [Para 11]

■

Therefore, computing the surviving/balance time limit, as per the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajeev Bansal (supra), it is found that the revenue had 58 days to issue notice under section 148 of the new regime in the instant case, i.e. till 20-7-2022, after issuance of the show cause notice issued under section 148A(b) on 23-5-2022. However, undisputedly, in the instant case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 27-7-2022, i.e., after the surviving/balance time period as per the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajeev Bansal (supra). [Para 12]

■

Therefore, in the light of the decision of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1(SC)/ 444 ITR 1 (SC), it is viewed that the notice issued under section 148 on 27-7-2022 is barred by the limitation period specified under section 149. Accordingly, it is viewed that the notice issued under section 148 on 27-7-2022 for the assessment year 2013-14 is void ab initio and bad in law. Therefore, the same is quashed. Consequently, the entire reassessment proceedings and the assessment order passed under section 147 read with section 144 for the assessment year 2013-14 is also quashed. [Para 13]

■

Even in the assessment year 2014-15, the notice under section 148 under the new regime was issued on 27-07-2022, which is beyond the surviving/balance time period as per the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajeev Bansal (supra). Accordingly, findings/conclusions as rendered in assessee's appeal for the assessment year 2013-14 shall apply mutatis mutandis to the appeal for the assessment year 2014-15. Accordingly, the notice issued under section 148 on 27-07-2022 for the assessment year 2014-15 is void ab initio and bad in law. Therefore, the same is quashed. Consequently, the entire reassessment proceedings and the assessment order passed under section 147 read with section 144 for the assessment year 2014-15 is also quashed. [Para 15]

In the instant appeal, the assessee raised cross objection and submitted that the notice under section 148 was issued on 18-7-2022, however, the time limit available as per erstwhile section 149 expired on 31-3-2022 thus was beyond the period of limitation and provisions of TOLA werre not applicable. It was, thus, prayed by the assessee that the notices issued in the instant case for assessment year 2015-16 under section 148 being after 1-4-2021, therefore, the same deserved to be dropped and consequently the reassessment order be quashed.

The assessee was HUF and proprietor of 'T' Ltd. The assessee filed its return of income declaring certain taxable income on 31-3-2003 which was processed under section 143(1). Subsequently the case was reopened under section 147/148 and assessment was completed under section 143(3) read with section 147.

A survey under section 133A was carried out in the business premises of 'T' Ltd. in which the Karta of the assessee HUF was a director. During the survey, a printout of cash book of 'T' Ltd. for the period 1-4-2001 to 28-6-2001 was found. As per the said printout the Assessing Officer of the said company found that there was an excess payment of Rs. 11,44,658/- and accordingly, the addition of the said amount was made in the hands of the company for want of satisfactory explanation. The said addition was confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) vide his order dated 15-7-2009.

The Tribunal deleted said addition in the hands of 'T' Ltd. by holding that the said document belongs to 'T' proprietorship of the assessee HUF and the income if any arising from such transactions was held to be assessed in the hands of assessee instead of 'T' Ltd.

Based on the findings of the Tribunal in the case of 'T' Ltd. vide order dated 26-3-2010 the Assessing Officer initiated proceedings under section 147 and issued a notice under section 148 on 30-7-2010.

The assessee filed objections against the initiation of the proceedings under section 148 which was rejected by the Assessing Officer. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment under section 143(3) read with section 147 on 1-12-2011. The assessee challenged the action of the Assessing Officer including the validity of reopening before the Commissioner (Appeals) but could not succeed.

The assessee filed instant appeal submitting that the notice issued under section 148 on 30-7-2010 was barred by limitation as provided under section 149 read with section 150. It was further contended that the notice under section 148 was issued on 30-7-2010 and as per restrictions provided under section 150(2) the time limit prescribed under section 149 had already expired on 31-3-2009. Thus, reassessment proceedings were illegal and void.
Reassessment under section 148 invalid as notice issued after prescribed limitation date :HC

As regards the validity of notice issued under section 148, the first condition laid down in section 148(1) for issuance of notice is that it should be issued before making assessment, re-assessment and re-computation of income. In the instant case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 25-10-1988 and the assessment was completed on 22-8-1990. Thus, the notice issued under section 148 was valid as it was issued before the assessment was made. Then, according to the provisions envisaged and limitation laid down in section 149(1), no notice under section 148 would be issued in cases falling under clause (a) of section 147 for the relevant assessment year if eight years had elapsed from the end of that year. In the instant case, the relevant assessment year was 1987-88 and 8 years from the end of that year would elapse in 1996. But the notice under section 148 was already issued on 25-10-1988 and was, therefore, well within the prescribed time limit of eight years, i.e., before 31-3-1990. The assessee’s contention that the notice under section 148 issued prior to 31-3-1990 could not take the right of the assessee to file the return under section 139(4) was also not tenable as, in the instant case, no return was furnished before the issuance of notice under section 148. Moreover, there was no provision in the Act to invalidate the notice under section 148 by furnishing of return after the issue of such notice.

The notice issued under section 148 was in the nature of notice under section 139(2) and it was issued as no return was filed by the assessee and the Assessing Officer had reason to believe that income had escaped assessment as per section 147(a) of the Act. The notice under section 148 was issued on 25-10-1988 and the return of income was filed by the assessee on 30-3-1989. As the return was filed after the issue of notice under section 148, it was certainly a return submitted in response to the notice under section 148. Although the return was filed before 31-3-1990 and it was a belated return, it could not be treated as a return furnished under section 139(4), as it was not filed voluntarily by the assessee. There was no clash between the provisions of sections 139(1) and 139(4) on the one hand and section 139(2), on the other. A person who has not furnished a return under section 139(1) and (2) is authorised to file the return under section 139(4). In the instant case, as the assessee has furnished the return in response to a notice under section 148 which was treated as a notice under section 139(2), the assessee was not entitled to furnish a return under section 139(4). Therefore, the return furnished by the assessee was to be treated as a return filed under section 139(2)/section 148 and not a return under section 139(4). The assessee had contended that the assessment was barred by limitation, as the return was filed on 30-3-1989 and the assessment should have been completed by 31-3-1990 while it was completed on 22-8-1990. This contention of the assessee was based on the argument that the return furnished on 30-3-1989 should be treated as a return under section 139(4). As the latter contention of the assessee was rejected and the return furnished on 30-3-1989 was treated as a return under section 148/139(2), the former contention was also not tenable and could not be accepted under any provisions of law. As the assessment was re-opened under section 147(a), provisions of section 153(2)(a) were applicable. According to these provisions, no assessment is to be made after the expiry of four years from the end of the assessment year in which the notice under section 148 was served. In the instant case, as the notice under section 148 was served on 26-10-1988, the limitation for assessment expired on 31-3-1993, i.e., four years from the end of assessment year 1988-89. In view of the foregoing, it was to be held that the notice issued under section 148 was a valid notice, the return furnished in compliance with the notice under section 148 was to be treated as a return furnished under section 139(2) and the assessment made was within limitation and, therefore, was a valid assessment.

As regards the point of commencement of limitation, a plain reading of the provisions contained in clause (i) of sub-section (1)(a) of section 149 conveys the message that the relative adjective ‘that’ used in that provision has reference to the words ‘assessment year’ used in the opening lines of sub-clause (i). It suggests that the period of eight years is to commence from the end of the relevant assessment year. Nowhere in section 149(1)(a)(i ) has the term ‘financial year’ been used The position has been made clear by the use of the same term ‘assessment year’ in both sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 151. It is, thus, abundantly clear that the prescribed period of eight years or 16 years, as the case may be, is to be reckoned from the end of the relevant assessment year and not the financial year.

As regards the question of issue and service of notice, for the purposes of application of the provisions of section 149, a notice under section 148 should be issued and served within the time prescribed by section 149. For proper administration of sections 149 and 153 and to satisfy the legislative intention in enacting those provisions, the words `issued’ and ‘served’ used in sections 149 and 153, respectively, should be regarded and interpreted as inter-changeable. It is difficult to accept that the Legislature would have intended that the issuance of notice under section 148 within the period of limitation prescribed by section 149 without there being the effective service of such notice as required by section 153 within the prescribed period, would satisfy the pre-condition for making a valid assessment as per the provisions of section 147 read with sections 149 and 153. Such an interpretation of the word ‘issued’ used in section 149 would be too oppressive for the assessees. For the decision to issue notice under section 148 is taken by the ITO behind the back of an assessee as there is no requirement of law to hear the assessee before the issue of a notice under section 148 to him If the meaning of the word ‘served’ as used in section 153 is not considered to be hidden in the meaning of the word ‘issued’ used in section 149 and vice versa, it may lead to unwanted consequences. For, before the end of eight or sixteen years, as the case may be, from the relevant assessment year, an ITO may issue a notice under section 148 and allow it to be kept in his file for an indefinite period, for the period of limitation prescribed by section 153 for completing the assessment is to commence from the date of service of the notice under section 148 and not before. The ITO may, thus, keep the sword of democles, hanging on the head of an assessee for an indefinite period, Such could not be the intention of the Legislature in enacting the provisions of sections 149 and 153. Both the sections prescribe limitation for an integrated purpose. They should, therefore, be read together in order to meet that purpose.

It therefore, logically follows that the word issued’ used in section 149 is required to carry the meaning of the expression ‘issued and served’ within the prescribed period of limitation.

As regards the validity of notice under section 148, the relevant assessment year in this appeal was 1975-76 which came to an end on 31-3-1976. The starting point of limitation under section 149(1)(c) was 1-4-1976 and the eighth year from that date expired on 31-3-1984. Since the notice under section 148, according to the assessee himself, was served on him by affixation on 30-3-1984, the notice issued and the assessment proceedings initiated on the basis of such notice were not hit by the provisions of section 149. Since the service of the notice under section 148 on 30-3-1984 was proved, the subsequent service on 3-4-1984 of another notice of the same type would not adversely affect the validity of the notice served on 30-3-1984. Therefore, the notice issued in this case under section 148 was quite valid and not hit by the provisions of section 149.

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer issued the original notice under section 148, for assessment year 2015-16 and consequent to the directions given by the Supreme Court in the case of Ashish Agrawal (supra), the said notice was deemed as notice issued under section 148A. The Assessing Officer after passing the order under section 148A(d) issued the notice under section 148. The contention of the assessee is that the said notice is barred by limitation as per the first proviso to the unamended provisions of section 149(1). [Para 6]

A combined reading of the observations of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC) and the findings of Delhi High Court in the case of IBIBO Group (P.) Ltd. v. ACIT [W.P. 17639 of 2022, dated 13-12-2024] makes it clear that the test for checking the validity of notices issued under section 148 under new regime for assessment years 2021-22 or prior years is whether the period of six years has expired at the time of issue of such notice and in that case the notice under section 148 becomes invalid. These observations also makes it clear that the time limit of ten years as per the amended provisions of section 149(1)(b) can be applied only prospectively. In assessee''s case when this test is applied for assessment year 2015-16, the period of six years has expired on 31-3-2022 and therefore the notice dated 28-7-2022 under section 148 for assessment year 2015-16 is invalid since it is barred by limitation. Accordingly the assessment completed under section 147 is liable to be quashed. [Para 7]

Under the Surtax Act the limitation is to be spelt out from service of the notice rather than issuance of the same. Since the impugned notice was served on the assessee after the limitation date, it was not valid, and the consequential reassessment should be cancelled.

A notice for reassessment for the relevant assessment year was served on the assessee under section 148 alleging escapement of income, within the meaning of section 147, on 27-1-1967. The assessee denied the allegations, and without prejudice to his rights, filed a return on the basis of the original return. No action was taken until 1-2-1971 when another notice dated 1-2-1971 was issued under section 139 requiring the assessee to produce books of accounts and documents. The assessee filed the writ petition contended that as the impugned notice under section 148 was issued in exercise of powers under section 147(1)(b), the notice under section 139 was issued beyond the prescribed period of limitation and, and such, no proceeding could be initiated or continued by virtue of the said impugned notice. The Single Judge upheld the assessee's contention and quashed the reassessment proceedings.

On appeal:

No return had been filed by the assessee as per the provisions of the Act and the so-called return filed beyond the time-limit prescribed under section 139(4) on 16-2-2000 was an invalid and non est return in the eyes of law. The proceedings to fasten liability on the assessee-company was commenced by the department for the assessment year 1997-98 by issue of a notice under section 142(1) dated 24-8-1998 for the first time. Prior to it, no notice or proceeding had started. Subsequently, several notices had been issued by the department under section 142(1) but all these notices were apparently issued after the end of the assessment year, i.e., 31-3-1998. As per the provisions of section 147, the income would be treated as escaped assessment at the end of the assessment year where no return had been filed. In the instant case, in the absence of return, the provisions were to tax income that escaped assessment and not to tax income which was not assessed as on 1-4-1998. Thus, the income could be assessed only by issuance of notice under section 148 and in the instant case, no such notice had been issued by the department under section 148. Mere issuance of notice under section 142(1) after the end of the assessment year in the absence of voluntary return by the assessee could not give rise to valid proceedings under the Act.

Explanation 2(a ) to section 147 includes non-filing of return in the expression ‘escaped assessment’. The scope of Explanation 2(a) has to be restricted to the failure of the assessee to file a return suo motu or a voluntary return under section 139(1) or section 139(4) within the prescribed time-limit and not to cases where a notice under section 142(1) requiring the assessee to file return has already been issued. Otherwise even on the first day of the assessment year itself the Assessing Officer can issue notice under section 148 when the process of assessment itself has not yet come into being. It would thus be too wide a proposition to be accepted. As regards the outer limit of issuing notice under section 142(1)(i), there is apparently no time-limit prescribed, but other provisions give an impression that the outer limit is one year from the end of the assessment year. Otherwise, the assessee’s failure to submit the return under section 142(1) would not entitle him to file the return thereafter. Once that time-limit is over and the assessee has not filed any return, it becomes a case of income escaping assessment and for that, issuance of notice under section 148 is a must. As per section 153, time-limit for completing assessment is two years from the end of the assessment year in which it was first assessable. This limit comes into play when the proceedings for assessment have been initiated by filing a return suo motu under section 139(1) or by issuance of a valid notice under section 142(1). Clause (i) of sub-section (1) of section 142 was amended by Finance Act, 1990, so that if a person fails to furnish a return of income by the due date mentioned in section 139(1), a notice calling upon him to file the return can be sent to him within the relevant assessment year itself. If no such initiation was taken within the assessment year, it would be a case of escaped assessment within the meaning of Explanation 2 to section 147 and, therefore, a notice under section 148 would be a must to empower the Assessing Officer to proceed with the assessment.

In the instant case, the assessee had not filed the return suo motu within a time prescribed under section 139(1), the revenue had not issued any notice under section 142(1) before the end of the assessment year and return furnished by the assessee under section 139(4) on 16-2-2000 had been filed beyond the time-limit prescribed under section 139(4) and was invalid return. Therefore, a notice under section 148 had to be issued when an assessment, reassessment or recomputation was to be made under section 147 to tax income which had escaped assessment. This was a case of assessment without there being an earlier assessment. Therefore, the assessment completed without issuing notice under section 148 was invalid and bad in law.

Accordingly, the assessment order stood annulled.

While confirming the order of the Commissioner (Appeals), the Tribunal observed that genuineness of investments could only be considered in the relevant assessment year 1988-89, because the same fell outside the purview of accounting period relevant to the assessment year 1989-90. But nowhere the Tribunal had given any direction that the Assessing Officer should reopen the assessment for the relevant assessment year. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was wrong in holding that the assessment was reopened as per the directions of the Tribunal. As per provisions of clause (b ) of section 149(1), the assessment could have been reopened within a period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year, as the income escaping assessment was more than Rs. 1 lakh. The relevant assessment year ended on 31-3-1989. Therefore, the assessment could have been reopened on or before 31-3-1995. But in the instant case, notice under section 148 was issued on 14-2-2001 and was served upon the assessee on 21-2-2001. Such notice was beyond time and was barred by period of limitation. Therefore, the assessment completed by the Assessing Officer by issue of notice under section 148 was without jurisdiction and void ab initio. Even though the assessment year involved was 1988-89 and amended provisions came into being only with effect from 1-4-1989, i.e., assessment year 1989-90, the law applicable would be one, as it existed on the date of issue of notice. In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and legal position, the assessment order was to be quashed as bad in law and resultant order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was also to be quashed.

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.

According to him, the service of a notice though extremely relevant, yet is a matter of procedure so that its absence or a defect therein would not invalidate the ensuing proceedings, but only make them irregular, i.e., where there is a valid assumption of jurisdiction to assess. Accordingly, the Accountant Member upheld the validity of reassessment proceedings on the basis of notice issued as on 28-3-2005. The Judicial Member, however, accepted the assessee's contention that the issuance of notice on 29-6-2005 was a fresh notice. He thus, set aside the reassessment proceedings holding that said notice was issued beyond the prescribed time-limit. In view of difference of opinion between the Members of the Tribunal, the matter was referred to the Third Member.

HELD (AS PER THIRD MEMBER)

The issue before the Division Bench as could be seen from the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) itself is narrowed down as to the validity of the assessment made by the Assessing Officer under sections 143(3) and 147 in the light of the initiation of reassessment proceedings by issuance of notice. The provisions of sections 147 to 151 are specific provisions which enable the department to reassess any income that has escaped assessment. These provisions underwent significant changes with effect from 1-4-1989. In the light of these changes, each and every initiation of assessment proceedings made on or after 1-4-1989 must be governed by the amended provisions as held by the decision of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Rakesh Aggarwal v. Asstt. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 496 /[1996] 87 Taxman 306 . Under section 148(1), before making an assessment, reassessment and computation under section 147, the Assessing Officer is required to serve on the assessee a notice requiring him to furnish a return of income. Under section 148(2), the Assessing Officer, before issuing any notice under section 148(I), is required to record his reasons for doing so. The provisions relating to the time-limit for issuance of notice are set out in section 149. [Para 15]

A notice issued within the period prescribed under section 149, even though served thereafter, gives a perfectly valid initiation.

■

A plain reading of the ruling of the Bombay High Court in the case of Godrej Industries Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2024] 160 taxmann.com 13 (Bombay) would make it clear that the validity of a notice under section 148 must be judged on the basis of the law as existing on the date of which the notice is issued. In the instant case, the deadline for issuance of notices for assessment year 2014-15 had expired on 31-3-2021. Consequently, and evidently, the notice issued in the instant case was hopelessly barred by limitation. Therefore, the notice issued indeed deserves to be quashed as being barred by limitation. VALIDITY OF NOTICE UNDER SECTION 148 ISSUED DURING PENDENCY OF REASSESSMENT PROCEEDINGS :

In CIT v. Ram Kishan Leela [2007] 207 CTR (Raj.) 463, the Rajasthan High Court considered similar issue and held that second notice issued during the pendency of the reassessment proceedings cannot be treated to be legally justified.

In view of the said decision and on the facts and circumstances of the case, it was to be held that the reopening of the assessment by the second notice could not be justified and the assessment completed on the basis of such illegal notice did not have legal legs to stand on. The assessment was, therefore, liable to be quashed on this ground.

VALIDITY OF NOTICE UNDER SECTION 148 ISSUED BEYOND PERIOD OF 4 YEARS FROM RELEVANT ASSESSMENT YEAR :

Subsequent notice under section 148 was issued on 31-3-2003. The assessment pertained to the assessment year 1996-97. Notice issued on 31-3-2003 was, therefore, after the expiry of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year as the fourth year had expired on 31-3-2001.

In view of the proviso to section 147, no action can be taken for reassessment after the expiry of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year, unless any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for such assessment year by reason of the failure on the part of the assessee to make a return under section 139 or in response to a notice issued under sub-section (1) of section 142 or section 148 or to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment, for that assessment year.

In the instant case, the assessee had disclosed all the facts relating to deduction under section 80HHC during the original assessment and the Assessing Officer had preferred to accept her claim. Therefore, it could not be said that there was any failure on the part of the assessee in disclosing material facts. Since the instant case was covered by the proviso to section 147, both the conditions, viz., firstly, the Assessing Officer must have reason to believe that income, profit or gains chargeable to income-tax have escaped assessment, and secondly, he must also have reason to believe that such escapement has occurred by reason of either omission or failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully or truly all material facts necessary for his assessment of that year, were required to be satisfied. As the assessee had disclosed the material facts, the second condition was not satisfied and, therefore, it could be said that the reassessment had been made only on the basis of change of opinion.

Thus, the reassessment made after the expiry of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year could not be justified in law because the department had not been able to bring out any material to show that there was any failure on the part of the assessee to disclose material facts truly and fully to the Assessing Officer during the assessment proceedings. Thus, in view of the proviso to section 147, the reopening of the assessment could not be justified and, consequently, the notice issued under section 148 was to be held to be invalid. The entire reassessment proceedings were, therefore, null and void and on this basis, the reassessment order was liable to be quashed. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be set aside and the reassessment was to be quashed.

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.

The Settlement Commission directed the Assessing Officer having jurisdiction in the matter to take action in accordance with law. Even if the direction issued by the Settlement Commission was the reason which impelled the Assessing Officer to issue notice under section 148, he could have recorded that reason either in the notice issued to the assessee, or even in the file maintained by him in his office. Though a counter-affidavit had been filed on behalf of the Revenue, there was no averment in the counter-affidavit that reasons had been separately recorded in the file. On this short ground alone the notice issued under section 148, must be quashed.

There was yet another reason why the notice and the order passed consequent thereto, could not be upheld. It was not disputed that so far as the assessment year 1981-82 was concerned, the period of limitation prescribed was ten years for the issuance of notice under section 148. The said period, therefore, expired on 31-3-1992. The notice was, therefore, ex-facie barred by limitation. The Revenue, however, relied upon section 150 and submitted that in view of the direction issued by the Settlement Commission, the question of limitation could not stand in the way of the Assessing Officer issuing a notice under section 148. No doubt the submission was misconceived.

Resort to sub-section (1) of section 150 can be taken only in cases where it becomes necessary to make assessment or reassessment or recomputation in consequence of, or to give effect to, any finding or direction pursuant to an appellate order passed by the appellate authority or pursuant any order in reference or revision or by a court in any proceeding under any other law.

Obviously, the appeal, reference or revision or any other proceeding before a court must relate to the assessee in question, and not any direction or assessment made in appeal, reference or revision in the case of any other assessee, or in a proceeding in which the assessee in question is not a party. The assessee before the Settlement Commission was different and distinct from the assessee in the instant case. Certain findings were arrived at by the Settlement Commission and that gave rise to a belief in the mind of the Settlement Commission that the petitioner and others might have earned income which had escaped assessment. It was, therefore, observed that necessary action be taken in accordance with law. Such an order could not be construed to be an order passed under this Act by way of appeal, reference or revision so as to necessitate reassessment for the assessment year 1981-82. Sub-section (2) of section 150 makes it quite clear that the provisions of sub-section (1) shall not apply in any case if the order which was the subject-matter of the appeal, reference or revision, could not have been made by reason of any other provision limiting the time with in which any action for assessment, reassessment or recomputation may be taken.

It, therefore, follows that if the original order which was the subject-matter of the appeal, reference or revision could not have been passed, when it was purported to have been passed by reason of its being barred by limitation, the same cannot be revived under sub-section (1) of section 150. In the instant case, that question did not arise, because there was no assessment order for the assessment year 1981-82, which had been taken in appeal, reference or revision before any authority under the Act. The order of the Settlement Commission could have only justified issuance of the notice, if that was the reason for issuance of the notice, but beyond that it could not operate to revive a proceeding which was barred by limitation.

In these circumstances, the notice issued under section 148 and the assessment made pursant thereto was wholly without juriseiction being barred by limitation. The notice issued under section 148 was bad for non-compliance with the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 148, as the Assessing Officer failed to record his reasons while issuing the said notice.

The instant petition was accordingly allowed and the impugned notice issued under section 148 was quashed.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The petitioner/assessee by way of instant petition has challenged the impugned section 148 Notice as in force till 31-3-2021, impugned order dated 30-7-2022 passed under section 148-A(d) and fresh impugned section 148 Notice dated 30-7-2022 as in force with effect from 1-4-2021.

■

The impugned notice dated 31-3-2021 was served on the petitioner on 12-4-2021, i.e., after the new reassessment regime under the Finance Act, 2021 came into effect. For assessment year 2015–16, the standard 4-year limitation under section 149(1)(a) (old law) had already expired on 31-3-2020. However, under the extended 6-year period provided in the proviso to section 147 (as it then stood), the limitation to issue such notice continued until 31-3-2022. Hence, the notice dated 31-3-2021 was within time under the old regime.

■

Subsequently, pursuant to the Supreme Court’s decision in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183/444 ITR 1 (SC), the impugned notice dated 31-3-2021 was deemed to be a show-cause notice under section 148A(b) of the new regime. The Assessing Officer accordingly proceeded to pass an order under section 148A(d) on 30-7-2022, and issued a fresh notice under amended section 148 on the same date.

■

In the meantime, the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 (TOLA) extended time limits for various tax actions, including issuance of notices and obtaining approvals under section 151, for the period between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021, due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

■

With effect from 1-4-2021, sections 147 to 151 of the Income-tax Act were amended. The first proviso to section 149(1), as amended, barred issuance of reassessment notices for assessment years beginning on or before 1-4-2021 if such notices were already time-barred under the old regime. However, since the notice dated 31-3-2021 was issued within the extended time permitted under the old law, the bar under the first proviso to section 149(1) did not apply.

■

Thus, the petitioner’s challenge was centered around whether the reassessment proceedings, initiated by the notice dated 31.03.2021 and followed by subsequent action under the new regime, were barred by limitation or valid under the combined effect of the old provisions, TOLA, and the amended law

, it was naturally considering defences such as limitation when the notice is issued say after 30th June, 2021 and is beyond three years and the escapement is below 50lakh. Otherwise, almost all the 90,000 notices were issued between the extended period of limitation and it cannot be that the Supreme court converted such notices to section 148A(b) notices only for them to travel upto the Supreme Court again and be quashed on the grounds of limitation.

2. A step by step process to understand the above controversy is below:

A.

The old reassessment notices issued within the extended period i.e. on or after 1st April, 2021-30th June, 2021 are converted to show-cause notices under section 148A(b) pursuant to the decision in Ashish Agarwal. Hence, for any fresh notice to be issued under section 148 post passing of the section 148A(d) order, the same cannot be beyond limitation on a plain reading of section 149, otherwise the said judgment in Ashish Agarwal converting the notices will be rendered nugatory or of no effect inasmuch as for obvious reasons the fresh notices to be issued under section 148 will invariably and always without doubt be beyond limitation. For this reason to reconcile the issue, the fresh notice under section 148 must travel back in time to the original date when they were issued i.e. the date of the old notice and limitation should be computed accordingly. The rationale is that the Supreme court judgment cannot be rendered nugatory and must not be defeated by holding that the fresh section 148 notices are beyond limitation.

B.

Hence, when the Supreme Court stated that all defences including limitation will be kept open, it was considering only those cases where the notice is issued after 30th June, 2021 only, for AY 2017-2018 and AY 2016-2017. For example for AY 2017-2018 if the section 148 notice is issued on say 2nd July, 2022, the notice will be beyond limitation if the income escaped assessment is less than Rs. 50 lakh and Ashish Agarwal applies only to these cases, otherwise the Supreme Court would not have sanctioned the reassessment notices by converting them to section 148A(b) notices.

C.

It cannot possibly be said that the defence of limitation can be taken against those notices issued under the extended period under TOLA, 2020 otherwise all the notices would be beyond limitation and there would be no purpose in converting them to show-cause notices. In Ashish Agarwal the period under consideration was precisely that beyond 1st April, 2021. Again, the judgment in Ashish Agarwal would stand defeated and reduced to a mere piece of paper if the notifications extending the limitation are quashed, or it is held that the notices issued during that period are beyond limitation. The notices must travel back in time to the original date failing which the section 148 notices would invariably be beyond limitation and the judgment in Ashish Agarwal will be rendered nugatory.

3.

The next question is of sanction of the 'specified authority'. This is mandated by the Act. However, pursuant to the decision in Ashish Agarwal if the old notices are converted to SCN's as per the judgment, then the defence of sanction becomes a double edged sword in the hands of the assessee. To illustrate, if sanction is incorrectly given for the old notice, it is liable to be quashed and there can be no further proceedings. However, if sanction is given appropriately for the old notice but inappropriately given for the fresh section 148 notice, the fresh notice is invalid and would have to be quashed and reissued if the law permits. The section 148A(d) order must receive sanction from the specified authority being the proper authority and once the appropriate sanction for the section 148A(d) order is obtained, there is no need to obtain fresh sanction for the section 148 notice under proviso 2 to section 1484. As rightly held in the above case, the fresh sanction was provided by the PCIT and not the authorities mentioned under section 151(ii) hence the sanction was bad in law.

Conclusion

The issue of limitation was not dealt with elaborately in the above case but some principles on limitation have been provided to enable a better understanding of the controversy on reassessment which has engulfed both assessee and Department. The issue of sanction was in ,my view, correctly decided by the Hon'ble Court. In my view, the judgment has dealt with the issue of sanction in great detail by analysing all the relevant provisions and has laid down the law correctly. There are other observations made by the learned Judge on change of opinion on the facts of the case. However, to clear all doubts, in my view, sanction can be tested upon the old notice since it is covered by the decision of Ashish Agarwal where all defences are to be kept open, and the issue of fresh sanction under section 148A(d)/section 148 can also be raised before the Courts. Further, it is now well settled that the concept of change of opinion has also been carried forward to the new regime of reassessment

Section 143

Finance Act, 2006

Time limit for issue of notice under section 143(2) for the purposes of making assessment or reassessment under section 147

7.3 Section 148(1) provides that before making any assessment, reassessment or re-computation under section 147, the Assessing Officer shall serve a notice under section 148, on the assessee, requiring him to furnish his return of income and the provisions of the Act shall apply as if the return furnished in response to such notice were a return required to be furnished under section 139.

The Tribunal has held that assessment under section 147 is invalid if the notice under section 143(2) is not issued within 12 months from the end of the month in which return under section 147 was filed (after issuance of notice under section 148). [See Raj Kumar Chawla v. ITO [2005] 94 ITD 1 (Delhi)(SB)]

To cure such time barred assessments, the law has been amended retrospectively. Two new provisos to sub-section (1) have been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-10-1991 to provide as follows:

(a)

Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2) as it stood immediately before the amendment of said sub-section by the Finance Act, 2002, but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

(b)

Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2)(ii) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2)(ii), but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

Further, an Explanation has been inserted, with effect from 1-10-2005 in section 148(1) so as to clarify that the provisions of the aforesaid provisos shall not apply in relation to any return which has been furnished on or after 1-10-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148(1).

Thus, so far as returns furnished on or after 1-10-2005 are concerned, the pre-amendment law will apply and the notices will have to be served within a period of 12 months specified in section 143(2).
