INCOME TAX: Where assessee entered into a Joint Development Agreement in previous year and Tribunal quashed reassessment for earlier year on grounds that there was no finding or direction under section 150(1), invocation of section 150(1) for reopening subsequent year was without jurisdiction and, as limitation under section 149 had expired, reassessment notice and orders were void and unsustainable in law.

A notice under section 148 was issued to the assessee on 21-7-2022 for the alleged escaped income of Rs. 39 lakhs and finally reassessment order was passed on 31-5-2023 against the assessee and consequential notice of demand was also issued.

In instant writ petition to the High Court, the assessee contended that entire reassessment proceeding be quashed and set aside and all consequential orders passed pursuant to issuance of notice under section 148A which had been issued beyond limitation period prescribed under section 149 be also quashed.

INCOME TAX: Where reassessment initiation for a firm was based on information from prior year’s return and financials rather than material relating to relevant year, absence of information pertaining to relevant assessment year rendered issuance of notice under section 148A invalid, vitiating subsequent proceedings under section 148.

INCOME TAX: Where Assessing Officer issued notice under section 148 beyond surviving limitation period of 22 days reckoned from date of assessee’s reply under law laid down in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC), reassessment proceedings held time-barred and liable to be quashed.

INCOME TAX : Where notice under section 148 dated 28-03-2021 for assessment year 2015-16 was issued with sanction of Commissioner (Exemption), though by virtue of section 3(1) of TOLA four-year limitation under old section 151 stood extended till 31-03-2021, since approval was required from Joint Commissioner as per section 151(2), notice and consequential reassessment were to be quashed

barred by time factor [Rajesh Sunderdas Vaswani v. DCIT [2017] 88 taxmann.com 602 (Guj.)].

Where AO issued and dispatched a reopening notice against assessee on last date of expiry of period of limitation, even though notice was franked by Postal department later, said notice was not barred by limitation [Rajmannar Ramaswamy v. ITO [2021] 130 taxmann.com 431 (Mad.)]. Digitally signing the notice is not issuance of notice - Considering the provisions of sections 282 and 282A of the 1961 Act and the provisions of section 13 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and meaning of the word 'issue', firstly, notice shall be signed by the assessing authority and then it has to be issued either in paper form or be communicated in electronic form by delivering or transmitting the copy thereof to the person therein named by modes provided in section 282 which includes transmitting in the form of electronic record. Section 13(1) of the IT Act, 2000 provides that unless otherwise agreed, the dispatch of an electronic record occurs when it enters into computer resources outside the control of the originator. Thus, the point of time when a digitally signed notice in the form of electronic record is entered in computer resources outside the control of the originator, i.e., the assessing authority, that shall be the date and time of issuance of notice u/s 148 r/w s. 149. Thus, mere digitally signing the notice is not the issuance of notice [Daujee Abhushan Bhandar (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2022] 136 taxmann.com 246/286 Taxman 623 (All.)].

Date of issue of notice in case of e-mail - Reassessment notices would be said to be digitally issued on date when same were e-mailed to petitioner [Sharad Garg v. ITO [2022] 136 taxmann.com 360/287 Taxman 207 (Delhi)].

For time-barring of digitally issued reassessment notices, date on which they were issued by email sent is important and not the date of receipt by assessee [Malavika Enterprises v. CBDT [2022] 137 taxmann.com 398/287 Taxman 693 (Mad.)].

In case of legal representatives - Section 159(2)(b) would require a separate notice to be issued u/s 148 within time prescribed u/s 149(1)(b) as against legal representatives directly and if such proceedings are initiated beyond time prescribed u/s 149(1)(b), such proceedings would not be valid [Mrs. Vanitha Gopal Shetty v. Asstt. CIT [2021] 129 taxmann.com 163 (Kar.)].

Notice served within extended period of limitation – Where assessee was served with a reassessment notice within extended period of limitation, first proviso of s. 149(1) (as amended by Finance Act, 2021) would not be attracted in facts of this case [Kusum Gupta v. ITO [2022] 145 taxmann.com 231/[2023] 290 Taxman 172 (Delhi)].

Where time period for issuance of reassessment notice for assessment year 2013-14 stood extended by s. 3 of TOLA, until 30-6-2021 and alleged escaped income of assessee was beyond Rs. 50 lakh, first proviso of s. 149 (as amended by Finance Act, 2021) would not be attracted and thus reassessment proceeding initiated during time limit extended by TOLA was within limitation [Salil Gulati v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 150 taxmann.com 49/455 ITR 24 (Delhi), SLP dismissed in Salil Gulati v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 150 taxmann.com 50/293 Taxman 75/455 ITR 29 (SC)].

Law applicable if limitation period has expired - In a matter of reassessment proceedings under the Act, if the limitation has already expired, then the amended law would not revive the matters by taking into consideration the amended provisions of law. The provisions of the amended Act would therefore be applicable only in those cases where the limitation under the old law has not expired [Chandi Ram v. ITO [1996] 87 Taxman 418 (Raj.)].
INCOME TAX : Where reassessment notice under section 148 was issued on 31-8-2022 after expiry of limitation on 16-6-2022, it was held to be time-barred.
Reassessment for s.56(2)(vii)(b) addition held time-barred as 148A(d) order and 148 notice were beyond limitation; assessment quashed: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer issued reopening notice beyond three years on ground that property purchased for Rs. 90 lakhs had stamp duty value of Rs. 1.25 crore, since reassessment was completed by making addition of Rs. 35.13, which was much below limit prescribed by provisions of section 149(1), reassessment notice and consequent order under section 148A(d), being barred by limitation, were to be quashed

INCOME TAX : Where notice under section 148 was issued by Assessing Officer just one day prior to expiry of limitation period on e-mail through ITBA portal, but said e-mail was sent to e-mail account which did not belong to assessee and was bounced and, thus, notice under section 148 was never served on assessee within period of limitation, assessment order passed under section 147 without service of notice under section 148 was to be declared as invalid and was to be quashed
Reassessment notice void as CIT(A) direction expunged and notice issued beyond sec. 149 time limit: ITAT

INCOME TAX: Where reassessment notice under section 148 was issued on or after 1-4-2021 for income escaping assessment relating to A.Y. 2015-16, such notice was time-barred and thus not valid as per statutory time limits under section 149.
Reassessment notice quashed due to issuance after expiry of limitation period as per amended provisions: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a trust, had its income assessed under section 148A(d) after filing its return and about five years later, Assessing Officer issued a reassessment notice under section 148, alleging that trust had paid legal and professional fees without receiving any actual services, reopening notice issued beyond period of limitation was liable to be quashed

INCOME TAX: Where notice under section 148 was issued beyond three years from end of relevant assessment year, since approval was obtained from Principal Commissioner instead of specified authority prescribed under section 151, notice and consequential reassessment proceedings were without jurisdiction

INCOME TAX: Where assessee challenged fresh notice issued under section 148 as time-barred, and it was found that although an earlier notice had been issued within extended period allowed under TOLA, Assessing Officer issued fresh notice after legally permitted time had expired, such notice was invalid as it was issued beyond period of limitation
Reassessment notice beyond limitation for AY 2015-16 held void; consequential actions quashed: HC

29-03-2022.

The scheme provides that assessment, reassessment or recomputation under Section 147 and issuance of notice under Section 148 shall be done:

(a)

Through automated allocation, in accordance with the risk management strategy formulated by the Board as referred to in Section 148 for issuance of notice; and

(b)

In a faceless manner, to the extent provided in Section 144B with reference to making an assessment or reassessment of total income or loss of assessee. 7.4-2i Section 152 - This provision provides that where an assessment has been reopened, the assessee (if he has not preferred an appeal or applied for revision) can claim that the re-assessment proceedings shall be dropped if he shows that:

(a)

He had been assessed on an amount which is not lower than what he would be rightly liable for, even if income alleged to have escaped assessment had been taken into account;

(b)

The assessment or computation had been properly made.

7.4-2j Section 153 - The time limits have been prescribed in this provision for summary assessment, scrutiny assessment, best judgment assessment and income escaping assessment. If an assessment is not completed within the prescribed time limit, it becomes time-barred.

7.4-2k Important judicial precedence - The following are the important rulings on the pre-amended reassessment provisions under Sections 147 to 151:

(a)

Where faceless mechanism has become mandatory, the issue of notice under Section 148 and order under Section 148A(d) by the Jurisdictional AO are not valid [Sundaram Multi Pap Ltd. v. ACIT [2024] 164 taxmann.com 608 (Bombay); Swarn Singh v. ITO [2024] 163 taxmann.com 745 (Amritsar - Trib.); Pravina Jagdish Patel v. ITO [2024] 164 taxmann.com 659 (Bombay); Sushila Sureshbabu Malge v. ITO [2024] 164 taxmann.com 633 (Bombay); Venus Jewel v. ACIT [2024] 164 taxmann.com 414 (Bombay); Jatinder Singh Bhangu v. UOI [2024] 165 taxmann.com 115 (Punjab & Haryana); Jasjit Singh v. UOI [2024] 165 taxmann.com 114 (Punjab & Haryana); Triton Overseas (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2023] 156 taxmann.com 318 (Calcutta). There should not be even any name of the officer issuing the notice, Ram Narayan Sah v. UOI [2024] 163 taxmann.com 478 (Gauhati)];

(b)

Where a notice under Section 148 was not issued in a proper manner, it will be deemed invalid [Brett Lee v. ACIT [2024] 163 taxmann.com 71 (Delhi - Trib.); GRS Hotel (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2024] 160 taxmann.com 125 (Allahabad); Mandeep Malli v. ACIT [2024] 162 taxmann.com 637 (Amritsar - Trib.)];

(c)

Not providing adequate time to respond to notice under Section 148A(b) invalidates the subsequent proceedings [Skipper Infrabuilders (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2024] 163 taxmann.com 10 (Calcutta); Ninaben Tusharbhai Shah v. ITO [2024] 161 taxmann.com 442 (Gujarat)];

(d)

The absence of approval from a specified sanctioning authority renders reassessment proceedings invalid [Ashok Kumar Makhija v. UOI [2024] 162 taxmann.com 514 (Delhi); Cipla Pharma and Life Sciences Ltd. v. DCIT [2024] 164 taxmann.com 663 (Bombay); Agnello Oswin Dias v. ACIT [2024] 161 taxmann.com 16 (Bombay)];

(e)

Where a notice under Section 148 issued after 01-04-2021 under the old law was treated as notice under Section 148A(b) as per the decision of Apex Court in Ashish Agarwal's case, but no fresh notice under Section 148 was issued thereafter, the reassessment proceedings were invalid [Ranjit Singh v. ITO [2024] 164 taxmann.com 629 (Amritsar - Trib.)];

(f)

Even in cases of reopening arising on the basis of information emanating under Section 135A, it is necessary for the AO to verify the information before issuing a notice under Section 148 as it is not necessary that information received through an electronic mechanism would be correct and would not require verification. [Benaifer Vispi Patel v. ITO [2024] 165 taxmann.com 5 (Bombay)];

(g)

Reassessment ● Notice Period

5.2 Under section 148 of the Act, an assessment can be reopened and for the purpose a notice can be issued to an assessee for filing a return of his income within a specified period, not being less than thirty days. At present, in the printed form of notice under section 148, the assessee is required to furnish a return of his income 'within thirty days'. As per Memorandum explaining provision of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, notices issued under section 148 have been held to be invalid by the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal on the ground that whereas the statute allows the taxpayer a time, 'not being less than thirty days', the notice gives the direction to file a return 'within a period of thirty days'. The Bombay High Court in the case of CIT v. Ekbal & Co. [1945] 13 ITR154 (Bom.) decided a similar issue by laying down that the expressions within thirty days' and 'not less than thirty days' are two quite different things. The above legal position, as such, invalidates all the proceedings initiated through such printed notice(s), which could have been avoided by changing the form of notice.

However, to get over the situation, section 148 of the Act has been amended, with retrospective effect from 1-4-1989 whereby the words 'not being less than 30 days' have been omitted.

The effect of the deletion of the words is that now an Assessing Officer can require an assessee to file a return pursuant to a notice under section 148 of the Act within such period as may be specified in the notice. Thus, now, a notice could be for a shorter period as the minimum time constraint has been removed.

Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996 states that this amendment will also apply to any notice which has already been issued, on or after 1-4-1989.

However, one does not find any specific words or mention of it in the amendment so as to show that such notices have been validated.

The concerned assessees may be adversely affected and may have to agitate the proceedings afresh. In such a situation a question could arise as to whether a mere insertion of the amendment with retrospective effect is sufficient to validate the invalid notice which has been issued needs to be validated. It is felt that the latter action would be necessary. Otherwise, one can validate or invalidate an action at any point of time with no remedy for taxpayers.

Further, it appears that those assessees who had questioned such validity may be able to agitate this issue. However, in cases where pursuant to notices issued after 1-4-1989 reassessment is concluded, it may not be now possible to take a plea that the notices were invalid. In other words, in such cases, it appears that the retrospective amendment would support the case of revenue.

Limitation period for completion of assessments and reassessments

5.3 Section 153 of the Act lays down the time limit for making an order of assessment (two years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable). Also, Explanation 1 below section 153 of the Act sets out certain circumstances in which certain periods as specified are excluded from the period of limitation.

In a case where an audit under section 142(2A) is ordered, the assessee is required to furnish a report of such audit within the prescribed time. In such a case, the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited under section 142(2 A) and ending with the date on which the assessee furnishes a report of such audit is excluded while reckoning the period of limitation for completion of the assessment, as per Explanation 1(iii) below section 153 of the Act.

As per the Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, in a case where the report is not prepared and, therefore, not furnished, the normal time limit of two years is operative and the Assessing Officer does not get any additional time for the purpose of making an assessment because the time taken for furnishing the audit report is not excluded. Exclusion of the period in terms of Explanation 1(iii) could operate only if the report of such audit is furnished.

To obviate the difficulty, the said Explanation has been amended, with effect from 1-4-1997, to provide that the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited and ending on the date on which the report of such audit was required to be furnished, shall be excluded from the period of limitation.

This would enable extension of the limitation period, at least, by the time permitted, although, the audit report is not furnished.

Author's views

1.

The issue of notice under section 148 is no doubt to be carried out in a faceless manner as provided under the e-Assessment of Income Escaping Assessment Scheme, 2022. However, it is pertinent to note the underlying objective of incorporating the faceless proceedings regime. The object was largely, almost wholly, to eliminate the interface between the assessee and Department in order to mitigate the levels of corruption and to have an effective and transparent system resulting in no further losses of revenue. As such, the issue of a section 148 notice in a faceless manner does not support the underlying objective i.e. to have a transparent process. It is only when there are hearings and evidence needs to be supplied or some proceeding takes place that the said proceedings have to be undertaken in a faceless manner- in other words, in my view, the requirement of issue of a section 148 notice in a faceless manner is only a directory provision, having no underlying objective and distant from the main objective. The issue of a section 148 notice whether in a faceless manner or in physical form would ultimately make no difference as long as it is issued by an Assessing Officer competent to issue the said notice.

2.

It is settled law that no fresh notice can be issued under section 148 unless it is within limitation. Hence, while the Revenue is not completely barred from issuing a fresh notice, since in some cases the notices would have been issued early and there would be application of the 5th proviso to section 149, the fresh notices could be within limitation. However, this is subject to the discretion of the Court as well.

3.

Assuming that there is no SLP filed by the Department before the Supreme Court, it is obvious that there can be no recovery from the assessees since the very assessment orders passed by the jurisdictional assessing officers are liable to be set aside in appeal. In the event, the judgment is stayed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the recovery can be carried out depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case and subject to the directions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court. For example, if the Supreme Court directs no recovery, when the judgment is stayed, there cannot be any recovery though it is difficult to imagine if the Hon'ble Supreme Court would make such an observation.

Service vs. issue of notice - Section 148 of enjoins that the AO must serve on the assessee a notice requiring him to furnish a return of his income, in respect of which he/she is assessable under the 1961 Act during the PY corresponding to the relevant AY. In stark contrast, s. 149 speaks only of the issuance of a notice under the preceding section within a prescribed period. S. 149 does not mandate that such a notice must also be served on the assessee within the prescribed period [Mayawati v. CIT [2010] 321 ITR 349 (Delhi)].

Limitation provided u/s 149 for issuance of notice commences from date when notice is issued and not when notice served [Synfonia Tradelinks (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2021] 127 taxmann.com 153/281 Taxman 557 (Del.); Sadhna Tolasariya v. ITO [2021] 127 taxmann.com 127/281 Taxman 354 (Mad.)].

Time-limit applies for issue of notice - The word 'issued' in section 149 should be given its natural meaning and not the strained wider meaning of 'served'. Consequently, where the notice was issued within time but was served on the assessee after the expiry of the time-limit, it could not be held to be invalid [Jai Hanuman Trading Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 110 ITR 36 (P&H - FB)].

It is date of issue of notice u/s 148, and not actual receipt of notice by assessee which is relevant to return a finding as to whether reassessment proceedings have been initiated within period of limitation [CIT v. K. G. Singhania [2012] 24 taxmann.com 208/209 Taxman 45 (P&H)].

Mere generation of notice do not constitute issue of notice – Function of generation of notice on ITBA portal and digital signing of notice is executed by Assessing Officer while function of drafting of e-mail to which notice is attached and triggering e-mail to assessee is performed by ITBA e-mail software system. Thus, mere generation of notice u/s 148 on ITBA software cannot in fact or in law constitute issue of notice, it is only upon due despatch that notice can be said to have been issued. 'Despatch' as per section 13 of Information Technology Act of 2000 is sine qua non for issuance of notice through electronic mail for purpose of s. 149 [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/[2023] 290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Date of issuance of notice in case of Postal department - Date of issue of notice would be the date on which the same was handed over for service to the proper officer or Postal Department. Since the Income-tax Department is covered by 'book now pay later' scheme, the further requirement of properly stamping envelope with adequate postal stamp, would not be germane. Therefore, where reassessment notice was handed over to Postal Department before stipulated time, it would not be barred by time factor [Rajesh Sunderdas Vaswani v. DCIT [2017] 88 taxmann.com 602 (Guj.)].

Where AO issued and dispatched a reopening notice against assessee on last date of expiry of period of limitation, even though notice was franked by Postal department later, said notice was not barred by limitation [Rajmannar Ramaswamy v. ITO [2021] 130 taxmann.com 431 (Mad.)].

Returns & Assessment*

Quoting of PAN

7.1 Section 139A has been amended with effect from 1-6-2006 to provide that the requirement of quoting of PAN is now extended to all quarterly statements prepared and delivered or caused to be delivered in accordance with section 200(3) or proviso to section 206C(3).

Clarificatory amendment regarding the time limit for issue of notice under section 142

7.2 Section 142(1), inter alia, provides that for the purposes of making assessment in a case where a person has not made a return of his income within the time specified under section 139(1), the Assessing Officer may serve a notice under the said sub-section on such person requiring him to furnish the return of his income in the prescribed form and manner.

Clause (i) of section 142(1) has been amended with effect from 1-4-2006 to provide that in a case where a person has not made a return of his income before the end of the relevant assessment year, the Assessing Officer may serve a notice after the end of the relevant assessment year under the said sub-section requiring such person to furnish his return of income.

Further a proviso to the said clause (i) has been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-4-1990, so as to provide that where any notice has been served on or after 1-4-1990 under sub-section (1) after the end of the relevant assessment year to any person who has not made a return of his income before the end of the relevant assessment year, such notice shall be deemed to be a notice served in accordance with the provisions of the said sub-section (1).

The amendment has been made to neutralise the decision in Motorola Inc. v. Dy. CIT [2005] 95 ITD 269 (Delhi)(SB), where it was held that the notice under section 142(1) calling for a return of income has to be issued after end of the period in section 139(1) and before end of the relevant assessment year and if no return of income is filed by an assessee till the end of the assessment year, a notice issued after the said date is invalid.

The amendment thus regularises the notices which were not served within the stipulated time period under the pre-amendment law.

Time limit for issue of notice under section 143(2) for the purposes of making assessment or reassessment under section 147

7.3 Section 148(1) provides that before making any assessment, reassessment or re-computation under section 147, the Assessing Officer shall serve a notice under section 148, on the assessee, requiring him to furnish his return of income and the provisions of the Act shall apply as if the return furnished in response to such notice were a return required to be furnished under section 139.

The Tribunal has held that assessment under section 147 is invalid if the notice under section 143(2) is not issued within 12 months from the end of the month in which return under section 147 was filed (after issuance of notice under section 148). [See Raj Kumar Chawla v. ITO [2005] 94 ITD 1 (Delhi)(SB)]

To cure such time barred assessments, the law has been amended retrospectively. Two new provisos to sub-section (1) have been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-10-1991 to provide as follows:

(a) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2) as it stood immediately before the amendment of said sub-section by the Finance Act, 2002, but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

(b) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2)(ii) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2)(ii), but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

Once the matter reaches Court, it is the legislation and its language, and the interpretation offered to that language as may primarily be decisive to govern the outcome of the proceeding. To read practicality into enacted law is dangerous. Also, it would involve legislation by the Court, an idea and exercise we carefully tread away from.

(vii) As to the decision of the Chhattisgarh High Court, with all respect, we are unable to persuade ourselves to that view. According to us, it would be incorrect to look at the delegation legislation i.e. Notification dated 31-3-2021 issued under the Enabling Act, to interpret the principal legislation made by Parliament, being the Finance Act, 2021. A delegated legislation can never overreach any Act of the principal legislature. Second, it would be over simplistic to ignore the provisions of, either the Enabling Act or the Finance Act, 2021 and to read and interpret the provisions of Finance Act, 2021 as inoperative in view of the fact circumstances arising from the spread of the pandemic COVID-19. Practicality of life de hors statutory provisions, may never be a good guiding principle to interpret any taxation law. In absence of any specific clause in Finance Act, 2021, either to save the provisions of the Enabling Actor the Notifications issued thereunder, by no interpretative process can those Notifications be given an extended run of life, beyond 31 March 2020. They may also not infuse any life into a provision that stood obliterated from the statute with effect from31-3-2021. Inasmuch as the Finance Act, 2021 does not enable the Central Government to issue any notification to reactivate the pre-existing law (which that principal legislature had substituted), the exercise made by the delegate/Central Government would be dehors any statutory basis. In absence of any express saving of the pre-existing laws, the presumption drawn in favour of that saving, is plainly impermissible. Also, no presumption exists that by Notification issued under the Enabling Act, the operation of the pre-existing provision of the Act had been extended and thereby provisions of Section 148A of the Act (introduced by Finance Act2021) and other provisions had been deferred. Such Notifications did not insulate or save, the pre-existing provisions pertaining to reassessment under the Act.

(viii)

In view of the above, all the writ petitions must succeed and are allowed. It is declared that the Ordinance, the Enabling Act and Sections 2 to 88 of the Finance Act 2021, as enforced w.e.f. 1-4-2021, are not conflicted. Insofar as the Explanation appended to clause A(a), A(b), and the impugned Notifications dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021 (respectively) are concerned, we declare that the said Explanations must be read, as applicable to reassessment proceedings as may have been in existence on 31-3-2021 i.e. before the substitution of Sections 147, 148, 148A, 149, 151 & 151A of the Act. Consequently, the reassessment notices in all the writ petitions are quashed. It is left open to the respective assessing authorities to initiate reassessment proceedings in accordance with the provisions of the Act as amended by Finance Act, 2021, after making all compliances, as required by law.

Concluding Remarks

Friends, the above entire discussion, is a classic example of a glaring and unfortunate mismatch between the perceived legislative intent of reducing the time barring limitation period of reopening of already concluded assessments u/s 148 from 6 years to 3 years w.e.f. 1-4-2021, aimed at reducing uncertainty, and the practical ground-level implementation of the said policy decision, during the transition to the substituted reassessment regime.

The taxpayer friendly image on account of reduction of the time period for reopening the already concluded assessments and the wishful act of extending the pre-amended time barring limitation period of issuance of notice under the old section 148, beyond 31-3-2021, by way of delegated legislation, so as to cover the entire 6 years, even in the newly substituted reassessment regime, can't go hand in hand.

ISSUE/SERVICE OF NOTICE

Service of notice is mandatory - The notice prescribed by section 148 cannot be regarded as a mere procedural requirement. It is only if the said notice is served on the assessee that the ITO would be justified in taking proceedings against the assessee. If no notice is issued or if the notice issued is shown to be invalid, then the proceedings taken by the ITO would be illegal and void [Y. Narayana Chetty v. ITO [1959] 35 ITR 388 (SC); CIT v. Thayaballi Mulla Jeevaji Kapasi [1967] 66 ITR 147 (SC); CIT v. Kurban Hussain Ibrahimji Mithiborwala [1971] 82 ITR 821 (SC)].

Section 148 provides for service of notice as a condition precedent to making the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested in the AO to proceed to reassess. The mandate of section 148 is that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued [R. K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 33 Taxman 229 (SC)].

Signature of authority – Where a reopening notice u/s. 148 was issued upon assessee without signature of Assessing Officer affixed on it either digitally or manually, said notice was invalid and same would not vest Assessing Officer with any further jurisdiction to proceed to reassess income of assessee [Prakash Krishnavtar Bhardwaj v. ITO [2023] 150 taxmann.com 60/293 Taxman 132/451 ITR 27 (Bom.)].

Date of issue/service of notice – While issuing notice u/s 148, date of issue of notice is not important, it is date of signing notice which is important [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices u/s 148 are sent through registered e-mail ID of respective Assessing Officers, though not digitally signed, it will be held to be valid service of notice. However, date and time of dispatch as recorded in ITBA portal will be taken as date of issuance of notice in this regard [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices u/s 148 were only uploaded in e-filing portal of assessees without any real time alert, date and time when assessees viewed notices in e-filing portal, as recorded in ITBA portal will be construed as date of service of notice [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices u/s 148 were manually despatched, date and time when notices were delivered to post office for dispatch was to be construed as date of issuance of notice [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Where notices were sent to unrelated e-mail addresses, date on which notice was first viewed by assessee on e-filing portal was to be construed as date of issuance of notice [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Issue before getting approval u/s 151 – There is no need for paper containing approval being received physically before issuing notice and Assessing Officer can proceed to issue a notice u/s 148 if approving authority has granted his approval and approval has been communicated to Assessing Officer in any manner including by uploading approval on portal of department. Thus, reopening notice could not be vitiated on ground that paper containing approval u/s 151 was received by Assessing Officer after issuing notice [Sahara Credit Cooperative Society Ltd. v. DCIT/Asstt. CIT [2022] 141 taxmann.com 384 (All.)].

Where assessment proceedings are pending - Notice cannot be issued during pendency of assessment proceedings [Jhunjhunwala Vanaspati Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 137 Taxman 336 (All.)].

In the Ashish Agarwal ruling, the Supreme Court did not address whether or not the reassessment notices were issued within the time limits prescribed under the provisions of the 1961 Act, read with the relaxations provided under TOLA. Thus, in Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70/301 Taxman 238/469 ITR 46 (SC), setting aside various judgments1, the Supreme Court held that:

(a)

Section 3(1) of TOLA applies to the issuance of reassessment notices under section 148 of the 1961 Act. While TOLA did not amend the four and six-year time limits under the Act, it provided a relaxation for issuing reassessment notices during the COVID-19 period. TOLA does not apply if the time-limit under section 149 expires before 20-3-2020. When issuing a reassessment notice, the revenue must check both section 149 time limit and TOLA's relaxation period. For example, the six-year limit for AY 2013-14 expired on 31-3-2020, but TOLA extended it to 30-06-2021.Accordingly, after 1-4-2021, the 1961 Act has to be read along with the substituted provisions. TOLA will continue to apply to the Income-tax Act after 1-4-2021, if any action or proceeding specified under the substituted provisions of the 1961 Act falls for completion between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021.

(b)

TOLA will extend the time-limit for the grant of sanction by the authority specified under section 151. The test to determine whether TOLA will apply to section 151 of the new regime is this: if the time-limit of three years from the end of an assessment year falls between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021, then the specified authority under section 151(i) has extended time till 30-6-2021 to grant approval. In the case of section 151 of the old regime, the test is: if the time-limit of four years from the end of an assessment year falls between 20-3-2020 and 31-3-2021, then the specified authority under section 151(2) has extended time till 31-3-2021 to grant approval. Thus, the Assessing Officers were required to issue the reassessment notice under section 148 of the new regime within the time-limit surviving under the 1961 Act read with TOLA. All notices issued beyond the surviving period are time-barred and liable to be set aside.

Findings of the Hon'ble Bombay High Court

The first proviso to section 148 of the Act refers to the approval of the specified authority being obtained before a notice under section 148 of the Act can be issued. Explanation 3 to section 148 of the Act specifies that the meaning of the term 'specified authority' as provided for in section 151 of the Act is to apply for the purpose of section 148. section 148A(d) also requires the Assessing Officer to pass an order after considering the reply of the assessee as to whether or not it is a fit case to issue a notice under section 148 and such an order under section 148A(d) has to be passed with the prior approval of the specified authority. The Explanation to section 148A of the Act also incorporates the meaning of 'specified authority', as provided for in section 151. As per section 151 of the Act, the 'specified authority' who has to grant his sanction for the purposes of section 148 and section 148A is the Principal Chief Commissioner or Principal Director General or where there is no Principal Chief Commissioner or Principal Director General, the Chief Commissioner or Director General if more than three years have elapsed from the end of the relevant assessment year. The present petition relates to the AY 2016-17, and as the impugned order and impugned notice are issued beyond the period of three years which elapsed on 31st March, 2020 the approval as contemplated in section 151(ii) of the Act would have to be obtained which has not been done by the Assessing Officer. The impugned notice mentions that the prior approval has been taken of the 'Principal Commissioner of Income-tax – 8' which is bad in law as the approval should have been obtained in terms of section 151(ii) and not section 151(i) of the Act and the PCIT-8 cannot be the specified authority as per section 151 of the Act. Further, even in the affidavit-in-reply, the department has accepted that the approval obtained is of the 'Principal Commissioner of Income-tax – 8' and, hence, such an approval would be bad in law.

TOLA only seeks to extend the period of limitation and does not affect the scope of section 151.

CBDT's observations in paragraph 6.1 of Instruction No. 1/2022 dated 11th May 2022 cannot be countenanced as it is not open to them to clarify that the law laid down by the Apex Court means that the extended reassessment notices will travel back in time to their original date when such notices were to be issued and, then, the new section 149 of the Act is to be applied as this is contrary to the judgment of this court in Tata Communications (supra) wherein it is held that TOLA does not envisage traveling back of any notice. Even assuming that it is held that these notices travel back to the date of the original notice issued on 25th June 2021, even then the approval of the Principal Chief Commissioner of Income-tax should be obtained in terms of section 151(ii) of the Act as a period of three years from the end of the relevant assessment year ended on 31st March 2020 for AY 2016-17.

In Dr. Mathew Cherian v. Asstt. CIT3 it was held that whether it is under the old or new regime of reassessment, issues settled should not be given a go by in the garb of reassessment. Hence, the concept of change of opinion should not be removed and the present case is a clear change of opinion on the part of the Assessing Officer.

Author's views

In my view, the issue of sanction which was strongly considered in the said judgment has been rightly decided and is without blemish. However, I have provided inputs on some interesting principles of limitation as well in addition to sanction and are noted below:

1.

The decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ashish Agarwal (supra) is binding on every Court in India being a judgment of the Supreme Court. In the said judgment, not only did the Hon'ble Supreme Court convert approximately 90,000 notices issued under the old regime to show-cause notices under section 148A(b), it also dispensed with an enquiry under section 148A(a) and proceeded to direct the passing of an order under section 148A(d). Hence, for all purposes, once there is such conversion of notices, it is not for namesake or for the asking, it is on account of the wisdom of the Hon'ble Supreme Court which must be followed. It follows, that the notices are to be proceeded with and an order under section 148A(d) passed. When the Supreme Court mentioned that all defences must be kept open, it was naturally considering defences such as limitation when the notice is issued say after 30th June, 2021 and is beyond three years and the escapement is below 50lakh. Otherwise, almost all the 90,000 notices were issued between the extended period of limitation and it cannot be that the Supreme court converted such notices to section 148A(b) notices only for them to travel upto the Supreme Court again and be quashed on the grounds of limitation.

7.4-4 New Reassessment provisions in brief

(1)

There is no change in Section 147. Therefore, AO can assess, by virtue of Explanation to Section 147, any other item of escaped income for which no notice under Section 148A has been issued.

(2)

Before initiating reassessment proceedings, the AO has to issue a notice under Section 148A(1). Such notice has to be issued on the basis of information suggesting that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment.

(3)

The notice should enclose all the information that suggests that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment.

(4)

The information in the case of the assessee shall be in accordance with the Risk Management Strategy formulated by the Board, audit objections, information received under Section 90 or 90A, an order of the Tribunal or Court or material gathered in a survey. However, no notice is required to be issued if information is emerging under the scheme framed under Section 135A.

(5)

Notice under Section 148A can be issued for the relevant assessment year within three or five years from the end of the relevant assessment year. The five-year limitation period will be available if information suggests an escaped income of Rs. 50 lakh or more based on asset, entry or expenditure as per books of account.

(6)

In FY 2024-25, notice under Section 148A can be issued for the AY 2021-22 and not for earlier assessment years. It can be issued for AY 2019-20 onwards if the escaped income is Rs. 50 lakh or more, and it is based on asset, entry or expenditure as per books of account.

(7)

No inquiry or approval is required before issuing notice under Section 148A(1). The concept of deemed information has been done away with.

(8)

The assessee has to furnish a reply in response to such notice as provided under Section 148A(2).

(9)

The AO has to pass an order under Section 148A(3) on the basis of information and reply received from the assessee in response to notice under Section 148A(1) determining whether it is a fit case or for issue of notice under Section 148(1).

(10)

Approval for passing the order under Section 148A(3) and issue of notice under Section 148 has to be obtained from Addl. CIT/Addl. DIT/ JCIT/JDIT. The approval is no longer required from senior officers like CIT/PCIT/CCIT/PCCIT/DGIT.

(11)

Notice under Section 148 will be issued along with the order under Section 148A.

(12)

Notice under Section 148 can be issued for the relevant assessment year within 'three years and three months' or 'five years and three months' from the end of the relevant assessment year. (iii) two years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable, where such assessment year is an assessment year commencing on or after the 1st day of April, 1969 ; or

(b) the expiry of eight years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable, in a case falling within clause (c) of subsection (1) of section 271 ; or

(c) the expiry of one year from the date of the filing of a return or a revised return under sub-section (4) or sub-section (5) of section 139,

whichever is latest.

(a) where the assessment, reassessment or recomputation is to be made under clause (a) of that section, after the expiry of four years from the end of the assessment year in which the notice under section 148 was served ;

(b) where the assessment, reassessment or recomputation is to be made under clause (b) of that section, after—

(i) the expiry of four years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable, or

(ii) the expiry of one year from the date of service of the notice under section 148,

whichever is later.

Implementation of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183 1. Hon'ble Supreme Court, vide its judgment dated 04.05.2022 [2022] 138 taxmann.com 64/286 Taxman 183, in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal has adjudicated on the validity of the issue of reassessment notices issued by the Assessing Officers during the period beginning on 1st April, 2021 and ending with 30th June 2021, within the time extended by the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 [hereinafter referred to as "TOLA"] and various notifications issued thereunder (these reassessment notices hereinafter referred to as "extended reassessment notices").

2. These extended reassessment notices were issued by the Assessing Officers under the provision of section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") following the procedure prescribed under various sections pertaining to reassessment namely sections 147 to 151, as they existed prior to their amendment by the Finance Act, 2021 (hereinafter referred to as "old law"). With effect from 1st April 2021, the old law has been substituted with new sections 147-151 (hereinafter referred to as the "new law").

3. Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that these extended reassessment notices issued under the old law shall be deemed to be the show cause notices issued under clause (b) of section 148A of the new law and has directed Assessing Officers to follow the procedure with respect to such notices. It has also held that all the defences available to assessees under section 149 of the new law and whatever rights are available to the Assessing Officer under the new law shall continue to be available. Hon'ble Supreme Court has passed this order in exercise of its power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India.

4. The implementation of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court is required to be done in a uniform manner. Accordingly, in exercise of its power under section 119 of the Act, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (hereinafter referred to as "the Board") directs that the following may be taken into consideration while implementing this judgment.

5. Scope of the judgment:

5.1 Taking into account the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in various paragraphs. it is clarified that the judgment applies to all cases where extended reassessment notices have been issued. This is irrespective of the fact whether such notices have been challenged or not.

6. Operation of the new section 149 of the Act to identify cases where fresh notice under section 148 of the Act can be issued:

6.1 With respect of operation of new section 149 of the Act, the following may be seen:

Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that the new law shall operate and all the defences available to assessees under section 149 of the new law and whatever rights are available to the Assessing Officer under the new law shall continue to be available.

16.3C-4a No reassessment if the assessment year was time-barred at the time the assessment proceedings were initiated - Section 150(2)(a) largely mirrors the existing provision of section 150(2). It refers to the time when the original order (which was subsequently challenged in appeal, reference, or revision) was made. The implication remains consistent with the current law: if, at the time the initial assessment order was passed, the assessment year was already time-barred under other provisions of the Act, then section 150(1) cannot be used to reopen it, even if a higher authority later gives a finding or direction.

Section 150(2)(b) introduces a new reference point for checking the time limitation for assessment proceedings that are the subject of court proceedings. This clause significantly broadens the circumstances under which section 150(1) cannot be invoked. It shifts the focus from the date of the final order to the date of initiation of proceedings relating to assessment or reassessment. If the proceedings were initiated at a time when the limitation period to issue notice for an assessment year had expired under the general provisions (like Section 149 or section 153), then even if a subsequent court order gives a finding or direction, section 150(1) would be rendered inapplicable. This would prevent the reopening of old cases based on findings from court proceedings.

16.3C-4b Time-limit to issue notice under section 148 - Sub-section (3) of section 150 provides the time limit within which the notice under section 148 can be issued pursuant to the findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority. It provides that the notice under section 148 shall be issued within 3 months from the end of the quarter in which the certified copy of the order of the authority or the Court, as the case may be, is received by the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. This provision puts the limitation period within which such notice should be issued, and if not issued within such period, the assessment becomes time-barred, and section 150(1) cannot come to its rescue.

Facts of the case

The assessee was issued a notice under section 148 for assessment year 2013-14 and thereafter assessment order was passed. The assessee filed a writ petition seeking a writ or order to quash notice under section 148 as also sanction authorizing issue of such notice and also impugned assessment order. The High Court considering order in Daujee Abhushan Bhandar (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2022] 136 taxmann.com 246/286 Taxman 623/444 ITR 41 (All.) disposed writ petition directing the respondent-authority concerned to decide the objection of the assessee against the notice under section 148, in accordance with law on the point of date of issuance of notice.

Following said direction of the High Court, the respondent No. 4/Assessing Officer rejected objection of the assessee observing that though High Court had quashed such notices issued under section 148 on or after 1-4-2021 but department had filed SLP before the Supreme Court on this issue and therefore till outcome of issue pending before the Supreme Court, it could not be said that notice under section 148 issued to the assessee was not valid.

Held that:

From the averments made by respondent in the short counter-affidavit, it is evident that the notice under section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for the assessment year 2013-14 was issued to the petitioner on April 1, 2021, whereas the limitation of issuing the notice expired on March 31, 2021. Thus notice under section 148 of the Income tax Act, 1961 was time barred and consequently it was without jurisdiction

The High Court having noticed that order passed by the respondent No. 4 in connection with disposal of objection of the assessee was highly contemptuous, whimsical and against all settled principles of propriety directed respondent No. 4 to file a personal affidavit to explain the things.

"In view of law laid down by the hon'ble Supreme Court and High Court, the principles of judicial discipline and propriety and binding precedent, we hold as under:

(a)

Judicial discipline and propriety are the two significant facets of administration of justice. The principles of judicial discipline require that the orders of the higher appellate authorities should be followed unreservedly by the subordinate authorities. The mere fact that the order of the appellate authority is not "acceptable" to the Department in itself an objectionable phrase or that is the subject matter of an appeal can furnish no ground for not following it unless its operation has been suspended by a competent court. If this healthy rule is not followed, the result will only be undue harassment to assessees and chaos in administration of tax laws.

(b)

Just as the judgments and orders of the Supreme Court have to be faithfully obeyed and carried out throughout the territory of India under article 141 of the Constitution, so should be the judgments and orders of the High Court by all inferior courts and tribunals subject to supervisory jurisdiction within the State under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution.

(c)

If an officer under the Income-tax Act, 1961 refuses to carry out the clear and unambiguous direction in a judgment passed by the hon'ble Supreme Court or High Court or the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal then in effect, it is denial of justice and is destructive of one of the basic principles in the administration of justice based on hierarchy of the court.

(d)

Unless there is a stay obtained by the authorities under the Income-tax Act, 1961 from higher forum, the mere fact of filing appeal or Special Leave Petition will not entitle the authority not to comply with the order of the High Court. Even though the authority may have filed an appeal or Special Leave Petition but either could not obtain a stay or the stay is refused, the order of the High Court must be complied with. Mere filing of an appeal or Special Leave Petition against the judgment or order of the High Court does not result in the assailed judgment or order becoming inoperative and unworthy of being complied with.

In view of the principles settled by the hon'ble Supreme Court and by High Courts in the judgments, we direct the respondents to maintain judicial discipline and follow the doctrine of binding precedent and be careful in future, having due regard to the authorities of the court, keeping in mind the judicial propriety and discipline."

INTRODUCTION

Section 147 of the Income Tax Act , 1961 (hereinafter referred to as 'IT Act, 1961') empowers the Assessing Officer ('AO') to assess or reassess such income or recompute the loss or the depreciation allowance or any other allowance or deduction for a particular assessment year of an assessee, if any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for that assessment year.

Section 148 of the IT Act, 1961 mandates the issuance of notice by AO income escaping assessment.

Section 148A of the IT Act, 1961, which was inserted by the Finance Act, 2021 prescribes the procedural requirement which the AO must adhere to before issuing notice under Section 148 of the IT Act, 1961.

TIME LIMIT FOR ISSUANCE OF NOTICE UNDER SECTION 148 OF THE INCOME TAX, ACT.

Section 149 of the IT Act, 1961 provides for the time limit for issuance of notice under Section 148. The normal time limit for issuing notice under Section 148 is three years from the end of the relevant assessment year. It also provides that a notice can be issued even beyond three years but not more than ten years from the end of the relevant assessment year if the AO has in his possession books of account or other documents or evidence which reveal that the income chargeable to tax which has escaped assessment amounts to or is likely to amount to fifty lakh rupees or more, in the form of

a.

an asset,

b.

expenditure in respect of transactions or in relation to an event or occasion, or

c.

an entry or entries in the books of amount.

CAN A NOTICE UNDER SECTION 148 OF THE IT ACT, 1961 BE ISSUED TWICE FOR THE SAME ASSESSMENT YEAR?

There are several decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India and various High Courts that the principle of res-judicata as stated in Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 does not apply in taxation matters. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Radhasoami Satsang, Saomi Bagh, Agra v. CIT [1992] 60 Taxman 248/193 ITR 321 has held that : -

"16. We are aware of the fact that strictly speaking res judicata does not apply to income tax proceedings. Again, each assessment year being a unit, what is decided in one year may not apply in the following year but where a fundamental aspect permeating through the different assessment years has been found as a fact one way or the other and parties have allowed that position to be sustained by not challenging the order, it would not be at all appropriate to allow the position to be changed in a subsequent year."

Therefore, it can be argued that since the principle of res-judicata does not apply in matters pertaining to taxation, the AO is empowered to issue several notices under Section 148 for the same Assessment Year.

In T. Krishnamurthy v. ITO [2020] 116 taxmann.com 476, the Hon'ble Madras High Court had held that the Assessing Officer has the power to issue notice under Section 148 of the IT Act, 1961 for the second time. It held that the first notice under Section 148 was set-aside only on technical grounds and was not decided on merit and therefore the same did not bar the department from issuing notice u/s 148 for the second time.

Interestingly, the third proviso of Section 147 states that the Assessing Officer may assess or reassess such income, other than the income involving matters which are subject matters of any appeal, reference or revision, which is chargeable to tax and has escaped assessment.

There are several judgements of various High Courts on the same principle, wherein the High Courts have held that if a notice under Section 148 has been issued and the same is pending adjudication before the Assessing Officer or CIT (Appeals) or the Tribunal, then the second notice, if issued is bad in law and is liable to be quashed.

The Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Kamdhenu Enterprise v. ITO [2023] 146 taxmann.com 417 while relying on the judgement of CIT v. Sanjay Kumar Garg [2015] 64 taxmann.com 334 (Delhi) has held that it is settled law that during the subsistence of a reassessment proceedings, another reassessment notice cannot be issued for the same assessment year.

The Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Kamdhenu Enterprise v. ITO [2023] 146 taxmann.com 417 while relying on the judgement of CIT v. Sanjay Kumar Garg [2015] 64 taxmann.com 334 (Delhi) has held that it is settled law that during the subsistence of a reassessment proceedings, another reassessment notice cannot be issued for the same assessment year. Similarly, in Smt. Pushpa Rajawat v. CIT [D.B. IT Appeal No. 205 of 2015, dated 25-10-2017] the Hon'ble Rajasthan High Court has held that that the adjudicating authority could not have issued second show cause notice under Section 148 of the IT Act, 1961 when the adjudication of the first notice issued under Section 148 was pending before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals).

The Hon'ble Calcutta High Court in the case of Pr. CIT v. Coal India Ltd. [2023] 146 taxmann.com 546 held that when a notice under section 148 of the Act is issued, the original assessment proceedings are entirely opened up or left open and the finality which had occurred in the first assessment order does not exist any longer. Therefore, without disposing of the return of income filed by the assessee in response to the first notice, the assessing officer could not have issued a second notice for reopening of the assessment which, at the relevant point of time, did not exist in the eye of law.

In Elite Pharmaceuticals v. ITO [2023] 147 taxmann.com 378/291 Taxman 597, the Hon'ble Calcutta High Court held that the second notice under Section 148 issued by the Income Tax Department is bad in law when the assessee had filed its return with respect to the first notice under Section 148 and the Department without disposing the return so filed issued second notice under Section 148.

CONCLUSION

While it is true that the IT Act, 1961 is silent with respect to the number of times a notice under Section 148 can be issued for the same assessment year, there are judgements of various High Courts wherein the answer to the question concerned is answered in favour of the department provided an issue has escaped assessment and such issue comes to his notice subsequently in course of the proceedings. However, the third proviso to Section 147 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 clearly bars the issuance of the second notice under Section 148 when the first notice is pending adjudication.

10.6-2 Limitation period for assessment year prior to assessment year 2021-22

As noted, the limitation period, in such a case, needs to be determined as per section 149(1)(b) as existed prior to April 1, 2021 (the earlier provision).

To illustrate, suppose in respect of assessment year 2013-14, the escaped income exceeds Rs. 50 lakhs; the case falls under section under the new provision; however, limitation period provided for the same under the earlier provision is six years; accordingly, in such a case, in terms of the first proviso to section 149(1), the limitation period would be six years as per the earlier provision and not 10 years as per the amended section 149(1)(b). Hence, the assessment cannot be reopened under the new provision.

10.6-3 Search, requisition and other cases prior to April 1, 2021

Suppose, search etc. were carried out, say, in February 2021, that is, prior to the amendment. In such cases, the assessment or reassessment was governed by special provisions of sections 153A and 153C. The second proviso lays down that, in such a case, the provisions of section 149(1) would not apply. In such a case, a notice for assessment or reassessment would be issued under the said special provisions of sections 153A and 153C.

Well yes Friends, in current times, the most buzzing and critically debated and talked about tax issue, having PAN India relevance and some very high value stakes, doing rounds in all the tax circles and the coveted corridors of the hon'ble High Courts, is the issue of legal sanctity and validity of the reassessment notices issued under the old section 148 on or after 1-4-2021.

Till date, the two hon'ble High Courts viz. the Chhattisgarh High Court (single Judge Bench) and the Allahabad High Court (regular bench) have pronounced their final verdicts on this issue. While the single Judge bench of the hon'ble Chhattisgarh High Court has upheld the validity of old 148 notice in two cases, on the basis of doctrine of conditional legislation and practicality, the regular bench of the hon'ble Allahabad High Court has quashed all such old 148 notices, issued on or after 1-4-2021, in a batch of 74 writ petitions, by passing a very meticulous and comprehensive judgement on 30-9-2021.

Friends, if you don't have the patience and time to read and go through all the54 pages of this long and meticulously drafted judgement of the hon'ble Allahabad High Court, and still, you want to grasp the entire judgement, then this Taxalogue is definitely for you. But, frankly speaking guys, I have cherished and loved reading, every word of this very well represented and meticulously drafted judgement and so my humble advice to you all, is to definitely read this judgement in its entirety in your spare time.

On 30-9-2021, the hon'ble Allahabad High Court, hearing a batch of 74 writ petitions, (leading case being 'Ashok Kumar Aggarwal v. Union of India' [Tax No. 524 of 2021] , challenging the initiation of re-assessment proceedings, on or after 1-4-2021, pursuant to issue of notices under the old section 148, in its landmark judgement, have quashed the respective old 148 notices and have allowed all the 74 writ petitions, by holding that, "A delegated legislation can never overreach any Act of the principal legislature."

But before we delve deeper into the finer nuances of some of the very significant observations and ratios as propounded by the hon'ble Allahabad High Court in this judgement, it will be useful and fruitful to briefly rush through the newly substituted legislative provisions concerning the new reassessment regime as brought up in the Finance Act 2021 and the corresponding chronology of events in this regard.

In the Finance Act 2021, amendments have been made, to substitute the pre-existing sections 147, 148, 149 and 151 (effective upto 31-3-2021) of the Income-tax Act, with corresponding new sections w.e.f. 1-4-2021 and thereby reducing the time barring limitation period for reopening the already concluded assessments from 6 years to 3 years, in cases where the escaped income representing an asset is less than Rs. 50 lakhs, and stipulating the replacement of the existing mandatory condition of formation of an independent reason to believe by the assessing authority that income of the assessee has escaped assessment so as to assume lawful jurisdiction u/s 147, by the presence of any flagged information as per the risk management strategy of CBDT or the final audit objection of C&AG, suggesting that income of the assessee has escaped assessment. Further a new section 148A, has also been inserted and made applicable w.e.f. 1-4-2021, requiring the assessing authority to provide a suitable opportunity of being heard to the assessee and also mandating prior approval of the competent income tax authority at various levels and steps, before issuing notice under the substituted section 148 of the Income-tax Act.

Friends, this reduction in time period of reopening of the already concluded assessments from 6 years to 3 years, has been announced as a path breaking taxpayer friendly relaxation, with a lot of fanfare, in the budget speech.

Exact Quote of the Budget Speech of our Hon'ble FM, during the presentation of the annual budget for 2021-22 fiscal, is reproduced below, for ready reference:

"Honourable Speaker, presently an assessment can be re-opened up to 6 years and in serious tax fraud cases for up to 10 years. As a result, taxpayers have to remain under uncertainty for a long time. I therefore propose to reduce this time-limit for re-opening of assessment to 3 years from the present 6 years."

Limitation period for completion of assessments and reassessments

5.3 Section 153 of the Act lays down the time limit for making an order of assessment (two years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable). Also, Explanation 1 below section 153 of the Act sets out certain circumstances in which certain periods as specified are excluded from the period of limitation.

In a case where an audit under section 142(2A) is ordered, the assessee is required to furnish a report of such audit within the prescribed time. In such a case, the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited under section 142(2 A) and ending with the date on which the assessee furnishes a report of such audit is excluded while reckoning the period of limitation for completion of the assessment, as per Explanation 1(iii) below section 153 of the Act.

As per the Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, in a case where the report is not prepared and, therefore, not furnished, the normal time limit of two years is operative and the Assessing Officer does not get any additional time for the purpose of making an assessment because the time taken for furnishing the audit report is not excluded. Exclusion of the period in terms of Explanation 1(iii) could operate only if the report of such audit is furnished.

To obviate the difficulty, the said Explanation has been amended, with effect from 1-4-1997, to provide that the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited and ending on the date on which the report of such audit was required to be furnished, shall be excluded from the period of limitation.

This would enable extension of the limitation period, at least, by the time permitted, although, the audit report is not furnished.

Special procedure for assessment of search cases

5.4 The Finance Act, 1995, introduced a new scheme for assessment of Undisclosed Income ('UnI') determined as a result of search.*

The Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, provides as follows:

"Field experience in the implementation of the new procedure for block assessments has shown that difficulties are arising in certain areas."

These relate to:

◆ Assessment procedure

◆ Definition of "Block period"

◆ Taxation of firms and partners

◆ Limitation affected by Special Audit and stay granted by Courts

To obviate the difficulties, certain amendments have been made in the following provisions:

◆ Section 2(74) defining 'Assessing Officer' has been amended to include Assistant Director and Deputy Director within its ambit. This amendment comes into effect from 1-10-1996.

This amendment confers jurisdiction (not otherwise available) on them to make an assessment of UnI under the said Chapter, as per Explanation given in the Memorandum.

Consequent to the above, two other amendments made are:

-Section 120(4)(b) of the Act has been amended to include reference to a Deputy Director so that appropriate higher authority can exercise jurisdiction over him. This amendment comes into force from 1-10-1996.

-Proviso to section 158BG has been amended laying down that no order under the Chapter be passed without prior approval of the Commissioner of Income-tax or Director. The objective is that where an order under the Chapter is passed by a Deputy Director he has to obtain sanction of Director within whose jurisdiction he has to work. This amendment comes into force from 1-10-1996. (See para 5.4-1)

◆ Section 158B(a) defining block period has been amended to provide that it would include a period of previous years relevant to ten assessment years instead of ten previous years, as per the present definition.

This amendment comes into force with retrospective effect from 1-7-1995. (See para 5.4-2)

◆ Explanation (b) below section 158BB(1) of the Act presently providing for assessment of firm and partners as per the schemes prevailing during the relevant years in the block period is being substituted by a new Explanation (b) which provides that only firm would be assessable in respect of UnI and not the partners.

7.2-3f ABATEMENT OF PENDING ASSESSMENT OR REASSESSMENT - There could be several situations and implications. Some of them are discussed below :

Consider a case, where the search action takes place, say, on 1-7-2003. In the search, only certain documents are found showing receipts on sale of certain goods, relating to the financial year 2002 and 2003. Apart from that, nothing else is found. In this case, the Assessing Officer will have to issue the notice under section 153A to the assessee for filing the return for the specified period, i.e., assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04. The assessee has already filed returns under section 139 for all the above assessment years. Further, in respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments have been reopened pursuant to notice under section 148. In respect of assessment year 2001-02, the assessee has not received any notice for assessment under section 143(2). Further, for the assessment year 2000-01 no assessment was done under section 143(3). In respect of assessment year 1999-2000, the assessment was made under section 143(3). The assessment is pending in appeal. In respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, against the assessments made under section 143(3), an appeal was filed. In the appeal, the assessment for assessment year 1997-98 was set aside and the appeal for assessment year 1998-99 was decided with a direction to examine the claim of the assessee, for certain facts, and accordingly allow the claim.

The position, in respect of the above assessment years, as per the new procedure, could be as follows :

The Assessing Officer has to make assessments or reassessments for each of the assessment years under the new procedure. Thus, prima facie, the Assessing Officer will make assessments or reassessments for all the years covered in the specified period, that is, assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04.

In respect of the assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments whereof are reopened but reassessments are not completed, the reassessments can now be completed, pursuant to section 153A. The effect would be extension in the limitation period for making reassessment, since section 153A overrides the provisions of section 153.

The assessments for assessment years 2000-01 and 2001-02, though barred by limitation under section 153, can be made under section 153A. In the assessment, normal disallowance, etc., can be made. This may attract interest, if any, under section 234B, etc.

The assessment for assessment year 1999-2000 is completed. All the same, a fresh assessment can be made under section 153A. The new procedure would not affect the pending appeal.

The set aside assessment for the assessment year 1997-98 shall abate and the Assessing Officer will make the assessment under section 153A. However, while making reassessment, it may not be possible for him to ignore the directions, if any, of the Appellate Authority, in respect of the issue covered by the appellate order.

11.2-8e Notice can be issued if incomes escaping assessment spread over more than 1 year [Section 149(1A)]

After sub-section (1) the following sub-section is inserted:

"(1A) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where the income chargeable to tax represented in the form of an asset or expenditure in relation to an event or occasion of the value referred to in clause (b) of sub-section (1), has escaped the assessment and the investment in such asset or expenditure in relation to such event or occasion has been made or incurred, in more than one previous years relevant to the assessment years within the period referred to in clause (b) of sub-section (1), a notice under section 148 shall be issued for every such assessment year for assessment, re-assessment or recomputation, as the case may be."

The amended section 149(1)(b) provides that notice under Section 148 can be issued after 3 years but before 10 years if escaped income of Rs. 50 lakhs or more is represented in the form of an asset, expenditure, or entry. Sub-section (1A) introduced by the Finance Act, 2022 provides that if such escaped income, represented in the form of asset or expenditure in respect of transaction, event or occasion, is spread over more than 1 year and the total escaped income in all these years is Rs. 50 lakhs or more, then AO gets jurisdiction to issue a notice under Section 148 for all those years. It is now no longer necessary that escaped income of Rs. 50 lakh should be only in 1 year. It is only to be seen that the aggregate of such escaped income is Rs. 50 lakh or more, and in such a situation, notice under Section 148 can be issued for all such years.

It starts with a non-obstante clause to override the provisions of Section 149(1);

The amended section 149(1)(b) provides that notice under Section 148 can be issued after 3 years but before 10 years if escaped income of Rs. 50 lakhs or more is represented in the form of an asset, expenditure, or entry. It is now no longer necessary that escaped income of Rs. 50 lakh should be only in 1 year. It is only to be seen that the aggregate of such escaped income is Rs. 50 lakh or more, and in such a situation, notice under Section 148 can be issued for all such years.

7.2-3f ABATEMENT OF PENDING ASSESSMENT OR REASSESSMENT - There could be several situations and implications. Some of them are discussed below :

Consider a case, where the search action takes place, say, on 1-7-2003. In the search, only certain documents are found showing receipts on sale of certain goods, relating to the financial year 2002 and 2003. Apart from that, nothing else is found. In this case, the Assessing Officer will have to issue the notice under section 153A to the assessee for filing the return for the specified period, i.e., assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04. The assessee has already filed returns under section 139 for all the above assessment years. Further, in respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments have been reopened pursuant to notice under section 148. In respect of assessment year 2001-02, the assessee has not received any notice for assessment under section 143(2). Further, for the assessment year 2000-01 no assessment was done under section 143(3). In respect of assessment year 1999-2000, the assessment was made under section 143(3). The assessment is pending in appeal. In respect of assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, against the assessments made under section 143(3), an appeal was filed. In the appeal, the assessment for assessment year 1997-98 was set aside and the appeal for assessment year 1998-99 was decided with a direction to examine the claim of the assessee, for certain facts, and accordingly allow the claim.

The position, in respect of the above assessment years, as per the new procedure, could be as follows :

◆ The Assessing Officer has to make assessments or reassessments for each of the assessment years under the new procedure. Thus, prima facie, the Assessing Officer will make assessments or reassessments for all the years covered in the specified period, that is, assessment years 1997-98 to 2003-04.

◆ In respect of the assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99, the assessments whereof are reopened but reassessments are not completed, the reassessments can now be completed, pursuant to section 153A. The effect would be extension in the limitation period for making reassessment, since section 153A overrides the provisions of section 153.

◆ The assessments for assessment years 2000-01 and 2001-02, though barred by limitation under section 153, can be made under section 153A. In the assessment, normal disallowance, etc., can be made. This may attract interest, if any, under section 234B, etc.

◆ The assessment for assessment year 1999-2000 is completed. All the same, a fresh assessment can be made under section 153A. The new procedure would not affect the pending appeal.
