T.K. Basu, J. - In this application the petitioner challenges three notices all dated the 17th October, 1978, and issued under section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"). The notices are in respect of the assessment years 1970-71, 1971-72 and 1972-73, respectively.

Although the main challenge is that the condition precedent for the applicability of section 148 was not satisfied in the present case and it was pressed very strenuously and a large number of authorities were cited before me, the other point as to the limitation was also urged equally strenuously. Before I deal with the main challenge, I shall deal with the question of limitation.

On the question of limitation, it was submitted that section 153 of the Act provides the time-limit for the completion of assessments and reassessments. The issue of limitation, it was contended, is to be considered in the light of section 153(2) of the Act. It was pointed out that separate time-limits for the completion of an assessment were provided for under section 147(a) and under section 147(b) of the Act. The submission on the question of limitation was on the basis that the proceedings, which were impugned in the present case, fell under section 147(b) of the Act. This is because, although the point was not given up by Mr. Suhas Sen, appearing for the Revenue, he did not seriously try to justify the issue of the impugned notices under section 147(a) of the Act. In other words, Mr. Sen's main argument was an attempt to justify the issue of the notices under section 147(b) of the Act, an argument with which I shall deal later on.

On the question the following points were urged on both sides.

(a)

What is the period of limitation for the completion of reassessment proceedings initiated under section 147(b)/148 of the Act ?

(b)

Whether the reassessment proceedings under section 147(b) were already barred by limitation as provided in section 153(2)(b) of the Act, on or before 17th October, 1978, the date when the ITO issued notices under section 142(1) of the Act?

(c)

Where the reassessment proceedings cannot be completed because of the bar of limitation under section 153(2)(b) of the Act, should this court go into the question of limitation or leave it to be considered by the ITO?

(d)

Has section 153(2A)/153(3) any application in this case?

Sharma v. ITO [2002] 122 Taxman 426/254 ITR 772 wherein it was held that fiscal statute more particularly on a provision such as the present one regulating period of limitation must receive strict construction. Law of limitation is intended to give certainty and finality to legal proceedings and to avoid exposure to risk of litigation to litigant. Proceedings, which have attained finality under existing law due to bar of limitation cannot be held to be open for revival unless the amended provision is clearly given retrospective operation so as to allow upsetting of proceedings, which had already been concluded and attained finality. The amendment to sub-section (1) of Section 150 is not expressed to be retrospective and, therefore, has to be held as only prospective. The amendment made to sub-section (1) of Section 150 which intends to lift embargo of period of limitation under Section 149 to enable Authorities to reopen assessments not only on the basis of Orders passed in proceedings under the I.T. Act but also on Order of a Court in any proceedings under any law has to be applied prospectively. Therefore, even as per rule, strict construction and limitation of section 149 applies until and unless ingredients of section 150(1) is fulfilled. In the case before us, the ingredients of section 150(1), which the Revenue has made the basis for issue of notice under section 148, itself is not satisfied, therefore, issuance of notice under section 148 is directly hit by the provisions of section 149 limitation. We are, therefore, of the considered view that since issuance of 148 notice is barred by limitation, serving of notice itself is invalid and bad in law and, therefore, any consequent assessment or re-assessment is obviously null and void. We, therefore, set aside the order of the ld. CIT (A) and direct quashing of the re-assessment proceedings. Since the legal ground of validity of proceedings under section 147/148 itself is decided in favour of the assessee, all other grounds in the grounds of appeal becomes infructuous.

As regards the point of commencement of limitation, a plain reading of the provisions contained in clause (i) of sub-section (1)(a) of section 149 conveys the message that the relative adjective ‘that’ used in that provision has reference to the words ‘assessment year’ used in the opening lines of sub-clause (i). It suggests that the period of eight years is to commence from the end of the relevant assessment year. Nowhere in section 149(1)(a)(i ) has the term ‘financial year’ been used The position has been made clear by the use of the same term ‘assessment year’ in both sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 151. It is, thus, abundantly clear that the prescribed period of eight years or 16 years, as the case may be, is to be reckoned from the end of the relevant assessment year and not the financial year.

As regards the question of issue and service of notice, for the purposes of application of the provisions of section 149, a notice under section 148 should be issued and served within the time prescribed by section 149. For proper administration of sections 149 and 153 and to satisfy the legislative intention in enacting those provisions, the words `issued’ and ‘served’ used in sections 149 and 153, respectively, should be regarded and interpreted as inter-changeable. It is difficult to accept that the Legislature would have intended that the issuance of notice under section 148 within the period of limitation prescribed by section 149 without there being the effective service of such notice as required by section 153 within the prescribed period, would satisfy the pre-condition for making a valid assessment as per the provisions of section 147 read with sections 149 and 153. Such an interpretation of the word ‘issued’ used in section 149 would be too oppressive for the assessees. For the decision to issue notice under section 148 is taken by the ITO behind the back of an assessee as there is no requirement of law to hear the assessee before the issue of a notice under section 148 to him If the meaning of the word ‘served’ as used in section 153 is not considered to be hidden in the meaning of the word ‘issued’ used in section 149 and vice versa, it may lead to unwanted consequences. For, before the end of eight or sixteen years, as the case may be, from the relevant assessment year, an ITO may issue a notice under section 148 and allow it to be kept in his file for an indefinite period, for the period of limitation prescribed by section 153 for completing the assessment is to commence from the date of service of the notice under section 148 and not before. The ITO may, thus, keep the sword of democles, hanging on the head of an assessee for an indefinite period, Such could not be the intention of the Legislature in enacting the provisions of sections 149 and 153. Both the sections prescribe limitation for an integrated purpose. They should, therefore, be read together in order to meet that purpose.

It therefore, logically follows that the word issued’ used in section 149 is required to carry the meaning of the expression ‘issued and served’ within the prescribed period of limitation.

As regards the validity of notice under section 148, the relevant assessment year in this appeal was 1975-76 which came to an end on 31-3-1976. The starting point of limitation under section 149(1)(c) was 1-4-1976 and the eighth year from that date expired on 31-3-1984. Since the notice under section 148, according to the assessee himself, was served on him by affixation on 30-3-1984, the notice issued and the assessment proceedings initiated on the basis of such notice were not hit by the provisions of section 149. Since the service of the notice under section 148 on 30-3-1984 was proved, the subsequent service on 3-4-1984 of another notice of the same type would not adversely affect the validity of the notice served on 30-3-1984. Therefore, the notice issued in this case under section 148 was quite valid and not hit by the provisions of section 149.

The Commissioner (Appeals) opined that the service of notice on 17-6-2005 was beyond the time-limit and, therefore, the assessment was bad in law. On revenue's appeal, the accountant member opined that the notice dated 28-3-2005 which was issued by the Assessing Officer after due receipt of necessary approval under section 151(2), a valid notice under section 148. According to him, the service of a notice though extremely relevant, yet is a matter of procedure so that its absence or a defect therein would not invalidate the ensuing proceedings, but only make them irregular, i.e., where there is a valid assumption of jurisdiction to assess. As regards the notice dated 17-6-2005, the Accountant Member was of view that the law does not contemplate multiple issue of notices conferring jurisdiction under section 148(1) so that there could be no reissue of an already validly issued notice. Accordingly, the Accountant Member upheld the validity of reassessment proceedings on the basis of notice issued as on 28-3-2005. The Judicial Member, however, accepted the assessee's contention that the issuance of notice on 29-6-2005 was a fresh notice. He thus, set aside the reassessment proceedings holding that said notice was issued beyond the prescribed time-limit. In view of difference of opinion between the Members of the Tribunal, the matter was referred to the Third Member.

HELD (AS PER THIRD MEMBER)

The issue before the Division Bench as could be seen from the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) itself is narrowed down as to the validity of the assessment made by the Assessing Officer under sections 143(3) and 147 in the light of the initiation of reassessment proceedings by issuance of notice. The provisions of sections 147 to 151 are specific provisions which enable the department to reassess any income that has escaped assessment. These provisions underwent significant changes with effect from 1-4-1989. In the light of these changes, each and every initiation of assessment proceedings made on or after 1-4-1989 must be governed by the amended provisions as held by the decision of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Rakesh Aggarwal v. Asstt. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 496 /[1996] 87 Taxman 306 . Under section 148(1), before making an assessment, reassessment and computation under section 147, the Assessing Officer is required to serve on the assessee a notice requiring him to furnish a return of income. Under section 148(2), the Assessing Officer, before issuing any notice under section 148(I), is required to record his reasons for doing so. The provisions relating to the time-limit for issuance of notice are set out in section 149. [Para 15]

A notice issued within the period prescribed under section 149, even though served thereafter, gives a perfectly valid initiation.

INCOME TAX: Where Assessing Officer issued order under section 148A(d) and notice under section 148 on 29.07.2022 for income escaping assessment, as original notice under section 148 was deemed issued on 24.06.2021 and limitation expired on 16.06.2022, subsequent proceedings were invalid as time barred.

As regards the validity of notice issued under section 148, the first condition laid down in section 148(1) for issuance of notice is that it should be issued before making assessment, re-assessment and re-computation of income. In the instant case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 25-10-1988 and the assessment was completed on 22-8-1990. Thus, the notice issued under section 148 was valid as it was issued before the assessment was made. Then, according to the provisions envisaged and limitation laid down in section 149(1), no notice under section 148 would be issued in cases falling under clause (a) of section 147 for the relevant assessment year if eight years had elapsed from the end of that year. In the instant case, the relevant assessment year was 1987-88 and 8 years from the end of that year would elapse in 1996. But the notice under section 148 was already issued on 25-10-1988 and was, therefore, well within the prescribed time limit of eight years, i.e., before 31-3-1990. The assessee’s contention that the notice under section 148 issued prior to 31-3-1990 could not take the right of the assessee to file the return under section 139(4) was also not tenable as, in the instant case, no return was furnished before the issuance of notice under section 148. Moreover, there was no provision in the Act to invalidate the notice under section 148 by furnishing of return after the issue of such notice.

The notice issued under section 148 was in the nature of notice under section 139(2) and it was issued as no return was filed by the assessee and the Assessing Officer had reason to believe that income had escaped assessment as per section 147(a) of the Act. The notice under section 148 was issued on 25-10-1988 and the return of income was filed by the assessee on 30-3-1989. As the return was filed after the issue of notice under section 148, it was certainly a return submitted in response to the notice under section 148. Although the return was filed before 31-3-1990 and it was a belated return, it could not be treated as a return furnished under section 139(4), as it was not filed voluntarily by the assessee. There was no clash between the provisions of sections 139(1) and 139(4) on the one hand and section 139(2), on the other. A person who has not furnished a return under section 139(1) and (2) is authorised to file the return under section 139(4). In the instant case, as the assessee has furnished the return in response to a notice under section 148 which was treated as a notice under section 139(2), the assessee was not entitled to furnish a return under section 139(4). Therefore, the return furnished by the assessee was to be treated as a return filed under section 139(2)/section 148 and not a return under section 139(4). The assessee had contended that the assessment was barred by limitation, as the return was filed on 30-3-1989 and the assessment should have been completed by 31-3-1990 while it was completed on 22-8-1990. This contention of the assessee was based on the argument that the return furnished on 30-3-1989 should be treated as a return under section 139(4). As the latter contention of the assessee was rejected and the return furnished on 30-3-1989 was treated as a return under section 148/139(2), the former contention was also not tenable and could not be accepted under any provisions of law. As the assessment was re-opened under section 147(a), provisions of section 153(2)(a) were applicable. According to these provisions, no assessment is to be made after the expiry of four years from the end of the assessment year in which the notice under section 148 was served. In the instant case, as the notice under section 148 was served on 26-10-1988, the limitation for assessment expired on 31-3-1993, i.e., four years from the end of assessment year 1988-89. In view of the foregoing, it was to be held that the notice issued under section 148 was a valid notice, the return furnished in compliance with the notice under section 148 was to be treated as a return furnished under section 139(2) and the assessment made was within limitation and, therefore, was a valid assessment.

Once notices under section 148 have been issued, the proceedings initiated through them have to be taken to their logical end. In other words, either assessments should be framed on the basis of those proceedings or the Assessing Officer may specifically drop the proceedings, may be on the ground that no sufficient material was available for holding that income liable to tax had escaped assessment. Even if an assessee does not comply with those notices by fling the income-tax returns, the remedy which is open to the revenue is not to issue fresh notices under section 148 but to issue notices under section 142(1) or to have completed the assessments under section 144. Thus, if the assessments have got barred by limitation, they cannot be revived by issuing fresh notices. In the instant case, this position was clear to the Assessing Officer and other officers of the department as could be gathered from a DO letter written by ITO to his IAC in which he had written that in this case, the assessment for the assessment year 1972-73 had been completed on a total income of Rs. 2,53,400 on 20-2-1985 as a result of which a demand was created. He had further mentioned that this matter was discussed with the Commissioner and that according to the Commissioner the demand was unrealisable and assessment was likely to be annulled.

As per the said printout the Assessing Officer of the said company found that there was an excess payment of Rs. 11,44,658/- and accordingly, the addition of the said amount was made in the hands of the company for want of satisfactory explanation. The said addition was confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) vide his order dated 15-7-2009.

The Tribunal deleted said addition in the hands of 'T' Ltd. by holding that the said document belongs to 'T' proprietorship of the assessee HUF and the income if any arising from such transactions was held to be assessed in the hands of assessee instead of 'T' Ltd.

Based on the findings of the Tribunal in the case of 'T' Ltd. vide order dated 26-3-2010 the Assessing Officer initiated proceedings under section 147 and issued a notice under section 148 on 30-7-2010.

The assessee filed objections against the initiation of the proceedings under section 148 which was rejected by the Assessing Officer. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment under section 143(3) read with section 147 on 1-12-2011. The assessee challenged the action of the Assessing Officer including the validity of reopening before the Commissioner (Appeals) but could not succeed.

The assessee filed instant appeal submitting that the notice issued under section 148 on 30-7-2010 was barred by limitation as provided under section 149 read with section 150. It was further contended that the notice under section 148 was issued on 30-7-2010 and as per restrictions provided under section 150(2) the time limit prescribed under section 149 had already expired on 31-3-2009. Thus, reassessment proceedings were illegal and void.

HELD: The Assessing Officer proposed to reopen the assessment of the two assessment years i.e. 2001-02 & 2002-03 vide notice under section 148 dated 30-07-2010. Thus, it is apparent that the notice issued under section 148 for initiation of reassessment proceedings is beyond the limitation provided under section 149 as exists at the relevant point of time.

It is clear that no notice under section 148 shall be issued in any case after the expiry of 6 years, however, the limitation provided under section 149 is applicable in a situation where the Assessing Officer on its own on the basis of fresh material or information forms an opinion that the income assessable to tax has escaped assessment. Section 150 provides the assessment or reassessment in pursuant to an order of appeal, revision or reference and therefore, the limitation provided under section 149 for reopening of the assessment is not per se applicable when the reopening is based on the directions of the appellate or revisional authority or as per the directions of the Court.

While confirming the order of the Commissioner (Appeals), the Tribunal observed that genuineness of investments could only be considered in the relevant assessment year 1988-89, because the same fell outside the purview of accounting period relevant to the assessment year 1989-90. But nowhere the Tribunal had given any direction that the Assessing Officer should reopen the assessment for the relevant assessment year. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was wrong in holding that the assessment was reopened as per the directions of the Tribunal. As per provisions of clause (b ) of section 149(1), the assessment could have been reopened within a period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year, as the income escaping assessment was more than Rs. 1 lakh. The relevant assessment year ended on 31-3-1989. Therefore, the assessment could have been reopened on or before 31-3-1995. But in the instant case, notice under section 148 was issued on 14-2-2001 and was served upon the assessee on 21-2-2001. Such notice was beyond time and was barred by period of limitation. Therefore, the assessment completed by the Assessing Officer by issue of notice under section 148 was without jurisdiction and void ab initio. Even though the assessment year involved was 1988-89 and amended provisions came into being only with effect from 1-4-1989, i.e., assessment year 1989-90, the law applicable would be one, as it existed on the date of issue of notice. In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and legal position, the assessment order was to be quashed as bad in law and resultant order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was also to be quashed.

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.

Therefore, on the date when the order which formed the subject matter of appeal before the Tribunal came into existence, the assessment for AY 2008-09 had already become time-barred.

9.12 Section 150(2) expressly provides that section 150(1) shall not apply in such circumstances. The legislative intent is clear. Section 150 cannot be utilised as a mechanism to revive a dead assessment or to reopen an assessment which had already become barred by limitation on the relevant date. The provision only saves those cases where the assessment was still alive and capable of being reopened on the date contemplated under section 150(2) of the Act. Therefore, even assuming for the sake of argument that the Tribunal order contained a finding or direction, the Revenue would still be confronted with the statutory bar contained in section 150(2) of the Act. Since the limitation for reopening AY 2008-09 had expired on 31.03.2015 and no time was available on 02.02.2017, the extended jurisdiction contemplated under section 150(1) stood expressly excluded by operation of section 150(2) of the Act.

9.13 In view of the foregoing discussion, we hold that the Tribunal order for AY 2007-08 did not contain any finding or direction within the meaning of section 150(1) of the Act. Consequently, invocation of section 150(1) by the AO for reopening AY 2008-09 was without jurisdiction. Even otherwise, the reopening is independently barred by section 150(2) of the Act since the limitation prescribed under section 149 had already expired on 31.03.2015 and no valid reassessment could have been made on the date of the CIT(A)'s order dated 02.02.2017, which was the order forming the subject matter of appeal before the Tribunal. Therefore, the notice issued under section 148 dated 19.03.2018 and the consequential reassessment framed pursuant thereto are void ab initio, barred by limitation and unsustainable in law. Accordingly, we quash the notice issued under section 148 of the Act as well as the consequential reassessment order. Since we have allowed the legal grounds challenging the assumption of jurisdiction itself, the other grounds raised on merits become academic and do not call for adjudication. The first proviso to Section 149(1)(b) requires the determination of whether the time limit prescribed under section 149(1)(b) of the old regime continues to exist for the assessment year 2021-2022 and before. Resultantly, a notice under Section 148 of the new regime cannot be issued if the period of six years from the end of the relevant assessment year has expired at the time of issuance of the notice. This also ensures that the new time limit of ten years prescribed under section 149(1)(b) of the new regime applies prospectively. For example, for the assessment year 2012-2013, the ten year period would have expired on 31 March 2023, while the six year period expired on 31 March 2019. Without the proviso to Section 149(1)(b) of the new regime, the Revenue could have had the power to reopen assessments for the year 2012-2013 if the escaped assessment amounted to Rupees fifty lakhs or more. The proviso limits the retrospective operation of Section 149(1)(b) to protect the interests of the assesses.

7. A combined reading of the above observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and the findings of Hon'ble Delhi High Court makes it clear that the test for checking the validity of notices issued under section 148 under new regime for AYs 2021-22 or prior years is whether the period of six years has expired at the time of issue of such notice and in that case the notice under section 148 becomes invalid. These observations also makes it clear that the time limit of ten years as per the amended provisions of section 149(1)(b) can be applied only prospectively. In assessee's case when we apply this test for AY 2015-16, the period of six years has expired on 31.03.2022 and therefore the notice dated 28.07.2022 under section 148 of the Act for AY 2015-16 is invalid since it is barred by limitation. Section 148 provides provisions for initiation of the reassessment proceedings. The initiation has to be made with the issue of a notice under section 148 on the assessee concerned. In the instant case from the facts alone, the notice for the assessment year 1981-82 was barred by limitation under section 149(1)(a)(ii ) and as such the assessment done in pursuance of time-barred notice was liable to be quashed. Mere acceptance, acquiescence and participation in such a proceeding where notice is served beyond the period of statutory limitation cannot remedy the defect for not issuing the notice within the period of limitation, and that does not confer authority on the Assessing Officer to assume jurisdiction. Service of notice within the statutory period is a sine qua non and is an indispensable requisite for the initiation of assessment proceeding under section 148 where income has escaped assessment. The Assessing Officer, in the instant case, having failed to comply with the statutory requirement, could not assume jurisdiction and as such, the assessment order for the assessment year 1981-82 in the assessment proceedings passed by him pursuant to such time-barred notice for the said assessment year could not be sustained and no appellate authority including the Tribunal could give authority or jurisdiction to the Assessing Officer in such cases, as no life could be given to a dead horse. Further, in all the notices of the assessment years 1982-83 to 1986-87 including the assessment year 1981-82, there was no mention as to the status of the assessee even though the department was aware of the status of the assesee as individual having already assessed the assessee in the said status, i.e., in the ‘individual’ capacity only on salary income.

If the department sought to assess him in the status of ‘oral trust’, the status should have been mentioned in the notice itself. Without mentioning the status in the notice itself, the said notice could not be taken advantage of to start proceedings under section 148 against the ‘oral trust’. Therefore, the assessment for all the years under consideration made pursuant to such invalid notice, must be quashed.

Whatever and howsoever noble may be the purpose of any trust (religious or evangelic), they cannot escape themselves from the responsibility of accountability before the revenue. Otherwise, the very purpose of the existence of the revenue to control the source of funds and expenditures of any person/assessee would be futile.

The primary onus to furnish the accounts to the Income-tax Department like all other law-abiding citizens irrespective of caste, creed, colour, community and religion heavily lies on the person/assessee. In the instant case the assessee as an individual might be receiving salary for the work done by him sincerely on propagation of Christianity but that did not mean that the department would close its eyes to the accounts maintained by him for the funds received from abroad and expenditures thereof.

In the result, the appeals were to be allowed.

The Assessing Officer has to serve a demand notice on the assessee under section 156 only if any tax, etc., is payable in consequence of any order passed under the Act. It was not denied that reassessment order passed on 28-3-2002 did not raise any demand of tax. The Assessing Officer was, therefore, not liable to serve any demand notice upon the assessee pursuant to the reassessment order. The issue of the demand notice on 17-5-2002 was unnecessary and had to be ignored as superfluous. [Para 8]

The argument, that the assessee could not challenge the ‘nil’ demand order made by the Assessing Officer, could not be appreciated. Even if no demand is created, but the assessee feels aggrieved by the reassessment order, then it is open to it to file an appeal and challenge the correctness of the order. [Para 9]

However, the contention of the assessee, that the notice under section 148 had been issued beyond the period prescribed, had force and was required to be accepted. The reasons recorded in the notice showed that there was no allegation that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment because of the failure of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts. On the contrary, the assessee had disclosed the dividend income and interest income in the profit and loss account and was alleged to have claimed deduction thereon under section 80-I in respect of the ‘A’ unit. That was only a legal position taken by the assessee after furnishing all the material facts. It is open to the assessee to put forth a legal contention or claim after furnishing all the material particulars. The assessee cannot be shut out from doing so. He cannot be said to have furnished untrue particulars or incomplete particulars for having raised a legal plea. The inference from the facts is for the Assessing Officer to draw. The duty of the assessee, even under the proviso to section 147, extends only to the furnishing of all the material facts. It is not for him to advice the Assessing Officer as to what inference should be drawn therefrom. The assessee, having filed the basic facts, may raise his own inference therefrom and put forth the same to the Assessing Officer which the Assessing Officer may, in his wisdom, accept or reject. But rejection of the assessee’s inference from the material facts cannot be equated with furnishing of untrue or incomplete particulars necessary for the assessment. In that view of the matter, the assessment order passed on 28-3-2002 was invalid, the notice under section 148 having been issued beyond the period of limitation, prescribed under the proviso to section 147. It is now well-settled that the issue of a valid notice under section 148 is a condition precedent for the validity of the reassessment. Therefore, the assessee was right in saying that the limitation for rectification under section 154 should be reckoned from the date of the original assessment order passed on 29-11-1996. In that case, the 4 years period expired on 31-3-2001. The order under section 154 having been passed on 28-2-2003 was barred by limitation and, hence, invalid. [Para 10]

Time limit for issue of notice under section 143(2) for the purposes of making assessment or reassessment under section 147

7.3 Section 148(1) provides that before making any assessment, reassessment or re-computation under section 147, the Assessing Officer shall serve a notice under section 148, on the assessee, requiring him to furnish his return of income and the provisions of the Act shall apply as if the return furnished in response to such notice were a return required to be furnished under section 139.

The Tribunal has held that assessment under section 147 is invalid if the notice under section 143(2) is not issued within 12 months from the end of the month in which return under section 147 was filed (after issuance of notice under section 148). [See Raj Kumar Chawla v. ITO [2005] 94 ITD 1 (Delhi)(SB)]

To cure such time barred assessments, the law has been amended retrospectively. Two new provisos to sub-section (1) have been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-10-1991 to provide as follows:

(a) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2) as it stood immediately before the amendment of said sub-section by the Finance Act, 2002, but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

(b) Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2)(ii) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2)(ii), but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

Further, an Explanation has been inserted, with effect from 1-10-2005 in section 148(1) so as to clarify that the provisions of the aforesaid provisos shall not apply in relation to any return which has been furnished on or after 1-10-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148(1).

Thus, so far as returns furnished on or after 1-10-2005 are concerned, the pre-amendment law will apply and the notices will have to be served within a period of 12 months specified in section 143(2).

Reduction of the time limits provided for completion of assessment and reassessment

7.4 Section 153 provides for time limit for completion of assessments and reassessments of total income and FBT. Section 153B provides for the time limit for completion of assessment in cases where search has been initiated under section 132 or books of account, other documents or any assets have been requisitioned under section 132A.

The time limits specified for completion of assessments and re-assessments in the aforesaid sections 153 and 153B have been amended with effect from 1-6-2006 to provide that the time limits specified under the aforesaid sections, shall be reduced by three months. To illustrate, for assessment year 2005-06, the regular assessment under section 143 or a best judgment assessment under section 144 would have to be completed by 31-12-2007 as against 31-3-2008 earlier.

However, where a notice under section 148 has been served after 1-4-2005, no reassessment order under section 147 can be passed after the expiry of nine months from the end of the financial year in which it has been served.

2025 (5) TMI 722 - BOMBAY HIGH COURT Other Citation: 2025:BHC - GOA:868 - DB GURPREET SINGH VERSUS DEPUTY COMMISSIONER OF INCOME 'TAX) Reopening of assessment u/s 147 - period of limitation - notices issued u/s 148 of the old regime - HELD THAT:- A notice under Section 148 of the IT Act accompanied by an order under Section 148A (d) is required to be issued within the time stipulated under Section 149 of the IT Act. Section 148A (d) does not govern the computation of time as contemplated in terms of Section 149 of the IT Act. The entire process under Section 148A(a) to (d) and the issuance of notice under Section 148 has to be completed within the total time available in terms of Section 149 (1) of the IT Act for issuance of notice under Section 148. A notice issued under Section 148 of the IT Act which is beyond the time line stipulated under Section 149 (1) is non-complaint and invalid. The timeline under Section 148A (d) is for the Assessing Officer to comply with the stipulations and the streamlining contemplated under Section 148A. This is primarily to bring in transparency and accountability into the system and is intended for the benefit of the assessees. However, to suggest that Section 148A (d) extends the time limit u/s 149 (1) and/or has a bearing on the time under Section 149 (1) is a submission which is misconceived and lacks legal sanctity. Delhi High Court in Ram Balram Buildhome Pvt. Ltd. [2025 (2) TMI 55 - DELHI HIGH COURT] applying the ratio of the decisions in Ashish Agarwal and Rajeev Bansal (supra) came to the conclusion that the remainder period with the Assessment Officer was twenty-nine days from 01/06/2021 when the reassessment proceedings commenced for issuing notice under Section 148 of the IT Act. The limitation for passing of the order under Section 148A (d) expired on 12/07/2022. Accordingly, the notice under Section 148A of the IT Act issued on 30/07/2022 was held to be beyond limitation and the same was quashed. The Delhi High Court also relied on the observations made in the case of Raminder Singh [2023 (9)' TMI 985 - DELHI HIGH COURT] wherein it was held that one month from the end of the month in which the time available to the assessee to respond to the notice under clause (b) of Section 148A expires is available to the Assessment Officer to pass an order under Section 148A (d) of the IT Act. It was further held that notice under Section 148 of the IT Act that is not accompanied by an order under Section 148A (d) of the Act would be non-compliant with the IT Act and no such notice could be issued beyond the period as specified under Section 149 (1) of the IT Act. This decision of the Delhi High Court is consistent with our view based on the interpretation of the decisions in Ashish Agarwal [2022 (5) TMI 240 - SUPREME COURT] and Rajeev Bansal [2024 (10) TMI 264 - SUPREME COURT (LB)]. Thus, we hold that the notice issued by Respondent No. 1 under Section 148 of the IT Act is beyond the time period specified u/s 149 (1) of the IT Act. Assessee appeal allowed.

On appeal : HELD: Section 148 provides provisions for initiation of the reassessment proceedings. The initiation has to be made with the issue of a notice under section 148 on the assessee concerned. In the instant case from the facts alone, the notice for the assessment year 1981-82 was barred by limitation under section 149(1)(a)(ii ) and as such the assessment done in pursuance of time-barred notice was liable to be quashed. Mere acceptance, acquiescence and participation in such a proceeding where notice is served beyond the period of statutory limitation cannot remedy the defect for not issuing the notice within the period of limitation, and that does not confer authority on the Assessing Officer to assume jurisdiction. Service of notice within the statutory period is a sine qua non and is an indispensable requisite for the initiation of assessment proceeding under section 148 where income has escaped assessment. The Assessing Officer, in the instant case, having failed to comply with the statutory requirement, could not assume jurisdiction and as such, the assessment order for the assessment year 1981-82 in the assessment proceedings passed by him pursuant to such time-barred notice for the said assessment year could not be sustained and no appellate authority including the Tribunal could give authority or jurisdiction to the Assessing Officer in such cases, as no life could be given to a dead horse. Further, in all the notices of the assessment years 1982-83 to 1986-87 including the assessment year 1981-82, there was no mention as to the status of the assessee even though the department was aware of the status of the assesee as individual having already assessed the assessee in the said status, i.e., in the ‘individual’ capacity only on salary income.

If the department sought to assess him in the status of ‘oral trust’, the status should have been mentioned in the notice itself. Without mentioning the status in the notice itself, the said notice could not be taken advantage of to start proceedings under section 148 against the ‘oral trust’. Therefore, the assessment for all the years under consideration made pursuant to such invalid notice, must be quashed.

Whatever and howsoever noble may be the purpose of any trust (religious or evangelic), they cannot escape themselves from the responsibility of accountability before the revenue. Otherwise, the very purpose of the existence of the revenue to control the source of funds and expenditures of any person/assessee would be futile.

The primary onus to furnish the accounts to the Income-tax Department like all other law-abiding citizens irrespective of caste, creed, colour, community and religion heavily lies on the person/assessee. In the instant case the assessee as an individual might be receiving salary for the work done by him sincerely on propagation of Christianity but that did not mean that the department would close its eyes to the accounts maintained by him for the funds received from abroad and expenditures thereof.

In the result, the appeals were to be allowed.

On appeal, the assessee contended before the first appellate authority that assessments had become time-barred as they could not have been framed on the aforesaid dates on the basis of first set of notices issued on 9-10-1973. The appellate authority took the view that perusal of record did not reveal that any notice under section 148 had been issued on 9-10-1973 and the photocopy of the notices produced did not give reasons for initiating the proceedings. On second appeal:

HELD: Once notices under section 148 have been issued, the proceedings initiated through them have to be taken to their logical end. In other words, either assessments should be framed on the basis of those proceedings or the Assessing Officer may specifically drop the proceedings, may be on the ground that no sufficient material was available for holding that income liable to tax had escaped assessment. Even if an assessee does not comply with those notices by fling the income-tax returns, the remedy which is open to the revenue is not to issue fresh notices under section 148 but to issue notices under section 142(1) or to have completed the assessments under section 144. Thus, if the assessments have got barred by limitation, they cannot be revived by issuing fresh notices. In the instant case, this position was clear to the Assessing Officer and other officers of the department as could be gathered from a DO letter written by ITO to his IAC in which he had written that in this case, the assessment for the assessment year 1972-73 had been completed on a total income of Rs. 2,53,400 on 20-2-1985 as a result of which a demand was created. He had further written that the assessment was completed in pursuance of action initiated under section 148 subsequent to an action under section 148 got time- barred. He had further mentioned that this matter was discussed with the Commissioner and that according to the Commissioner the demand was unrealisable and assessment was likely to be annulled.

In the circumstances, it was to be held that since in the instant case valid Notices for the assessment years under consideration had been issued by The Assessing Officer on 9-10-1973 but he failed to complete the assessments within the time allowed under law, the assessments got barred by time for both the years. Introductory Remarks

1. The procedure for assessment is streamlined in Chapter XIV of the Income-tax Act (the Act). The provisions of sections 147 to 153 of the Income-tax Act (the Act) deal with assessments covering escapement of income, time limit for issuance of notice etc. The corresponding provision in the Indian Income-tax Act 1922 (the 1922 Act) was covered in section 34 of the 1922 Act. Virtually section 147 of the Act corresponds to section 34(1) and Explanation of the 1922 Act.

However, with regard to service of notice, the Supreme Court in the case of R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 33 Taxman 229/166 ITR 163 succinctly explained the difference between the Act and the 1922 Act.

"The scheme of the Act so far as notice for reassessment is concerned, is quite different. What used to be contained in section 34 of the 1922 Act has been spread out into three sections, being sections 147, 148 and 149 in the 1961 Act (as the Act stood then). A clear distinction has been made out between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice' under the 1961 Act. Section 34 of the 1922 Act conferred jurisdiction on the Assessing Officer to reopen an assessment subject to service of notice within the prescribed period. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It categorically prescribes that no notice under section 148 shall be issued after the prescribed limitation has lapsed. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as a condition precedent to making the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested in the Assessing Officer to proceed to reassess. The mandate of section 148(1) is that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued. In the present case, admittedly, the notice was issued within the prescribed period of limitation, as 31-3-1970 was the last day of that period. Service under the 1961 Act is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction in the Assessing Officer to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. As the Assessing Officer in the instant case had issued notice within limitations, the appeal was to be allowed and the order of the High Court was vacated."

The Finance Bill, 2021 proposes to insert a new section 148A which contains provisions for conducting an inquiry and providing an opportunity before issuance of notice under new section 148 of the Act. However, this procedure of enquiry, providing opportunity and passing an order, before issuing notice under new section 148 of the Act, shall not be applicable in search or requisition cases.

Section 149 of the Act is proposed to be amended with regard to time limit for issuance of notice.

Section 147 of the Act in simple words

2. If the Assessing Officer has reason to believe that any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment, he may assess/reassess such income. For this purpose, a notice shall be issued under section 148 of the Act. Once an assessment has been reopened, any other income which has escaped assessment and which comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer subsequently in the course of the proceeding under section 147 of the Act, can also be included in the assessment.

Conditions - There are two conditions -

1.

The Assessing Officer must have reason to believe that income or profits or gains chargeable to income-tax had escaped assessment.

2.

Such an escapement had occurred by reason of either omission or failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully or truly all material facts necessary for his assessment of that year

It may be noted that in the judgment of the Punjab & Haryana High Court, the starting point for the purpose of reckoning the period of limitation for issue of notice under section 148 was taken as the date of the appellate order which was the subject matter of appeal before the Tribunal. However, in ITO v. Eastern Coal Co. Ltd. [1975] 101 ITR 477 , the Calcutta High Court took the view that the expression "the order which was the subject matter of appeal, reference or revision" appearing in section 150(2) referred to the original order of assessment and held that it was with reference to the date of such an order that the period of limitation for issue of notice under section 148 has to be reckoned. This is clear from the observations of the court in page 487 of the report to the effect that on 29-12-1960 when the original order of assessment was passed, action could have been taken for reassessment for the assessment year 1958-59 as "that was the date when the order which was the subject-matter of appeal was passed". If this judgment is applied, our view in the preceding paragraph that on 22-3-1990 the Assessing Officer could have validly issued notice under section 148 to reopen the assessment for the assessment year 1980-81 would appear to be correct. The Andhra Pradesh High Court in CIT v. G. Viswanatham [1988] 172 ITR 401 was faced with the situation where both on the dates on which the assessment order and the appellate were passed, the notice of reassessment was found to have been barred by limitation. The High Court has taken the view that the expression "the order which was the subject matter of the appeal" referred to the original order of the assessment and not the appellate order, as is clear from the observations of the court towards the end of page 410 and the top of page 411 of the report. The High Court observed, vis-a-vis the judgment of the Calcutta High Court (supra) that the said judgment "...in fact, supports our proposition rather than militate against it." It was ultimately held that both with reference to the date of the assessment order as also with reference to the date of the appellate order, the notice of reassessment was invalid. Section 148, read with sections 142(1) and 147, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income escaping assessment - Issue of notice for - Assessment year 1997-98 - For assessment year 1997-98, Assessing Officer, on 24-8-1998, issued notice to assessee under section 142(1) - Assessee filed his return on 16-2-2000 - As return filed by assessee was beyond time limit prescribed under section 139(4), i.e., on or before 31-3-1999, Assessing Officer initiated reassessment proceedings against assessee under section 147 and completed assessment - Whether since in instant case revenue had not issued any notice under section 142(1) before end of assessment year and return furnished by assessee under section 139(4) on 16-2-2000 had been filed beyond time-limit prescribed under section 139(4) and was invalid return, in such circumstances, notice under section 148 had to be issued when an assessment, reassessment or recomputation was to be made under section 147 to tax income which had escaped assessment - Held, yes - Whether therefore, assessment completed without issuing notice under section 148 was invalid and bad in law - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1997-98, the Assessing Officer, on 24-8-1998, issued notice to assessee under section 142(1). The assessee filed his return on 16-2-2000. As the return filed by assessee was beyond time-limit prescribed under section 139(4), i.e., on or before 31-3-1999, the Assessing Officer initiated reassessment proceedings against the assessee under section 147 and completed the assessment. The assessee filed the instant miscellaneous application and contended that no notice under section 148 was ever issued before passing the assessment order. Hence, the assessment under section 147 became invalid.

HELD: No return had been filed by the assessee as per the provisions of the Act and the so-called return filed beyond the time-limit prescribed under section 139(4) on 16-2-2000 was an invalid and non est return in the eyes of law. The proceedings to fasten liability on the assessee-company was commenced by the department for the assessment year 1997-98 by issue of a notice under section 142(1) dated 24-8-1998 for the first time. Prior to it, no notice or proceeding had started. Subsequently, several notices had been issued by the department under section 142(1) but all these notices were apparently issued after the end of the assessment year, i.e., 31-3-1998. As per the provisions of section 147, the income would be treated as escaped assessment at the end of the assessment year where no return had been filed. In the instant case, in the absence of return, the provisions were to tax income that escaped assessment and not to tax income which was not assessed as on 1-4-1998. Thus, the income could be assessed only by issuance of notice under section 148 and in the instant case, no such notice had been issued by the department under section 148. Mere issuance of notice under section 142(1) after the end of the assessment year in the absence of voluntary return by the assessee could not give rise to valid proceedings under the Act.

HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had observed in the order for the assessment year 1998-99 'the Assessing Officer is, however, free to take action in assessment year 1997-98'. The above observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) could not be held as a direction. Following the decision of the Supreme Court in Rajinder Nath v. CIT [1979] 120 ITR 14 / 2 Taxman 204, it could safely be held that the Commissioner (Appeals) had not given any direction to the Assessing Officer to initiate reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98. Therefore, the notice issued under section 148 on 16-11-2004 was beyond the time-limit prescribed in the Act. In this case the assessment year ended on 31-3-1998 and, therefore, no notice under section 148 could have been issued after 31-3-2004. The appellate order for the assessment year 1998-99 had been passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) on 10-6-2004 and as per law, no reassessment for the assessment year 1997-98 could have been made after 31-3-2004. For argument's sake if it was admitted that the Commissioner (Appeals) had given direction to the Assessing Officer to initiate reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98 in his order dated 10-6-2004, even then under the law, the direction given by the Commissioner (Appeals) on 10-6-2004 was against the provisions of section 150(2).

In the instant case, initiation of the reassessment proceedings was barred by other provision of the Act on 10-6-2004 when the appellate order for the assessment year 1998-99 was passed. The assessment year 1997-98 had ended on 31-3-1998. Reopening of the assessment for the assessment year 1997-98 was permissible under the Act upto 31-3-2004. However, the appellate order, on the basis of which reassessment was initiated, had been passed on 10-6-2004. On the said date initiation of reassessment proceedings for the assessment year 1997-98 was prohibited by law, and, hence, reassessment proceeding initiated after 31-3-2004 was clearly barred by limitation.

Therefore, the reassessment order was time barred by limitation and, hence, was liable to be quashed.

In the result, the appeal was to be allowed.

We have considered the rival submissions and have gone through the material available on record. In this case, we are concerned with the issue as to whether the notices under section 148 of the Act issued in the month of March, 2001 were validly issued or not. It is not disputed that the then Assessing Officer had issued notice under section 148 of the Act for all the years under appeal in the month of February, 1997/March, 1998. Therefore, the machinery for reassessment is set in motion and the Assessing Officer has to adopt the prescribed procedure for making the reassessment. However, in the present cases, admittedly, the reassessment proceedings initiated by the above notices have not been concluded to a logical end. Be that as it may, the Assessing Officer issued fresh notices under section 148 of the Act in the month of March, 2001. In the case of Jai Dev & Co. v. ITO [2001] 116 Taxman 86 Trib., the Tribunal held that even if an assessee does not comply with the notices issued under section 148, the remedy which is open to the revenue is not to issue fresh notice under section 148 but to issue notice under section 142(1) or to have completed the assessment under section 144. If the assessment has got barred by limitation, the same cannot be revived by issuing fresh notice. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Trustees of H.E.H. the Nizam’s Supplemental Family Trust v. CIT [2000] 242 ITR 381 has laid down that the position of law is settled inasmuch as subsequent proceedings under section 148 of the Act cannot be commenced unless and until there is disposal of the earlier proceedings. Similar view was expressed by the Kerala High Court in the case of Smt. Niloter Hameed v. ITO [1999] 235 ITR 161 and also by the Chandigarh Bench of the Tribunal in the case of H.P. State Forest Corporation Ltd. v. JCIT [2002] 80 ITD 591 . No contrary decision of any High Court or the Supreme Court has been brought to our notice for taking a different view. The plea of the learned Departmental Representative that that the notices issued in March, 2001 are not during the pendency of the earlier notices issued and as such are fresh notices issued validly, cannot be accepted. The machinery for reassessment was already set in motion by the issuance of the earlier notices and if the reassessments were not completed for whatever reasons, such reassessments cannot be revived by issuing fresh notices as the time for completing the reassessments in pursuance to the earlier notices held already expired.

6. In the light of the above observations, we are of the opinion that the notices under section 148 issued in the month of March 2001 are not validly issued. Consequently the CIT(A) was justified in cancelling the assessments completed on the basis of the said notices.

7. In the result, the appeals are dismissed.

"In view of law laid down by the hon'ble Supreme Court and High Court, the principles of judicial discipline and propriety and binding precedent, we hold as under:

(a)

Judicial discipline and propriety are the two significant facets of administration of justice. The principles of judicial discipline require that the orders of the higher appellate authorities should be followed unreservedly by the subordinate authorities. The mere fact that the order of the appellate authority is not "acceptable" to the Department in itself an objectionable phrase or that is the subject matter of an appeal can furnish no ground for not following it unless its operation has been suspended by a competent court. If this healthy rule is not followed, the result will only be undue harassment to assessees and chaos in administration of tax laws.

(b)

Just as the judgments and orders of the Supreme Court have to be faithfully obeyed and carried out throughout the territory of India under article 141 of the Constitution, so should be the judgments and orders of the High Court by all inferior courts and tribunals subject to supervisory jurisdiction within the State under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution.

(c)

If an officer under the Income-tax Act, 1961 refuses to carry out the clear and unambiguous direction in a judgment passed by the hon'ble Supreme Court or High Court or the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal then in effect, it is denial of justice and is destructive of one of the basic principles in the administration of justice based on hierarchy of the court.

(d)

Unless there is a stay obtained by the authorities under the Income-tax Act, 1961 from higher forum, the mere fact of filing appeal or Special Leave Petition will not entitle the authority not to comply with the order of the High Court. Even though the authority may have filed an appeal or Special Leave Petition but either could not obtain a stay or the stay is refused, the order of the High Court must be complied with. Mere filing of an appeal or Special Leave Petition against the judgment or order of the High Court does not result in the assailed judgment or order becoming inoperative and unworthy of being complied with.

In view of the principles settled by the hon'ble Supreme Court and by High Courts in the judgments, we direct the respondents to maintain judicial discipline and follow the doctrine of binding precedent and be careful in future, having due regard to the authorities of the court, keeping in mind the judicial propriety and discipline."

The provisions of Sections 147 to 151 are specific provisions which enable the Department to reassess any income that has escaped assessment. These provisions underwent significant changes with effect from 1.4.1989. In the light of these changes, each and every initiation of assessment proceedings made on or after 1.4.1989 must be governed by the amended provisions as held by the decision of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Rakesh Aggarwal v. Asstt. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 496/[1996] 87 Taxman 306. Under Section 148(1), before making an assessment, reassessment and computation u/s 147, the Assessing Officer is required to serve on the assessee a notice requiring him to furnish a return of income. Under Section 148(2), the AO, before issuing any notice u/s 148(1), is required to record his reasons for doing so. Rajeev Bansal [2024] 167 taxmann.com 70 (SC), it was held that notices issued under the erstwhile section 148 for assessment years 2013-14 and 2014-15 shall be deemed to be valid, provided they fall within the permissible time frame (surviving period) as preserved under the directions laid down in the said judgment. The Supreme Court, in the case of Rajeev Bansal, has elaborated upon the concept of the ‘surviving period’ for determining the validity of notices issued under section 148 after the pronouncement of the judgment in Union of India v. Ashish Aggarwal (supra). This interpretation is specifically discussed in the said judgment. The period from the date of the issuance of the erstwhile notice till 4-5-2022, the date on which the Supreme Court had rendered the decision in Ashish Agarwal (supra) is required to be excluded. Additionally, the time provided till the date of providing the material, which should have accompanied a notice under section 148A(b), as well as the time available to the assessee to respond to the said notice was also required to be excluded. The ‘surviving period’ is required to be computed and separately added to determine the validity of the notice issued under section 148. The surviving period is calculated by taking into account the number of days between the original date of issuance of the deemed notice under section 148 and 30-6-2021, as clarified in judicial pronouncements following the judgment in Ashish Agarwal and considering the entire facts of the case and the law laid down by the Apex court in the case of UOI v Rajeev Bansal (supra), it is opined that in the instant case the surviving period was of twenty four days and the revised timeline for issue of notice under section 148 (under the new regime) expired on 26-6-2022 and the notice issued in the instant case on 25-7-2022, is clearly barred by limitation and the impugned reassessment proceedings dated 23-5-2023, passed under section 147 read with section 144 (with 144B), is not legally valid and the same is quashed. Pertinently, it is to be pointed out at this stage that 'if an order is passed by a judicial or quasi-judicial authority having no jurisdiction, it is an obligation of Appellate Court to rectify the error and set aside the order passed by the authority or forum having no jurisdiction'. Though the files pertaining to the reassessment proceedings of the appellant were transferred, the second respondent has no authority to continue the reassessment proceedings under section 129 and hence, the notice dated 14-12-2018 issued by him is also held to be invalid. Admittedly, no notice under section 148 was issued by the second respondent, who is the jurisdictional Assessing Officer, for reassessment of the return of income of the appellant, within the time frame stipulated under the Act. 7.3 Section 148(1) provides that before making any assessment, reassessment or re-computation under section 147, the Assessing Officer shall serve a notice under section 148, on the assessee, requiring him to furnish his return of income and the provisions of the Act shall apply as if the return furnished in response to such notice were a return required to be furnished under section 139.

The Tribunal has held that assessment under section 147 is invalid if the notice under section 143(2) is not issued within 12 months from the end of the month in which return under section 147 was filed (after issuance of notice under section 148). [See Raj Kumar Chawla v. ITO [2005] 94 ITD 1 (Delhi)(SB)]

To cure such time barred assessments, the law has been amended retrospectively. Two new provisos to sub-section (1) have been inserted retrospectively with effect from 1-10-1991 to provide as follows:

(a)

Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2) as it stood immediately before the amendment of said sub-section by the Finance Act, 2002, but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

(b)

Where a return has been furnished during the period from 1-10-1991 to 30-9-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148 and, subsequently a notice has been served under section 143(2)(ii) after the expiry of twelve months specified in the proviso to section 143(2)(ii), but before the expiry of the time limit for making the assessment or reassessment as specified in section 153(2), such notice shall be deemed to be valid notice.

Further, an Explanation has been inserted, with effect from 1-10-2005 in section 148(1) so as to clarify that the provisions of the aforesaid provisos shall not apply in relation to any return which has been furnished on or after 1-10-2005 in response to a notice served under section 148(1).

Thus, so far as returns furnished on or after 1-10-2005 are concerned, the pre-amendment law will apply and the notices will have to be served within a period of 12 months specified in section 143(2).

Service vs. issue of notice - Section 148 of enjoins that the AO must serve on the assessee a notice requiring him to furnish a return of his income, in respect of which he/she is assessable under the 1961 Act during the PY corresponding to the relevant AY. In stark contrast, s. 149 speaks only of the issuance of a notice under the preceding section within a prescribed period. S. 149 does not mandate that such a notice must also be served on the assessee within the prescribed period [Mayawati v. CIT [2010] 321 ITR 349 (Delhi)].

Limitation provided u/s 149 for issuance of notice commences from date when notice is issued and not when notice served [Synfonia Tradelinks (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2021] 127 taxmann.com 153/281 Taxman 557 (Del.); Sadhna Tolasariya v. ITO [2021] 127 taxmann.com 127/281 Taxman 354 (Mad.)].

Time-limit applies for issue of notice - The word 'issued' in section 149 should be given its natural meaning and not the strained wider meaning of 'served'. Consequently, where the notice was issued within time but was served on the assessee after the expiry of the time-limit, it could not be held to be invalid [Jai Hanuman Trading Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 110 ITR 36 (P&H - FB)].

It is date of issue of notice u/s 148, and not actual receipt of notice by assessee which is relevant to return a finding as to whether reassessment proceedings have been initiated within period of limitation [CIT v. K. G. Singhania [2012] 24 taxmann.com 208/209 Taxman 45 (P&H)].

Mere generation of notice do not constitute issue of notice – Function of generation of notice on ITBA portal and digital signing of notice is executed by Assessing Officer while function of drafting of e-mail to which notice is attached and triggering e-mail to assessee is performed by ITBA e-mail software system. Thus, mere generation of notice u/s 148 on ITBA software cannot in fact or in law constitute issue of notice, it is only upon due despatch that notice can be said to have been issued. 'Despatch' as per section 13 of Information Technology Act of 2000 is sine qua non for issuance of notice through electronic mail for purpose of s. 149 [Suman Jeet Agarwal v. ITO [2022] 143 taxmann.com 11/[2023] 290 Taxman 493 (Delhi)].

Date of issuance of notice in case of Postal department - Date of issue of notice would be the date on which the same was handed over for service to the proper officer or Postal Department. Since the Income-tax Department is covered by 'book now pay later' scheme, the further requirement of properly stamping envelope with adequate postal stamp, would not be germane. Therefore, where reassessment notice was handed over to Postal Department before stipulated time, it would not be barred by time factor [Rajesh Sunderdas Vaswani v. DCIT [2017] 88 taxmann.com 602 (Guj.)].

Where AO issued and dispatched a reopening notice against assessee on last date of expiry of period of limitation, even though notice was franked by Postal department later, said notice was not barred by limitation [Rajmannar Ramaswamy v. ITO [2021] 130 taxmann.com 431 (Mad.)].

FACT: For the assessment year 1987-88, the assessee’s return of income was due to be filed on 31-7-1987, but it was not filed even till 25-10-1988, when a notice under section 148 was issued. In response to the said notice, the assessee filed its return on 30-3-1989, and the assessment was completed on 22-8-1990 under section 143(3) read with section 147(a). The assessee appealed against the assessment order contending that the assessment officer was not competent to issue the notice under section 148 until the limitation for filing the return under section 139(4) expired and as such the return filed on 30-3-1989. even after the service of notice under section 148, was to be treated as a return under section 139(4) and the notice under section 148 was non est in law. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that as there was no valid return before the notice was issued, the notice under section 148 was valid and upheld the assessment order.

On second appeal, the assessee reiterating its earlier arguments, contended (i) that the notice under section 148 was invalid; and (ii) that the return filed in response to such notice was to be treated as a return under section 139(4), and hence, the assessment completed on 22-8-1990 was barred by limitation.

HELD: As regards the validity of notice issued under section 148, the first condition laid down in section 148(1) for issuance of notice is that it should be issued before making assessment, re-assessment and re-computation of income. In the instant case, the notice under section 148 was issued on 25-10-1988 and the assessment was completed on 22-8-1990. Thus, the notice issued under section 148 was valid as it was issued before the assessment was made. Then, according to the provisions envisaged and limitation laid down in section 149(1), no notice under section 148 would be issued in cases falling under clause (a) of section 147 for the relevant assessment year if eight years had elapsed from the end of that year. In the instant case, the relevant assessment year was 1987-88 and 8 years from the end of that year would elapse in 1996. But the notice under section 148 was already issued on 25-10-1988 and was, therefore, well within the prescribed time limit of eight years, i.e., before 31-3-1990. The assessee’s contention that the notice under section 148 issued prior to 31-3-1990 could not take the right of the assessee to file the return under section 139(4) was also not tenable as, in the instant case, no return was furnished before the issuance of notice under section 148. Moreover, there was no provision in the Act to invalidate the notice under section 148 by furnishing of return after the issue of such notice.

Insofar as the period of limitation is concerned, the present dispute relates to the assessment year 1992-93 and as per the then existing provision of limitation specified under Section 149 of the Act, the period of limitation was 10 years. Accordingly, the reassessment notice could be issued on or before 31.05.2001 whereas in the instant case reassessment notice under Section 148 of the Act was issued on 11.04.2001, which was within the period of limitation. Consequently, we are of the opinion that the notice issued under Section 148 of the Act was issued within the period of limitation.

17. In the light of the aforesaid, the question of invoking the provision of Section 150(1) of the Act does not arise and it is not necessary for us to dwell on this aspect of the matter. We may however, observe that Section 150 of the Act provides that the power to issue a notice under Section 148 of the Act in consequence of or giving effect to any finding or direction of the Appellate or Revisional Authority or the Court is subject to the provisions contained in Section 150(2) of the Act. Section 150(2) of the Act provides that the direction issued under Section 150(1) of the Act cannot be given by the Appellate or Revisional Authority or by the Court if on the date on which the order in appeal or revision was passed, the reassessment proceeding had become barred by time. Under Section 150(2) of the Act the Appellate or the Revisional Authority or the Court could give direction for reassessment only in respect of that assessment year. In respect of reassessment, proceedings could be initiated on the date of passing of the order in appeal. Since we have held that the notice was issued within the period of limitation, the provision of Section 150(1) of the Act is not applicable in the instant case.

18. In the light of the aforesaid, we do not find any error in the order passed by the Tribunal. The appeal fails and is dismissed. The questions of law are answered accordingly.

Under these circumstances section 292B was not held applicable. He contended before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner that the proceedings under section 147 was bad in law and should be quashed on the ground of non-service of notice under section 148 to him. On reference under section 256(2) it was held that the employee of the assessee appeared before the Assessing Officer only in response to a notice under section 142(1) and not in response to notice under section 148. Section 142 (1) dealt with the enquiry before assessment and the appearance of the employee was to produce accounts or documents before the ITO and the same could not be deem to be knowledge of proceedings under section 147 of the Act. Reassessment ● Notice Period

5.2 Under section 148 of the Act, an assessment can be reopened and for the purpose a notice can be issued to an assessee for filing a return of his income within a specified period, not being less than thirty days. At present, in the printed form of notice under section 148, the assessee is required to furnish a return of his income 'within thirty days'. As per Memorandum explaining provision of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, notices issued under section 148 have been held to be invalid by the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal on the ground that whereas the statute allows the taxpayer a time, 'not being less than thirty days', the notice gives the direction to file a return 'within a period of thirty days'. The Bombay High Court in the case of CIT v. Ekbal & Co. [1945] 13 ITR154 (Bom.) decided a similar issue by laying down that the expressions within thirty days' and 'not less than thirty days' are two quite different things. The above legal position, as such, invalidates all the proceedings initiated through such printed notice(s), which could have been avoided by changing the form of notice.

However, to get over the situation, section 148 of the Act has been amended, with retrospective effect from 1-4-1989 whereby the words 'not being less than 30 days' have been omitted.

The effect of the deletion of the words is that now an Assessing Officer can require an assessee to file a return pursuant to a notice under section 148 of the Act within such period as may be specified in the notice. Thus, now, a notice could be for a shorter period as the minimum time constraint has been removed.

Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996 states that this amendment will also apply to any notice which has already been issued, on or after 1-4-1989.

However, one does not find any specific words or mention of it in the amendment so as to show that such notices have been validated.

The concerned assessees may be adversely affected and may have to agitate the proceedings afresh. In such a situation a question could arise as to whether a mere insertion of the amendment with retrospective effect is sufficient to validate the invalid notice which has been issued needs to be validated. It is felt that the latter action would be necessary. Otherwise, one can validate or invalidate an action at any point of time with no remedy for taxpayers.

Further, it appears that those assessees who had questioned such validity may be able to agitate this issue. However, in cases where pursuant to notices issued after 1-4-1989 reassessment is concluded, it may not be now possible to take a plea that the notices were invalid. In other words, in such cases, it appears that the retrospective amendment would support the case of revenue.

Limitation period for completion of assessments and reassessments

5.3 Section 153 of the Act lays down the time limit for making an order of assessment (two years from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable). Also, Explanation 1 below section 153 of the Act sets out certain circumstances in which certain periods as specified are excluded from the period of limitation.

In a case where an audit under section 142(2A) is ordered, the assessee is required to furnish a report of such audit within the prescribed time. In such a case, the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited under section 142(2 A) and ending with the date on which the assessee furnishes a report of such audit is excluded while reckoning the period of limitation for completion of the assessment, as per Explanation 1(iii) below section 153 of the Act.

As per the Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance (No. 2) Bill, 1996, in a case where the report is not prepared and, therefore, not furnished, the normal time limit of two years is operative and the Assessing Officer does not get any additional time for the purpose of making an assessment because the time taken for furnishing the audit report is not excluded. Exclusion of the period in terms of Explanation 1(iii) could operate only if the report of such audit is furnished.

To obviate the difficulty, the said Explanation has been amended, with effect from 1-4-1997, to provide that the period commencing from the date on which the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited and ending on the date on which the report of such audit was required to be furnished, shall be excluded from the period of limitation.

This would enable extension of the limitation period, at least, by the time permitted, although, the audit report is not furnished.
