Section 150(1), with a non obstante clause, overrides the general time limits prescribed in section 149 for issuing notices under section 148. This provision enables issuing a notice under section 148 for re-assessment at any time for the purpose of giving effect to any finding or direction contained in an order passed by any authority in any proceeding by way of appeal, reference or revision or by a Court. While section 150(1) grants a broad power, section 150(2) imposes a restriction on that power. It states that the provisions of sub-section (1) (i.e., the power to issue notice "at any time") shall not apply in any case where the assessment, reassessment, or recomputation relates to an assessment year in respect of which such reassessment could not have been made at the time the order (which was the subject-matter of the appeal, reference, or revision) was made, by reason of any other provision limiting the time within which any action for reassessment may be taken. This provision ensures that this power cannot be used to revive an assessment year that was already time-barred when the original order (which was the subject of appeal or revision) was made.

The existing provision covered the scenario where an order (the subject of appeal or revision) was made, but did not cover the situation in which proceedings for assessment, reassessment, or recomputation had been initiated by the Assessing Officer, but no order had been passed. Further, section 150 did not specify the time limit within which the notice under section 148 pursuant to the findings or directions contained in any order of the court or authority must be issued.

The Apex Regulatory Body for Direct Taxes in India i.e. CBDT has brought in an Instruction dated 4.3.2021 bearing F.No. 225/40/2021/ITA-II, regarding Selection of Cases for Issue of Notice u/s 148 of the Income Tax Act.

The said CBDT Instruction directs that the undermentioned categories of cases are to be considered as 'potential cases' for taking action u/s 148 of the Act by 31.3.2021 for the AY 2013-14 to AY 2017-18 by the Jurisdictional Assessing Officer (JAO):

i.

Cases where there are Audit Objections (Revenue/Internal);

ii.

Cases of information from any other Government Agency/Law Enforcement Agency;

iii.

Potential cases including:

(a)

Reports of Directorate of Income-tax (Investigation),

(b)

Reports of Directorate of Intelligence & Criminal Investigation,

(c)

Cases from Non-Filer Management System (NMS) & other cases as flagged by the Directorate of Income-tax (Systems) as per risk profiling;

iv.

Cases where information arising out of field survey action, requiring action u/s 148 of the Act.

v.

Cases of information received from any Income-tax authority requiring action u/s 148 of the Act with the approval of Chief Commissioner of Income Tax concerned.

It has been further provided in the said CBDT Instruction that no other category of cases, except the above, shall be considered for taking action u/s 148 of the Act by the JAO.

It has also been clarified that these instructions shall not be applicable to the Central charges and International Taxation charges for which separate instructions are being issued.

Interestingly, the said CBDT Instruction also clarifies that action u/s 148 of the Act shall be taken by the Assessing Officer in respect of the above categories of cases after forming a reasonable belief that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment and 'reasons to believe' shall be recorded and required sanction as per section 151 of the Act shall be obtained before issuing notice u/s 148 of the Act.

It is pertinent to mention here that amendments have been proposed in the Finance Bill 2021, to substitute the existing sections 147 and 148 of the Income Tax Act, to reduce the time period for reopening the already concluded assessments from existing 6 years to 3 years. However, where the escapement of income is suggested to be of Rs 50 lakhs or more in a financial year in the form of undisclosed asset, then the maximum time period for reopening the already concluded assessments is 10 years.

No doubt that the proposed reduction in time period for reopening of assessments from 6 years to 3 years is a welcome and appreciable initiative. However, the issue of concern is the fact that the existing mandatory condition of formation of an independent reason to believe by the assessing authority that income of the assessee has escaped assessment so as to assume lawful jurisdiction u/s 147, is proposed to be substituted with the presence of any flagged information as per the risk management strategy of CBDT or the final audit objection of C&AG, suggesting that income of the assessee has escaped assessment.

However, a further clarification is desirable from CBDT that whether all the present "information" generated in Annual Information Return (AIR) u/s 285BA of the Income tax Act like share transactions, mutual fund transactions, cash deposits, credit card transactions, foreign travel, purchase of immovable property etc. would be considered as the "flagged information" suggesting escapement of income, so as to warrant assumption of jurisdiction under the newly proposed sections 148 and 147. If that being so, then naturally these amendments are of a lot of concern and apprehension because in such cases, suspicion arising out of such flagged information will substitute the existing mandatory condition of formation of reason to believe by the assessing authority.

Also, the existing proviso to section 147 requiring the mandatory condition of failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for the purpose of assessments for reopening the already concluded assessments beyond a period of 4 years and uptill 6 years, has found no place in the newly proposed section 147 and 148.

Further, the newly proposed section 148A, requiring the assessing authority to provide a suitable opportunity of being heard to the assessee and also mandating prior approval of the competent income tax authority before issuing notice u/s 148, and as such being perceived by the Legislature as an adequate safeguard, authorises the assessing authority to proceed with the issuing of notice u/s 148 merely if he thinks it fit to do so and it nowhere requires the formation of an independent reason to believe by such assessing authority, of the escapement of income.

It is expected that the investment by Indians in Cryptocurrency could touch $241 million by 2030. Currently, India has the highest number of crypto owners globally, at 10.07 crores1.

A bill was expected to be presented during the Winter Session of Parliament to regulate Cryptocurrencies. However, it was not introduced, and it is now expected that the Govt. may take up this bill in the Budget Session. If Govt. does not prohibit Indians from dealing in Cryptocurrencies, we expect that the Govt. could introduce a regressive tax regime for Cryptocurrencies.

Considering the size of the market, the amount involved, and the risk coupled with Cryptocurrencies, we expect that the following changes may be brought in the taxation of Cryptocurrencies:

2.1. TDS/TCS provisions

Both sale and purchase of Cryptocurrencies above the threshold limit should be brought within the ambit of TDS/TCS provisions. This will help the Govt. to get the footprints of the investors.

2.2. Reporting in SFT

Both sale and purchase of Cryptocurrencies should be brought within the ambit of reporting in the Statement of Financial Transactions. The trading companies already do similar reporting of sale and purchase of shares and units of mutual funds.

2.3. Higher tax rate

Similar to winnings from Lottery, Game Shows, Puzzle, etc., a higher tax rate of 30% should be levied on the income arising from the sale of Cryptocurrency.

2.4. Loss can't be set off

The losses from the sale of Cryptocurrency should not be allowed to be adjusted from other income and should also not be allowed to be carried forward.

3. Change in re-assessment provisions

The Finance Act 2021 introduced a paradigm shift in the fundamentals on which the entire scheme of re-assessment is based. It substituted sections 147, 148, 149 and 151 and inserted a new section 148A, making a complete change in the assessment proceedings relating to an income escaping assessment and search-related cases.

The new scheme of re-assessment inter-alia reduces the time limit for reopening the assessment from 6 years to 3 years. If the Assessing Officer has evidence in his possession, which reveals that the income escaping assessment, represented in the form of asset, amounts to Rs. 50 lakhs or more, the notice can be issued up to 10 years.

Further, the new scheme also specifies that before issuing a notice under section 148, the Assessing Officer shall conduct enquiries, if required, and provide an opportunity of being heard to the assessee. After considering his reply, the Assessing Officer shall decide, after passing an order, whether it is a fit case for the issue of notice under section 148 and serve a copy of such order along with such notice on the assessee.

The new provisions of re-assessment were made effective from 01-04-2021. Therefore, the notices issued on or after 01-04-2021 under section 148 must adhere to the new re-assessment provisions. However, the CBDT, exercising the powers conferred under section 3(1) of the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 vide Notification No. 20/2021, dated 31-3-2021, extended the timelines for issuing notice under the old provisions of section 148 to 30-04-2021. The date was again extended to 30-06-2021 vide Notification No. 38 /2021, dated 27-4-2021.

The assessees challenged the re-assessment notices issued during the extended time on the grounds of whether the CBDT has authority to issue such notifications extending the timelines where the provisions have already been substituted by the Finance Act 2021 with effect from 01-04-2021. It would be incorrect to look at the delegation legislation (Notifications) issued under the TLA Act, 2020 to interpret the principal legislation made by Parliament. A delegated legislation can never overreach any Act of the principal legislature. The delegated authority cannot override the Act by exceeding the authority or making provisions inconsistent with the Act.

(iii) The Act is a dynamic enactment that sustains through enactment of the Finance Act every year. Therefore, on 1st April every year, it is the Act as amended by the Finance Act, for that year which is applied. In the present case, it is the Act as amended by the Finance Act 2021, that confronted the Enabling Act as was pre-existing. In absence of any legislative intent expressed either under the Finance Act, 2021 or under the Enabling Act, to preserve any part of the pre-existing Act, plainly, reference to provisions of Sections 147 and 148 of the Act and the words 'assessment' and 'reassessment' appearing in the Notifications issued under the Enabling Act may be read to be indicating only at proceedings already commenced prior to 1-4-2021, under the Act (before amendment by the Finance Act, 2021). The delegated action performed under the Enabling Act cannot, itself create an overriding effect in favour of the Enabling Act.

(iv)

The delegation made could be exercised within the four corners of the principal legislation and not to overreach it. Insofar as the Enabling Act does not delegate any power to legislate - with respect to enforceability of any provision of the Finance Act, 2021 and those provisions (Sections 2 to 88) had come into force, on their own, on 1-4-2021, any exercise of the delegate under the Enabling Act, to defeat the plain enforcement of that law would be wholly unconstitutional. Reliance placed upon the judgements of the hon'ble Supreme Court in the cases of Chairman and Managing Director, Food Corpn. of India v. Jagdish Balaram Bahira [2017] 8 SCC 670 and Dilip Kumar Ghosh v. Chairman [2005] 7 SCC 567.

(v)

The Parliament being aware of all realities, both as to the fact situation and the laws that were existing, it had consciously enacted the Enabling Act, to extend certain time limitations and to enforce only a partial change to the reassessment procedure, by enacting section 151-A to the Act. It then enacted the Finance Act, 2021 to change the substantive and procedural law governing the reassessment proceedings. That having been done, together with introduction of section 148-A to the Act, legislative field stood occupied, leaving the delegate with no room to manipulate the law except as to the time lines with respect to proceedings that may have been initiated under the Act (both prior to and after enforcement of the Finance Act, 2021).The delegated legislation can never defeat the principal legislation. Observations & Principal Ratios propounded by the Hon'ble Allahabad High Court

The key observations and factual and legal propositions as pronounced by the hon'ble Allahabad High Court in the batch of these 74 writ petitions are being summarised as under:

(i)

There can be no exception to the principle - an Act of legislative substitution is a composite act. Thereby, the legislature chooses to put in place another or, replace an existing provision of law. It involves simultaneous omission and re-enactment. By its very nature, once a new provision has been put in place of a pre-existing provision, the earlier provision cannot survive, except for things done or already undertaken to be done or things expressly saved to be done.

(ii)

Undeniably, on 1-4-2021, by virtue of plain/unexcepted effect of Section 1(2)(a) of the Finance Act, 2021, the provisions of Sections 147, 148, 149, 151 (as those provisions existed upto 31-3-2021), stood substituted, along with a new provision enacted by way of Section 148A of that Act. In absence of any saving clause, to save the pre-existing (and now substituted) provisions, the revenue authorities could only initiate reassessment proceeding on or after 1-4-2021, in accordance with the substituted law and not the pre-existing laws.

(iii)

cedural laws define the rules with which substantive laws may be enforced.

In the present matter, the Court held that the failure to follow the procedure under section 144C (1) was not just aprocedural error but also a denial of substantive rights of the assessee. It was ruled that a legally valid draft order is the foundation for commencement of DRP proceedings which gives the substantive right to the assessee to argue for prospective reduction/increase in tax liability of the taxpayer.

Analysis and Conclusion The issue of non-compliance with section 144C first came to limelight with the decision of Hon'ble Andhra Pradesh High Court in the case of Zuari Cement3 wherein the assessment order was quashed for want of issue of a draft order. The Ruling was followed in Vijay Television4. In this case as well, a final order was passed without issue of a draft order. Later however a corrigendum was issued by the AO treating the final order as a draft order. The Hon'ble Madras High Court held :

The fact that taxable amount has been determined and a demand notice has been issued leads to a conclusion that the order passed is a final order and not a draft order;

Dispute Resolution Panel ('DRP') refused to entertain the assessee(or 'taxpayer') on the ground that the order objected to before it was not a draft order;

The procedure prescribed under section 144C of the Act is mandatory and failure to follow the same results in nullity of the order; there is a difference between nullity and irregularity/illegality; and

Life cannot be infused in a null and void order by issuing a corrigendum.

In arriving at its conclusion the court relied on the decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Kalyankumar Ray5 to buttress the proposition that determination of tax liability is conclusive of the fact that impugned order is final assessment order.

"Quashing" vs. "Remand back"

As of now it is a settled law that failure to comply with the procedure laid down under section 144C(1) of the Act would vitiate the proceedings and would render it to be treated as incurably defective and illegal.Similar approach has been adopted by the Delhi High Court where in a string of cases on the same issue; i.e., non-compliance with the requirement to pass a draft order under section 144C, the Court has set aside the assessment order and remanded back the matter to the Assessing Officer.However, it should be noted that the Delhi High Court has specifically directed that the matter be remanded to the AO whereas such a specific direction is missing in the judgement delivered by the Bombay High Court. The impact of such a difference in the wordings of judgment is that generally, an assessment can be revived only if the superior court specifically gives clear directions to do so.

"Expiry of Limitation Period"

Another point to be noted is that in cases where limitation period for proceedings has expired, the Revenue is normally left with no option but to forego proceedings for the relevant assessment year.It is a settled position of law that after the period of limitation has expired no proceedings can be taken to assess nor could any period of limitation laid down by the Act be extended merely by a superior Tribunal directing an inferior Tribunal to make an assessment or to take proceedings which result in assessment after the period of limitation is over.6

Strategy of Revenue Authorities in initial cases was to accept that it was a mistake to issue final order which stood rectified by issuing a corrigendum. This strategy did not bear any fruit.Recently in the case of GE Oil and Gas7, Revenue Authorities pleaded that non issuance of Draft Order was merely a clerical mistake in selecting the right option in the system whereby instead of selecting the option of draft order the option of final order was excercised. Hon'ble Court rejected the plea noting that the notice of demand as well as penalty notice was issued which led to a conclusion that a final order had been issued.

In the case of Alcatel Lucent8, Revenue Authorities improvised their strategy agreeing to treat the impugned assessment order as a Draft Order and the consequent notice of demand stood withdrawn. This resulted in an absolute redressal of petitioner's grievance with the petitioner agreeing to pursue the matter before DRP. Thereby the quashing of the assessment order was prevented.

Therefore, while it is clear that taxpayer cannot be denied the substantive right to a Draft Order and file objections before DRP, the exact response of the Courts has varied from case to case. For aggrieved taxpayers the plethora of favourable High Court Rulings may not necessarily work as precedents to secure access to DRP at lower levels and they may have to seek specificremedy from Jurisdictional High Courts in each instance. As the faceless assessment scheme evolves and comes of age in understanding and applying the mandatory procedural requirements, Courts stand as sentinels on alert to safeguard substantive rights and ensure that taxpayers get the statutory remedy they are entitled to.

by virtue of savings clause and not otherwise. The intention of the Legislature can be inferred from the savings clause making the provisions of pervious law applicable.

In a case where a particular provision in a statute is omitted and in its place another provision dealing with the same contingency is introduced without a saving clause in favour of pending proceedings then it can reasonably be inferred that the intention of the Legislature is that the pending proceeding shall not continue but a fresh proceeding for the same purpose may be initiated under the new provision. Thus, the effect of repealing a statute or deleting a provision is to eliminate it from the statute book such that it had never been passed, and the statute must be considered as a law that never existed.

2.3 State of Punjab v. Shreyans Indus Ltd. [Civil Appeal Nos. 2506 to 2521 of 2016, dated 4-3-2016]: The issue involved in this case was regarding interpretation of provisions of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948 (the Act). In terms of Section 11(3) of the Act, 1948, time-limit for completing the assessment provided is three years from the end of the year. In this case, the Assessing Officer, however, sent notices after the expiry of three years. The Assessing Officer relied on Section 11(10) of the Act whereby the Commissioner is empowered to extend the period of three years for passing the order of assessment for such further period as he may deem fit, after recording in writing the reasons for extending such period.

The question before the Supreme Court was "Whether the power to extend time is to be necessarily exercised before the normal expiry of the said period of three years run out?"

Three judge bench of the Supreme Court relying on income-tax decisions observed that once statutory period of limitation expires, the assessee is protected from being subject to assessment again, as the right to make assessment gets extinguished.

Thus, once an assessment is time barred there would be no question of extending the time for assessment.

Further, the department can demand service tax under the guise of thirty months at any time later on. Also, if the intention of the Government was to make the amendment applicable even after lapse of eighteen months, there should be savings clause to this effect or any clarification in this regard by the government.

advanced by the learned Additional Solicitor General of India that practicality dictates that the reassessment proceedings be protected. Practicality, if any, may lead to legislation. Once the matter reaches Court, it is the legislation and its language, and the interpretation offered to that language as may primarily be decisive to govern the outcome of the proceeding. To read practicality into enacted law is dangerous. Also, it would involve legislation by the Court, an idea and exercise we carefully tread away from.

(vii) As to the decision of the Chhattisgarh High Court, with all respect, we are unable to persuade ourselves to that view. According to us, it would be incorrect to look at the delegation legislation i.e. Notification dated 31-3-2021 issued under the Enabling Act, to interpret the principal legislation made by Parliament, being the Finance Act, 2021. A delegated legislation can never overreach any Act of the principal legislature. Second, it would be over simplistic to ignore the provisions of, either the Enabling Act or the Finance Act, 2021 and to read and interpret the provisions of Finance Act, 2021 as inoperative in view of the fact circumstances arising from the spread of the pandemic COVID-19. Practicality of life de hors statutory provisions, may never be a good guiding principle to interpret any taxation law. In absence of any specific clause in Finance Act, 2021, either to save the provisions of the Enabling Actor the Notifications issued thereunder, by no interpretative process can those Notifications be given an extended run of life, beyond 31 March 2020. They may also not infuse any life into a provision that stood obliterated from the statute with effect from31-3-2021. Inasmuch as the Finance Act, 2021 does not enable the Central Government to issue any notification to reactivate the pre-existing law (which that principal legislature had substituted), the exercise made by the delegate/Central Government would be dehors any statutory basis. In absence of any express saving of the pre-existing laws, the presumption drawn in favour of that saving, is plainly impermissible. Also, no presumption exists that by Notification issued under the Enabling Act, the operation of the pre-existing provision of the Act had been extended and thereby provisions of Section 148A of the Act (introduced by Finance Act2021) and other provisions had been deferred. Such Notifications did not insulate or save, the pre-existing provisions pertaining to reassessment under the Act.

(viii)

In view of the above, all the writ petitions must succeed and are allowed. It is declared that the Ordinance, the Enabling Act and Sections 2 to 88 of the Finance Act 2021, as enforced w.e.f. 1-4-2021, are not conflicted. Insofar as the Explanation appended to clause A(a), A(b), and the impugned Notifications dated 31-3-2021 and 27-4-2021 (respectively) are concerned, we declare that the said Explanations must be read, as applicable to reassessment proceedings as may have been in existence on 31-3-2021 i.e. before the substitution of Sections 147, 148, 148A, 149, 151 & 151A of the Act. Consequently, the reassessment notices in all the writ petitions are quashed. It is left open to the respective assessing authorities to initiate reassessment proceedings in accordance with the provisions of the Act as amended by Finance Act, 2021, after making all compliances, as required by law.

Update on Similar Recent Developments in Hon'ble Delhi & Mumbai High Courts

The Hon'ble Delhi Court has also commenced hearing in the batch of 1300 writ petitions challenging the validity and legal sanctity of reassessment notices issued under the old section 148, on or after 1-4-2021 on 28-9-2021.

The Hon'ble Bombay High Court has also listed the batch of similar writ petitions for hearing on 11-10-2021.

The Revenue Authorities have filed an application for transfer of these writ petitions before the Hon'ble Supreme Court Bench.

Friends, the above entire discussion, is a classic example of a glaring and unfortunate mismatch between the perceived legislative intent of reducing the time barring limitation period of reopening of already concluded assessments u/s 148 from 6 years to 3 years w.e.f. 1-4-2021, aimed at reducing uncertainty, and the practical ground-level implementation of the said policy decision, during the transition to the substituted reassessment regime.

The record referred to in section 154 does mean only the order is based and the ITO is entitled to the purpose of exercising his jurisdiction under section 154 to look into whole evidence and the law applicable to ascertain whether there was an error—Maharana Mills (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [1959] 36 ITR 350 (SC). ‘Record’ would mean the record of the case comprising the entire proceedings incumbent and material produced by the parties and taken on record by the authorities, which were available at the time of passing the order, which is the subject-matter of proceedings for rectification. The authorities cannot go beyond the record and look into fresh evidence and materials, which were not on the record at the time the order sought to be rectified, was passed—Gammon India Ltd. v. CIT [1995] 214 ITR 50/80 Taxman 591 (Bom.).

Record does not mean only the order of assessment, but it comprises of all proceedings on which assessment order is based—Maharana Mills (P.) Ltd.’s case (supra). The Tribunal’s finding is a part of records of appeal so as to empower the Deputy Commissioner to rectify his earlier order—Mahendra Mills Ltd. v. P.B. Desai, Asstt. CIT [1975] 99 ITR 135 (SC). Records of assessment of other assessment years can also be looked into—Indra Singh & Sons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [1967] 64 ITR 501 (Cal.).

By Successor Commissioner

3. Successor Commissioner cannot refuse to entertain rectification application in respect of the order passed by his predecessor on the ground that he being a succeeding Commissioner could not sit over the judgment of his predecessor to review his order under the guise of making rectification— Trustees of Indore Cancer Foundation Charitable Trust v. Union of India [2001] 248 ITR 730/116 Taxman 531 (MP).

The term ‘order’

4. Since the ‘order’ as mentioned has not been specified as original first order, it includes amended or rectified order and, therefore, where original assessment was subsequently rectified, a second application for rectification made within two years from date of first certificatory order was valid—Hind Wire Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1995] 212 ITR 639/80 Taxman 79 (SC). However, where mistake in original assessment is left untouched in subsequent reassessment, period of limitation should be counted from the date of original assessment and not from the date of reassessment—Mettur Chemical & Industrial Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1977] 110 ITR 822 (Mad.). Limitation period is applicable only to making of order and not to issue of demand notice—S.T. Velu v. CIT [1958] 33 ITR 463 (Mad.). Where the first rectification application has been dismissed by the Commissioner (Appeals), the successor Commissioner (Appeals) cannot admit a second application and allow the same in respect of the same alleged mistake—CIT v. J.K. Bankers [2000] 245 ITR 844/[2003] 130 Taxman 127 (All.).

Few examples for reference

5. In terms of section 74, there has to be mistake apparent from the record. In other words, a look at the record must show that there has been an error and that error may be rectified. For example, reference to documents outside the record and the law is impermissible when applying the provisions of section 74—CIT v. Keshri Metal (P.) Ltd. [1999] 237 ITR 165/104 Taxman 360 (SC).

If order is plainly and obviously inconsistent with the specific and clear provision amended retrospectively indisputably, there is a mistake apparent from record—CIT v. E. Sefton & Co. (P.) Ltd. [1989] 179 ITR 435/47 Taxman 392 (Cal.). A subsequent decision of the Supreme Court can validly form basis for rectifying an order of assessment under section 74, provided decision is given by the Apex Court within two years from the date of order—B.V.K. Seshavataram v. CIT [1994] 210 ITR 633/75 Taxman 491 (AP), Kil Kotagiri Tea & Coffee Estates Co. Ltd. v. ITAT [1988] 174 ITR 579/[1989] 42 Taxman 33 (Ker.). The CBDT has also issued Circular No. 68 dated November 17, 1971 in support of aforesaid view.

The assessment years concerned were 1967-68,1968-69 and 1970-71 to 1973-74. The Assessing Officer initiated re-assessment proceedings and issued notices under section 148 of the Act against which the assessee filed a writ before the Bombay High Court. The assessee contended that it had disclosed all facts and that failure of the Assessing Officer to investigate into the matter further could not be equated with omission or failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for assessment. The assessee further contended that prior to assessment year 1972-73 there was no column in the return of income for indicating method of stock valuation and therefore the Assessing Officer had no jurisdiction to issue the notices. The High Court held that the method of valuation of closing stock adopted by the assessee resulted in under-valuation of inventories and understatement of profit, thus resulting in income escaping assessment. The High Court further held that irrespective of the fact that there was no specific item for disclosure in the return of income, there was a failure on the part of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for its assessment. The High Court also held categorically that "it is not for the Court to judge whether sufficiency of reasons for the Assessing Officer to believe that by reason of failure of the assessee to make a true and full disclosure of material facts income has escaped assessment and the Assessing Officer was justified in reopening assessments for the relevant years under section 147(a) of the Act and in issuing notices under section 148 of the Act."

4.3 The facts in the case decided by the Karnataka High Court in CIT v. Faruk Anvar Co. [1993] 70 Taxman 369/199 ITR 433 were that in his order under section 263 of the Act for the assessment year 1980-81, the Commissioner of Income-tax observed that the assessee could claim weighted deduction under section 35B of the Act provided the expenses squarely fell within the provisions of section 35B of the Act and, accordingly, some of the items of expenses were not deductible. Treating this finding as source of information, the Assessing Officer initiated proceedings to re-open the earlier assessments under section 147(b) of the Act for the assessment years 1978-79 and 1979-80. The First Appellate Authority, however, accepted the assessee's contention that the order of the Commissioner of Income-tax could not be treated as 'information' so as to enable the assessing authority to re-open the assessment under section 147(b) of the Act in respect of another year. This view was confirmed by the Tribunal.

On reference (appeal to the Karnataka High Court) it was contended by the assessee that "the order of Commissioner of Income-tax cannot have a bearing on the concluded assessment sought to be reopened"

The High Court held as under-

"Applying the ratio of the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of A.L.A. Firm (supra) there could be no doubt that the Assessing Officer was entitled to be enlightened by any source which could be considered as an information for the purpose of re-opening the assessment under section 147(b) of the Act. The Commissioner of Income-tax certainly is a superior authority and his views can be taken as a source of information by a subordinate officer like the Assessing Officer.

So far as the question that the order of the Commissioner of Income-tax should have a bearing on the concluded assessment sought to be reopened was concerned, it was found that many of the items such as office expenses, packing materials, etc., were also referred to in the order of the Commissioner of Income-tax. This apart, the scope of section 35B of the Act itself was considered by the Commissioner of Income-tax, which certainly had a direct bearing on the deductions claimed by the assessee in the instant case. Therefore, it could not be said that the Commissioner of Income-tax's order had no bearing on the fact situation.

Therefore, the reopening of assessment was justified."

Stated Facts- Sawhney's Decision

On July 28, 2011, in terms of Section 132 of the Act, Income-tax search and seizure operations were carried out on the Assessee (substituted by wife of deceased Assessee). For the relevant assessment year ('AY'), notice under section 153A of Act was also issued to the Assessee requiring him to file tax return. Accordingly, the Assessee filed the income tax returns for the year under consideration.

The Assessing officer ('AO') had noted that as per the information received from the investigation wing, for the relevant AY 2006-07, the Assessee was allegedly having bank account with HSBC bank, Geneva. This information was claimed to have received from the competent authority under 'Exchange of Information' framework of DTAA/DTAC between India and France.

The information of maintaining foreign bank account was admitted by the son of the Assessee. Additionally, the AO noted that the said account details and the available funds of this account were not declared by the Assessee in the return of income.

The AO, on the basis of information received from the authorities in this matter, made an addition of Rs. 9,18,54,176/- on account of maximum outstanding balance lying in the bank account maintained with HSBC Bank, Geneva for the AY 2006-07. Thus, for the AY 2006-07, the Assessment Order was passed under section 153A read with section 143(3) of the Act.

For the remaining AY 2007-08 to 2011-12, the AO made addition on grounds of undeclared interest earned against the deposits in HSBC Bank, Geneva. The order of AO was confirmed by Hon'ble Commission of Income-tax (Appeals) ('CIT(A)').

Aggrieved, the Assessee filed an appeal before the Hon'ble Tribunal.

Contentions of the Appellant (Taxpayer)

The Assessee submitted that considering the date of the search & therefore, the last 'Panchnama' was drawn in the Financial Year ('F.Y.') 2011-2012. Thus, as per section 153B (1A) of the Act, the limitation period to pass the Assessment Order expired on March 31, 2014. However, the assessment order was passed post March 31, 2014 and hence, the same was barred by limitation.

The Assessee, inter alia, placed reliance on the decision of the Hon'ble ITAT, Delhi Benches in the case of PHI Seeds v. Dy. CIT [2015] 45 CCH 318, wherein the Hon'ble Tribunal had held that it had the jurisdiction to adjudicate whether an order of assessment under section 143(3) of the Act has been passed within the period of limitation or not and for that purpose legality of different aspects which are integral to the process can be challenged.

Further, the Assessee submitted that no incriminating evidence was recovered during the course of search. The Assessee had referred to 'Panchnama' executed which did not find mention of any incriminating material and therefore, the assessee submitted that no addition could be made against him.

Kabul Chawla [2015] 61 taxmann.com 412/234 Taxman 300/[2016] 380 ITR 573 wherein the Hon'ble High Court opined that already completed assessments can be interceded by the assessing officer under section 153A of the Act only on the basis of incriminating material found during the course of search proceedings.

Due date for filing of belated and revised ITR

If a return of income is not filed on or before the specified due date, it is regarded as a belated return. Further, the taxpayer has an option to revise a return to correct any error or omission in the original return. An assessee may file a revised or belated return for any previous year at any time before the expiry of the relevant assessment year or before completion of the assessment, whichever is earlier. Thus, as per the existing provisions, the last date to file the revised or belated return is 31st March of the relevant Assessment Year.

The Finance Bill, 2021 proposed amendments to Section 139(4) and 139(5), with effect from the assessment year 2021-22, to provide that the belated and revised return can be filed at any time within three months prior to the end of the relevant assessment year or before completion of the assessment, whichever is earlier.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) has redrafted the wordings of the proposed amendment although the intent remains the same. Now, it has been provided that the belated and revised return can be filed before three months prior to the end of the relevant assessment year or before the completion of the assessment, whichever is earlier.

Thus, pursuant to the amendment, a belated and revised return in respect of assessment year 2021-22 and subsequent assessment years can be filed up to 31st December of that assessment year.

15. New scheme of Re-assessment

15.1. Changes proposed by the Finance Bill, 2021

The Finance Bill, 2021 proposed a new re-assessment procedure for an income which has escaped the assessment and in search and seizure cases. The Explanatory Memorandum stated that the new scheme of assessment would result in less litigation and would provide ease of doing business to the taxpayers. The Finance Bill substituted existing Sections 147, 148, 149 and 151 and inserted a new section 148A making a complete change in the assessment proceedings relating to income escaping assessment and search related cases. Consequential amendments have also been proposed to Sections 151A, 153A and 153C.

The new Section 147 provides that the Assessing Officer can make the re-assessment of an income escaping assessment if the following conditions are satisfied:

(a)

Any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year; and

(b)

The Assessing Officer follows the provisions of sections 148 to 153.

If the above conditions are satisfied, the Assessing Officer can assess or reassess such income or recompute the loss or the depreciation allowance or any other allowance or deduction for such assessment year. It is imperative to note that in view of Explanation to Section 147 the Assessing Officer can assess or reassess all those incomes which have escaped assessment and which come to his notice subsequently in the course of such proceeding notwithstanding that the procedure prescribed in section 148A was not followed before issuing such notice for such income.

15.2. Power to assess or reassess for assessment or reassessment or recomputation

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) has also covered 'recomputation' within the scope of the said Explanation to Section 147. Thus, the Assessing Officer for the purpose of assessment or reassessment or recomputation can assess or reassess all those incomes which have escaped assessment and which come to his notice subsequently in the course of such proceeding notwithstanding that the procedure prescribed in Section 148A was not followed before issuing such notice for such income.

15.3. Information suggests income escaping in case of Survey

The new scheme of reassessment proposes that the Assessing Officer can initiate the proceedings if he has the information which suggests that some income has escaped the assessment. Explanations 1 and 2 of the proposed Section 148 define the situation in which an Assessing Officer shall be deemed to have the information which suggests that the income chargeable to tax has escaped the assessment.

Explanation 2 applies in the case of search, survey or requisition of books, documents or other assets. Explanation 1 applies in other cases.

Summary of Present Legal Position Key Takeaways for Practitioners

First, the clean slate principle remains the dominant rule. Where a resolution plan extinguishes all past tax liabilities, reassessment under Section 148 is unjustified—now fortified by the Supreme Court's SLP dismissal in AMW Auto Component.

Second, the VRDV Traders exception carves a narrow window: reassessment for investigating fraud through shell entities and reversal trades may survive, though any resulting recovery against the corporate debtor remains impermissible. The remedy, per the Telangana HC, may lie against erstwhile directors.

Third, timely claim-filing by the Revenue during the CIRP is critical. Failure to submit claims before the Resolution Professional results in permanent extinguishment, as seen in V Hotels and Vaibhav Goel.

Fourth, resolution applicants should ensure comprehensive tax extinguishment clauses in the resolution plan covering assessed and unassessed liabilities, TDS demands, penalties, prosecution risks, and related-party implications as demonstrated by the exhaustive clauses in the AMW Auto Component plan.

Conclusion

The jurisprudence on the interplay between IBC resolution plans and income tax reassessment has reached substantial clarity through Ghanshyam Mishra, Vaibhav Goel, and the AMW Auto Component SLP dismissal. The clean slate principle is now the settled norm. However, the VRDV Traders exception permitting reassessment where mala fide transactions through shell entities are suspected creates a narrow but significant carve-out that the Supreme Court has not yet directly addressed.

Taxpayers and professionals must carefully evaluate each case on its facts particularly the nature of transactions, the comprehensiveness of the resolution plan's extinguishment clauses, and whether tax claims were duly filed during the CIRP to determine whether the clean slate holds or whether the wound remains open.

The reassessment provisions introduced in the Income Tax Bill, 2025 appear to be a classic case of old wine in a new bottle. After the substantial overhaul brought by the Finance Act, 2021 - which was lauded for streamlining procedures, reducing litigation, and fostering taxpayer confidence—the proposed rollback to earlier mechanisms in the 2025 Bill is both perplexing and concerning.

The 2021 Reform: A Promised Shift Toward Efficiency and Fairness

The Finance Act, 2021 ushered in a new era of reassessment jurisprudence. One of its key features was a significant curtailment of the reassessment window-from six years to three years under Section 148—except in cases involving serious tax evasion where income chargeable to tax, represented in the form of assets, exceeded ₹50 lakh. Such cases were allowed to be reopened up to ten years. The post 2021 act aligns with the enhanced access to third-party data under Sections 285BA and 285BB, including Annual Information Statements (AIS) and reports from enforcement agencies electronically and thereby, reducing reassessment notice period.

The Hon'ble Finance Minister had highlighted, in her 2021 Budget Speech, that the reduction in the time limit was necessitated by the digitization and real-time availability of taxpayer information. The goal was clear: reduce uncertainty, curb harassment, and bring reassessment in tune with modern-day data access and compliance norms.

2025 Bill: Reinstating the Past

In a surprising move, the Income Tax Bill, 2025 appears to have reintroduced several elements reminiscent of the pre-2021 reassessment regime. Notably:

Time Limit Re-Expansion: The Bill resurrects the 4-year and 6-year time bars for issuing reassessment notices—now cloaked under Section 282 and linked to the issuance under the erstwhile Section 148, now proposed as Section 280. This reversion dilutes the sharpness and precision that the post 2021 act reform aimed to achieve. The 2025 bill shows a mirror image of the Pre-amended 2021 act.

Sanction approval u/s 151 Hierarchy Watered Down: One of the keystones of the 2021 amendments was the elevation of the sanctioning authority under Section 151—from (Joint Commissioner or Commissioner) to Commissioner & Principal Chief Commissioner or Principal Director General. This was a deliberate policy safeguard meant to prevent arbitrary and unjustified reopening of cases. The 2025 Bill, however, devolves the sanctioning authority back to the level of Joint Commissioner or Additional Commissioner, under Section 282, thereby weakening the supervisory checks envisioned in even in the Pre-2021 reform.

A Legislative Contradiction

The regression is more than just procedural. It strikes at the very legislative intent articulated in the Memorandum to the Finance Bill, 2021, which had explicitly emphasized reduced litigation, ease of doing business, and use of technology as the foundation for reassessment reform.

The 2025 proposal, by contrast, creates a legislative paradox—rolling back reform without revising the rationale. It ignores the earlier commitment made to taxpayers and professionals alike, and worse, creates a legal structure that is vulnerable to arbitrariness, lack of consistency, and increased litigation.

Conclusion: A Call for Legislative Introspection

As professionals, we look not only for legislative consistency but also for policy continuity that respects prior commitments. The proposed reassessment provisions in the Income Tax Bill, 2025, by reviving elements of the very system that was consciously discarded in 2021, represent a legislative volte-face. The finance ministry owes stakeholders an explanation: has the information ecosystem deteriorated, or was the 2021 reform premature?

In a tax administration increasingly reliant on data, precision, and transparency, going back to broad-brush tools of reassessment seems anachronistic. The hope is that reason will prevail before this retrogressive shift becomes law.

Hon'ble Income-tax Tribunal Decision

Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the Hon'ble ITAT held that it is not disputed that search was conducted and 'Panchnama' was executed in the present case. However, the 'Panchnama' did not disclose that any incriminating material to conclude that the bank account with HSBC Bank, Geneva was maintained by assessee.

The Hon'ble ITAT relied on the case of Kabul Chawla (supra), wherein it was observed that "AO can make amendments to already concluded assessments under section 153A on the basis of incriminating material made known during the course of search which were not produced or disclosed earlier."

Further, reliance was placed on Pr. CIT v. Meeta Gutgutia [2017] 82 taxmann.com 287/248 Taxman 384/395 ITR 526 (Delhi), wherein it was held that 'there was no justification at all for the AO to proceed on surmises and estimates without there being any incriminating material qua the AY for which he sought to make additions of franchisee commission.'

Furthermore, the Hon'ble ITAT held that the Swiss authorities could have provided information post the period 2011-12 but not for relevant period under consideration in the present case. Letter issued by Swiss Authorities to the Government of India specifically states that information could be provided for years commencing from 2011-12.

Therefore, the required information for the period prior to 2011 could not have been provided by the authorities as per Article 26 of DTAA between India and Switzerland. Thus, the ITAT held that the assessment order passed was beyond limitation period as the reference sought by the Income-tax authorities was erroneous and bad in law.

Our Comments

Back in 2016, when Panama Papers blew the lid off how money is parked in offshore tax haven jurisdictions, a number of countries including India introduced financial reforms and took a number of corrective actions to set things right. However, after the Panama Paper leak, even stringent laws and penalties were not sufficient to deter offenders from indulging in financial jugglery.

Panama Paper rocked the world in 2016 but the recent investigations under Pandora Papers provides twice as much information and is even larger and more global in scope than the earlier ICIJ's landmark Panama Paper Investigation.

There's nothing illegal with holding an offshore account unless it is done with the malafide intent of tax evasion. The courts while dwelling on the issue of "unaccounted money stashed outside India" would look into various aspects that are integral to the process.

The ITAT in the aforecited recent decision of Bhushan Lal Sawhney's case (supra) had observed that if no incriminating material could be found during the course of search to establish Assesee's connection with respect to foreign bank account, the additions would not sustain.

The Hon'ble ITAT, Kolkata Benches in Bishwanath Garodia v. Dy. CIT [2016] 76 taxmann.com 81, held the similar view and it observed that 'But in a case or circumstances where the proceedings have reached finality, assessment under section 143(3) read with section 153(3) has to be made as was originally made and in case certain incriminating materials were found indicating undisclosed income, then addition shall only be restricted to these documents/incriminating material.'

It is noteworthy to mention here that in the case of Bhushan Lal Sawhney (supra), the statement of Assesee's son was recorded by the AO who had admitted that Assessee had maintained bank account with HSBC Geneva. However, the same was denied by the assessee in his statement recorded by the AO.

It was observed by Delhi High court in Smt. Dayawanti v. CIT [2016] 75 taxmann.com 308/[2017] 245 Taxman 293/390 ITR 496 that "while adjudging the probative value of these statements, it is to be seen whether the assessee was able to give any explanation for the statement, its connection with the material seized, all are relevant, to judge if it is to be considered in an assessment."

return of income for the current year was filed at Nil income with the carry forward of loss of Rs. 10,00,000/-. Addition of Rs. 8,00,000/-, for instance, is made in the assessment order, and despite such addition so made, the assessed income of the current year would still be Nil and only carried forward loss would be reduced to Rs. 2,00,000/- in place of Rs. 10,00,000/-. Such situation is not covered under section 270A as there would not result any difference between the assessed income and the returned/processed income both being Nil. All that the difference, addition of Rs. 8,00,000/- has made, is in the quantum of carry forward of loss which was reduced to Rs. 2,00,000/- instead of earlier sum of Rs. 10,00,000. But, this situation is not contemplated under section 270A for the levy of penalty.

However, reduction of carried forward loss may impact the total income in the next year and in that situation, the position of 'under reported income' may emerge in that year inviting the consequences of penalty under section 270A in that year.

(e)

Since the 'under reported income' is computed having regard to assessed income and processed income, income additionally returned in the revised return filed under section 139(5) would also not invite penalty under section 270A. It however needs to be appreciated that unless assessing officer discards the revised return on any of the grounds mentioned under sub section (5) of section 139 that the revision was not as a result of 'discovery' of 'omission' or 'wrong statement', and hence such purported revised return cannot be treated as valid revised return, it may not be possible for the revenue to impose penalty qua the additional income returned through the revised return. Similarly, the income returned in belated return filed in time would also not be part of 'under reported income'.

Penalty under sub section (4) (5) of section 270A ghost of penalty under section 271(1)(c)

Plain reading of sub sections (4)(5) of section 270A deems such intangible additions on which no penalty was imposed in earlier year(s) which is taken advantage of by the assessee in explaining source of any deposit or investment or receipt in the following year. Such intangible additions would be 'under reported income' of the year(s) to which the intangible additions relate.

For example, if some investment made in A.Y. 2020-21 is sought to be explained with the help of some intangible addition made in A.Y. 2017-18 on which no penalty under section 270A was imposed, such explained amount of investment would be deemed to be 'under reported income' for A.Y. 2017-18 for the purpose of levy of penalty and assessing officer may direct such person to pay penalty under section 270A qua such 'under reported income' in A.Y. 2017-18.

But the question would arise as to whether such penalty can be initiated after the expiry of limitation period prescribed under section 275, more so when there is no provision in section 270A on the lines of the provision contained in sub section (1A) of section 271permitting the initiation of penalty even after the passing of the assessment order of those year(s).

In our considered opinion, since there is no validating provision in section 270A on the lines of the provision contained in sub section (1A) of section 271, any imposition of penalty under sub section (4) (5) of section 270A may hit the road block of limitation and penalty imposed in such circumstances may be liable to be held as barred by limitation under section 275.

Another question that has raged controversy in the interpretation of Explanation 2 to section 271(1)(c) would continue to remain so in the interpretation of sub section (4) (5) of section 270A that as to what is the meaning of the phrase appearing in these sub sections where 'no penalty was levied'. Whether it would cover a situation where penalty though was imposed qua intangible additions in those earlier year(s) but was cancelled/deleted in appeal either on merit or on legal ground, or where no penalty was imposed at all.

In our considered opinion, if penalty was levied but was cancelled for any reason including on legal grounds, yet it would be a case where penalty was levied and such intangible additions cannot be revisited with penalty under sub section (4)(5) of section 270A.
